abstract: The main point of this paper is that stochastic neural networks have a mathematical structure that corresponds quite closely with that of quantum field theory. Neural network Liouvillians and Lagrangians can be derived, just as can spin Hamiltonians and Lagrangians in QFf. It remains to show the efficacy of such a description.
originalAbstract: The main point of this paper is that stochastic neural networks have a mathematical structure that corresponds quite closely with that of quantum field theory. Neural network Liouvillians and Lagrangians can be derived, just as can spin Hamiltonians and Lagrangians in QFf. It remains to show the efficacy of such a description.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a mathematical connection between stochastic neural networks and quantum field theory. Its central claim concerns structure: equations describing neural systems with randomness can be organized in ways closely corresponding to mathematical descriptions used in field theory. The contribution is a framework for describing network dynamics.

Specifically, the author states that neural-network Liouvillians and Lagrangians can be derived, drawing a parallel with spin Hamiltonians and Lagrangians in quantum field theory. These named constructions express the proposed correspondence at the level of mathematical formulation. The emphasis is on establishing suitable descriptions of a neural system and its evolution, rather than reporting a new recognition or learning result.

The abstract explicitly leaves the usefulness of this description to be demonstrated. That separates the stated achievement from the remaining question: deriving a corresponding mathematical structure establishes a possible way to analyze stochastic networks, while showing that it provides effective explanations or calculations is a further step. The paper's significance rests on opening that theoretical connection.
summary.tldr: The paper derives field-theory-like mathematical descriptions for stochastic neural networks, while leaving their practical efficacy unresolved.

title: Stochastic Neurodynamics

abstract: We present a Parallel Distributed Semantic (PDS) Network architecture that addresses the problems of sequencing and ambiguity resolution in natural language understanding. A PDS Network stores phrases and their meanings using multiple PDP networks, structured in the form of a se(cid:173) mantic net. A mechanism called Propagation Filters is employed: (1) to control communication between networks, (2) to properly sequence the components of a phrase, and (3) to resolve ambiguities. Simulation results indicate that PDS Networks and Propagation Filters can successfully rep(cid:173) resent high-level knowledge, can be trained relatively quickly, and provide for parallel inferencing at the knowledge level.
originalAbstract: We present a Parallel Distributed Semantic (PDS) Network architecture that addresses the problems of sequencing and ambiguity resolution in natural language understanding. A PDS Network stores phrases and their meanings using multiple PDP networks, structured in the form of a se(cid:173) mantic net. A mechanism called Propagation Filters is employed: (1) to control communication between networks, (2) to properly sequence the components of a phrase, and (3) to resolve ambiguities. Simulation results indicate that PDS Networks and Propagation Filters can successfully rep(cid:173) resent high-level knowledge, can be trained relatively quickly, and provide for parallel inferencing at the knowledge level.

paragraphs: Understanding a phrase requires keeping its components in the right sequence and resolving competing interpretations. This paper introduces a Parallel Distributed Semantic network architecture to address both problems. It represents phrases and their meanings using multiple parallel distributed processing networks organized into a semantic-network structure.

The coordinating mechanism is called Propagation Filters. These filters control communication among the component networks, arrange the components of a phrase in the proper sequence, and resolve ambiguities. Communication control is therefore part of the interpretation process: how information moves between networks helps determine how the phrase is understood.

Simulation results indicate that the combined architecture can represent high-level knowledge, learn relatively quickly, and perform parallel inference at the knowledge level. The contribution brings distributed representations together with an explicit structure for coordinating them. It addresses the need for components to work concurrently while still respecting the ordering and interpretive constraints that arise in natural-language understanding.
summary.tldr: Propagation Filters coordinate distributed semantic networks to preserve phrase order, resolve ambiguity, and support parallel inference.

title: Propagation Filters in PDS Networks for Sequencing and Ambiguity Resolution

abstract: We have continued our study of a parallel perturbative learning method [Alspector et al., 1993] and implications for its implemen(cid:173) tation in analog VLSI. Our new results indicate that, in most cases, a single parallel perturbation (per pattern presentation) of the func(cid:173) tion parameters (weights in a neural network) is theoretically the best course. This is not true, however, for certain problems and may not generally be true when faced with issues of implemen(cid:173) tation such as limited precision. In these cases, multiple parallel perturbations may be best as indicated in our previous results.
originalAbstract: We have continued our study of a parallel perturbative learning method [Alspector et al., 1993] and implications for its implemen(cid:173) tation in analog VLSI. Our new results indicate that, in most cases, a single parallel perturbation (per pattern presentation) of the func(cid:173) tion parameters (weights in a neural network) is theoretically the best course. This is not true, however, for certain problems and may not generally be true when faced with issues of implemen(cid:173) tation such as limited precision. In these cases, multiple parallel perturbations may be best as indicated in our previous results.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many simultaneous parameter perturbations should be used during a learning step. In the neural-network setting, the parameters are connection weights, and perturbative learning changes them to obtain information useful for improvement. The authors consider the number of parallel perturbations made each time a training pattern is presented.

Their new theoretical results favor a single parallel perturbation per pattern presentation in most cases. This gives a concrete answer to an implementation choice: repeatedly perturbing the parameters during the same presentation is not generally the theoretically preferred strategy. The finding refines their earlier work on parallel perturbative learning and its possible realization in analog integrated circuits.

The conclusion has explicit exceptions. Certain problems favor multiple perturbations, and hardware constraints such as limited numerical precision may also change the preferred choice. In those circumstances, the authors' earlier support for multiple perturbations still applies. The practical lesson is that the theoretical choice and the hardware choice depend on the conditions under which learning operates, with precision identified as one relevant constraint.
summary.tldr: One parallel perturbation per training pattern is usually theoretically preferred, but problem structure and limited hardware precision can favor several.

title: A Study of Parallel Perturbative Gradient Descent

abstract: A training method based on a form of continuous spatially distributed optical error back-propagation is presented for an all optical network composed of nondiscrete neurons and weighted interconnections. The all optical network is feed-forward and is composed of thin layers of a Kerr(cid:173) type self focusing/defocusing nonlinear optical material. The training method is derived from a Lagrangian formulation of the constrained minimization of the network error at the output. This leads to a formulation that describes training as a calculation of the distributed error of the optical signal at the output which is then reflected back through the device to assign a spatially distributed error to the internal layers. This error is then used to modify the internal weighting values. Results from several computer simulations of the training are presented, and a simple optical table demonstration of the network is discussed. 772 Elizabeth C. Behrman 1 KERR TYPE MATERIALS Kerr-type optical networks utilize thin layers of Kerr-type nonlinear materials, in which the index of refraction can vary within the material and depends on the amount of light striking the material at a given location. The material index of refraction can be described by: n(x)=no+nzI(x), where 110 is the linear index of refraction, ~ is the nonlinear coefficient, and I(x) is the irradiance of a applied optical field as a function of position x across the material layer (Armstrong, 1962). This means that a beam of light (a signal beam carrying information perhaps) passing through a layer of Kerr-type material can be steered or controlled by another beam of light which applies a spatially varying pattern of intensity onto the Kerr-type material. Steering of light with a glass lens (having constance index of refraction) is done by varying the thickness of the lens (the amount of material present) as a function of position. Thus the Kerr effect can be loosely thought of as a glass lens whose geometry and therefore focusing ability could be dynamically controlled as a function of position across the lens. Steering in the Kerr material is accomplished by a gradient or change in the material index of refraction which is created by a gradient in applied light intensity. This is illustrated by the simple experiment in Figure 1 where a small weak probe beam is steered away from a straight path by the intensity gradient of a more powerful pump beam.

paragraphs: This paper develops a training method for a feedforward optical network whose processing is distributed continuously across space. The network consists of thin layers of Kerr-type material, where the refractive index depends on local light intensity. Consequently, one light pattern can influence how another beam travels through the material, providing a physical mechanism for nonlinear processing.

The authors derive learning from a Lagrangian formulation of constrained output-error minimization. This mathematical approach accounts for the network's physical constraints while determining how its internal weights should change. The resulting procedure computes a spatial pattern of error at the output and reflects that signal backward through the device to assign errors to internal layers.

Those internal error patterns guide updates to the weighting values. The contribution is therefore a formulation of backpropagation suited to continuous optical signals and nondiscrete neurons. The paper presents computer simulations of training and discusses a simple optical-table demonstration, connecting the mathematical derivation with simulated learning and a physical implementation concept.
summary.tldr: A constrained optimization formulation derives spatially distributed backpropagation for training a nonlinear optical network.

title: A Lagrangian Formulation For Optical Backpropagation Training In Kerr-Type Optical Networks

abstract: A new class of plug in classification techniques have recently been de(cid:173) veloped in the statistics and machine learning literature. A plug in clas(cid:173) sification technique (PaCT) is a method that takes a standard classifier (such as LDA or TREES) and plugs it into an algorithm to produce a new classifier. The standard classifier is known as the Plug in Classi(cid:173) fier (PiC). These methods often produce large improvements over using a single classifier. In this paper we investigate one of these methods and give some motivation for its success.
originalAbstract: A new class of plug in classification techniques have recently been de(cid:173) veloped in the statistics and machine learning literature. A plug in clas(cid:173) sification technique (PaCT) is a method that takes a standard classifier (such as LDA or TREES) and plugs it into an algorithm to produce a new classifier. The standard classifier is known as the Plug in Classi(cid:173) fier (PiC). These methods often produce large improvements over using a single classifier. In this paper we investigate one of these methods and give some motivation for its success.

paragraphs: A standard classifier can be used as a component inside a larger classification algorithm. This paper discusses that strategy through plug-in classification techniques, called PaCTs. The classifier inserted into the procedure is the plug-in classifier, or PiC. The distinction separates the underlying prediction method from the surrounding algorithm that turns it into a new classifier.

Examples of possible components include linear discriminant analysis and tree classifiers. The broader technique can therefore operate on established classification methods rather than requiring an entirely new component learner. The abstract notes that methods in this class often deliver large improvements over using one classifier alone, motivating closer examination of how the surrounding procedure contributes.

The paper investigates one such technique and offers motivation for its success. Its explanatory focus is the value created by the plug-in arrangement: classification performance depends on how a learner is used as well as on the learner itself. This provides a way to study improvements at the level of the overall algorithm while retaining a familiar classifier as its component.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates why embedding a standard classifier within a plug-in classification procedure can improve performance.

title: The Error Coding and Substitution PaCTs

abstract: We present exact analytical equilibrium solutions for a class of recur(cid:173) rent neural network models, with both sequential and parallel neuronal dynamics, in which there is a tunable competition between nearest(cid:173) neighbour and long-range synaptic interactions. This competition is found to induce novel coexistence phenomena as well as discontinuous transitions between pattern recall states, 2-cycles and non-recall states.
originalAbstract: We present exact analytical equilibrium solutions for a class of recur(cid:173) rent neural network models, with both sequential and parallel neuronal dynamics, in which there is a tunable competition between nearest(cid:173) neighbour and long-range synaptic interactions. This competition is found to induce novel coexistence phenomena as well as discontinuous transitions between pattern recall states, 2-cycles and non-recall states.

paragraphs: The paper studies recurrent neural networks whose connections operate at two spatial scales: between nearest neighbors and over longer distances. The relative influence of these interactions can be tuned. This makes competition between local and distant connections an explicit part of the model, allowing the authors to examine how it affects the network's recall behavior.

The authors obtain exact analytical equilibrium solutions for a class of these networks. Their treatment includes both sequential and parallel neuronal dynamics, covering models in which neurons update in sequence as well as models with simultaneous updates. The contribution is an analytical characterization of the modeled behavior, rather than solely observations from numerical runs.

The competition produces coexistence phenomena and abrupt transitions involving recall states, non-recall states, and two-cycles, which alternate between two states. Thus, changing the balance of interactions can change the kind of behavior the network exhibits discontinuously. Within the analyzed model class, the findings connect memory recall and cycling behavior to the interaction between local and long-range connections.
summary.tldr: Exact analysis shows that competing local and long-range connections can induce coexistence and abrupt transitions among recall, cycling, and non-recall states.

title: Discontinuous Recall Transitions Induced by Competition Between Short- and Long-Range Interactions in Recurrent Networks

paragraphs: Mixture models offer a statistical approach to clustering, and expectation-maximization is a common method for fitting them. The paper addresses a computational obstacle: EM repeatedly accesses the data, making its use expensive on enormous datasets. The proposed algorithm uses multiresolution kd-trees to reduce the cost of EM-based clustering.

The authors report a dramatic cost reduction, with savings increasing linearly with the number of data points. This claim concerns the growth of the savings; it should not be read as a claim that total runtime becomes independent of dataset size. The method is presented for maximum-likelihood estimation of Gaussian mixture models.

The abstract also identifies broader applications. Non-Gaussian models are covered when their class densities are monotonic in Mahalanobis distance. Other stated applications include clusters with mixed categorical and numerical data and Bayesian methods such as Autoclass. The contribution therefore combines an acceleration method for Gaussian mixture fitting with explicitly described routes to other clustering settings, including a condition on the non-Gaussian case.
summary.tldr: Multiresolution kd-trees substantially reduce EM clustering costs, with reported savings growing linearly with dataset size.

title: Very Fast EM-Based Mixture Model Clustering Using Multiresolution Kd-Trees

abstract: We calculate lower bounds on the size of sigmoidal neural networks that approximate continuous functions. In particular, we show that for the approximation of polynomials the network size has to grow as O((logk)1/4) where k is the degree of the polynomials. This bound is valid for any input dimension, i.e. independently of the number of variables. The result is obtained by introducing a new method employing upper bounds on the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension for proving lower bounds on the size of networks that approximate continuous functions.
originalAbstract: We calculate lower bounds on the size of sigmoidal neural networks that approximate continuous functions. In particular, we show that for the approximation of polynomials the network size has to grow as O((logk)1/4) where k is the degree of the polynomials. This bound is valid for any input dimension, i.e. independently of the number of variables. The result is obtained by introducing a new method employing upper bounds on the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension for proving lower bounds on the size of networks that approximate continuous functions.

paragraphs: This paper asks how large a neural network with sigmoidal units must be to approximate continuous functions. Its focus is on lower bounds: establishing required network size rather than constructing a particular approximation algorithm. Such a result concerns the resources that an approximation demands, even before choosing a method for learning the network.

For polynomial approximation, the authors report a required growth scale involving the fourth root of the logarithm of the polynomial degree. They state that the bound applies regardless of input dimension. This makes polynomial degree the explicit complexity quantity in the result, with the bound remaining valid independently of the number of variables.

The proof introduces a method that uses upper bounds on Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension to derive lower bounds on approximation size. It connects a measure of a model family's expressive capacity to the resources needed for continuous-function approximation. The contribution is both a size restriction for sigmoidal networks and a proof strategy for obtaining such restrictions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives lower bounds on sigmoidal-network size for continuous-function approximation using upper bounds on VC dimension.

title: Lower Bounds on the Complexity of Approximating Continuous Functions by Sigmoidal Neural Networks

abstract: We present an expressive agent design language for reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing that allows the user to constrain the policies considered by the learn(cid:173) ing process.The language includes standard features such as parameter(cid:173) ized subroutines, temporary interrupts, aborts, and memory variables, but also allows for unspecified choices in the agent program. For learning that which isn't specified, we present provably convergent learning algo(cid:173) rithms. We demonstrate by example that agent programs written in the language are concise as well as modular. This facilitates state abstraction and the transferability of learned skills.
originalAbstract: We present an expressive agent design language for reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing that allows the user to constrain the policies considered by the learn(cid:173) ing process.The language includes standard features such as parameter(cid:173) ized subroutines, temporary interrupts, aborts, and memory variables, but also allows for unspecified choices in the agent program. For learning that which isn't specified, we present provably convergent learning algo(cid:173) rithms. We demonstrate by example that agent programs written in the language are concise as well as modular. This facilitates state abstraction and the transferability of learned skills.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an agent programming language that lets a user restrict which policies reinforcement learning considers. A program can express parts of the desired behavior while leaving some choices unspecified. Learning then supplies those choices within the structure established by the program, combining explicit design with adaptation.

The language includes parameterized subroutines, temporary interrupts, aborts, and memory variables. These features support structured descriptions of agent behavior, including reusable components and changes in control flow. The authors also provide provably convergent learning algorithms for the portions left unspecified, giving a theoretical foundation for learning within the language.

Examples demonstrate that programs in the language can be concise and modular. The authors connect that modularity to state abstraction and the transfer of learned skills. The significance is a way to express useful behavioral structure without filling in every decision beforehand. The resulting learning problem is shaped by the programmer's constraints, with convergence guarantees applying to the learning algorithms presented for resolving the remaining choices.
summary.tldr: An agent language combines programmed behavioral structure with unspecified choices learned through provably convergent algorithms.

title: Programmable Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: We present the embedded trees algorithm, an iterative technique for estimation of Gaussian processes defined on arbitrary graphs. By exactly solving a series of modified problems on embedded span(cid:173) ning trees, it computes the conditional means with an efficiency comparable to or better than other techniques. Unlike other meth(cid:173) ods, the embedded trees algorithm also computes exact error co(cid:173) variances. The error covariance computation is most efficient for graphs in which removing a small number of edges reveals an em(cid:173) bedded tree. In this context, we demonstrate that sparse loopy graphs can provide a significant increase in modeling power rela(cid:173) tive to trees, with only a minor increase in estimation complexity.

By exactly solving a series of modified problems on embedded span(cid:173) ning trees, it computes the conditional means with an efficiency comparable to or better than other techniques. Unlike other meth(cid:173) ods, the embedded trees algorithm also computes exact error co(cid:173) variances. In this context, we demonstrate that sparse loopy graphs can provide a significant increase in modeling power rela(cid:173) tive to trees, with only a minor increase in estimation complexity.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an iterative estimation method for Gaussian processes represented on graphs that may contain cycles. Called the embedded-trees algorithm, it repeatedly solves modified problems on spanning trees contained within the graph. Each tree problem is solved exactly, and the series of solutions is used to perform estimation for the original graph.

The method computes conditional means with efficiency comparable to or better than other techniques. It also computes exact error covariances, providing uncertainty information alongside the estimated values. The abstract highlights this covariance calculation as a distinguishing capability, extending the result beyond obtaining point estimates alone.

Covariance computation is most efficient when removing only a small number of edges leaves a tree. In that setting, the authors demonstrate that sparse graphs with loops can substantially increase modeling power over trees with only a small increase in estimation complexity. The contribution therefore connects a richer dependency structure to a tractable estimation strategy, with the strongest efficiency advantage tied to graphs that are close to trees.
summary.tldr: The embedded-trees algorithm estimates Gaussian models on cyclic graphs and computes exact error covariances, especially efficiently for graphs close to trees.

title: Tree-Based Modeling and Estimation of Gaussian Processes on Graphs with Cycles

abstract: We consider an MDP setting in which the reward function is allowed to change during each time step of play (possibly in an adversarial manner), yet the dynamics remain fixed. Similar to the experts setting, we address the question of how well can an agent do when compared to the reward achieved under the best stationary policy over time. We provide efficient algorithms, which have regret bounds with no dependence on the size of state space. Instead, these bounds depend only on a certain horizon time of the process and logarithmically on the number of actions. We also show that in the case that the dynamics change over time, the problem becomes computationally hard.
originalAbstract: We consider an MDP setting in which the reward function is allowed to change during each time step of play (possibly in an adversarial manner), yet the dynamics remain fixed. Similar to the experts setting, we address the question of how well can an agent do when compared to the reward achieved under the best stationary policy over time. We provide efficient algorithms, which have regret bounds with no dependence on the size of state space. Instead, these bounds depend only on a certain horizon time of the process and logarithmically on the number of actions. We also show that in the case that the dynamics change over time, the problem becomes computationally hard.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision making when the rewards attached to actions and states can change at every step, potentially through adversarial choices. The environment's transition dynamics remain fixed. This separates uncertainty about what will be rewarding from changes in how actions move the agent through the environment.

The performance target is the reward that the best stationary policy would have achieved over time. A stationary policy uses the same decision rule throughout play. Regret measures the agent's shortfall relative to this reference, allowing the authors to ask how well an adaptive agent can compete despite changing rewards.

The authors provide efficient algorithms with regret bounds that do not depend on the number of states. Instead, the bounds depend on a particular horizon time of the process and only logarithmically on the number of actions. They also show computational hardness when the dynamics change over time. Fixed dynamics are thus a substantive condition of the positive result, rather than an incidental modeling choice.
summary.tldr: With fixed dynamics and changing rewards, efficient MDP algorithms achieve regret bounds independent of the number of states, while changing dynamics make the problem computationally hard.

title: Experts in a Markov Decision Process

abstract: We present a method for binary on-line classification of triggered but temporally blurred events that are embedded in noisy time series in the context of on-line discrimination between left and right imaginary hand-movement. In particular the goal of the binary classification problem is to obtain the decision, as fast and as reliably as possible from the recorded EEG single trials. To provide a probabilistic decision at every time-point t the presented method gathers information from two distinct sequences of features across time. In order to incorporate decisions from prior time-points we suggest an appropriate weighting scheme, that emphasizes time instances, providing a higher discriminatory power between the instantaneous class distributions of each feature, where the discriminatory power is quantified in terms of the Bayes error of misclassification. The effectiveness of this procedure is verified by its successful application in the 3rd BCI competition. Disclosure of the data after the competition revealed this approach to be superior with single trial error rates as low as 10.7, 11.5 and 16.7% for the three different sub jects under study.
originalAbstract: We present a method for binary on-line classification of triggered but temporally blurred events that are embedded in noisy time series in the context of on-line discrimination between left and right imaginary hand-movement. In particular the goal of the binary classification problem is to obtain the decision, as fast and as reliably as possible from the recorded EEG single trials. To provide a probabilistic decision at every time-point t the presented method gathers information from two distinct sequences of features across time. In order to incorporate decisions from prior time-points we suggest an appropriate weighting scheme, that emphasizes time instances, providing a higher discriminatory power between the instantaneous class distributions of each feature, where the discriminatory power is quantified in terms of the Bayes error of misclassification. The effectiveness of this procedure is verified by its successful application in the 3rd BCI competition. Disclosure of the data after the competition revealed this approach to be superior with single trial error rates as low as 10.7, 11.5 and 16.7% for the three different sub jects under study.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to distinguish imagined left-hand and right-hand movement from a single EEG trial as quickly and reliably as possible. The relevant activity follows a trigger, but its timing is blurred and the measurements are noisy. A useful classifier therefore needs to accumulate evidence while continuing to produce decisions as new measurements arrive.

The proposed method supplies a probabilistic decision at each time point by combining information from two sequences of features. Earlier decisions contribute through a weighting scheme that gives more emphasis to moments when the feature distributions for the two classes are easier to distinguish. This discriminatory strength is quantified using the Bayes error of misclassification.

The approach was successfully applied in the third BCI competition. Analysis after the data were disclosed supported its reported superiority, with single-trial error rates as low as 10.7%, 11.5%, and 16.7% for the three subjects studied. These findings support weighting accumulated evidence by its discriminatory value in this setting.
summary.tldr: The method combines EEG evidence over time, emphasizing moments that better distinguish imagined left-hand from right-hand movement.

title: Aggregating Classification Accuracy across Time: Application to Single Trial EEG

abstract: The risk, or probability of error, of the classifier produced by the AdaBoost algorithm is investigated. In particular, we consider the stopping strategy to be used in AdaBoost to achieve universal consistency. We show that provided AdaBoost is stopped after n iterations--for sample size n and < 1--the sequence of risks of the classifiers it produces approaches the Bayes risk if Bayes risk L > 0.
originalAbstract: The risk, or probability of error, of the classifier produced by the AdaBoost algorithm is investigated. In particular, we consider the stopping strategy to be used in AdaBoost to achieve universal consistency. We show that provided AdaBoost is stopped after n iterations--for sample size n and < 1--the sequence of risks of the classifiers it produces approaches the Bayes risk if Bayes risk L > 0.

paragraphs: This paper studies the probability that an AdaBoost classifier makes an error, focusing on how training should stop as the sample size increases. The central question is consistency: whether classifiers trained on increasingly large samples can approach the lowest error achievable for the underlying prediction problem. That benchmark is called the Bayes risk.

The stated result connects consistency to a stopping strategy whose iteration count depends on the training sample size. Under that strategy, the sequence of classifier risks approaches the Bayes risk when the Bayes risk is strictly positive. The supplied abstract has an incomplete rendering of the stopping formula, so its exact schedule cannot be reliably reconstructed from this evidence.

The significance is that stopping is part of the theoretical guarantee, rather than merely a choice about training time. The result concerns convergence of prediction error as more data become available. It does not promise zero error: with positive Bayes risk, even the best possible classifier has unavoidable error. AdaBoost's stated achievement is approaching that benchmark under the specified stopping condition.
summary.tldr: AdaBoost's error approaches positive Bayes risk under a sample-size-dependent stopping strategy.

title: AdaBoost is Consistent

abstract: This paper considers kernels invariant to translation, rotation and dilation. We show that no non-trivial positive deﬁnite (p.d.) kernels exist which are radial and dilation invariant, only conditionally positive deﬁnite (c.p.d.) ones. Accordingly, we discuss the c.p.d. case and provide some novel analysis, including an elemen- tary derivation of a c.p.d. representer theorem. On the practical side, we give a support vector machine (s.v.m.) algorithm for arbitrary c.p.d. kernels. For the thin- plate kernel this leads to a classiﬁer with only one parameter (the amount of regu- larisation), which we demonstrate to be as effective as an s.v.m. with the Gaussian kernel, even though the Gaussian involves a second parameter (the length scale).

paragraphs: The paper studies kernels intended to remain unchanged under translation, rotation, and changes of scale. Its central theoretical finding is that no nontrivial positive definite kernel can be both radial and dilation invariant. This rules out that particular combination of properties within the ordinary positive definite kernel class.

The authors consequently investigate conditionally positive definite kernels, which provide a different mathematical setting for the desired invariance. They develop new analysis, including an elementary derivation of a representer theorem for this class. They also give a support vector machine algorithm that can work with arbitrary conditionally positive definite kernels, connecting the theory to a usable classification method.

With the thin-plate kernel, the classifier needs only one parameter: the amount of regularization. The authors demonstrate effectiveness comparable to an SVM using a Gaussian kernel, which also requires a length-scale parameter. The practical finding is that this kernel choice can reduce the number of parameters while retaining comparable demonstrated classification effectiveness, alongside the paper’s precise restriction on ordinary positive definite kernels.
summary.tldr: Conditionally positive definite kernels enable an invariant-kernel SVM approach whose thin-plate version achieves demonstrated Gaussian-SVM effectiveness with one fewer parameter.

title: Learning with Transformation Invariant Kernels

abstract: We study the problem of domain transfer for a supervised classification task in mRNA splicing. We consider a number of recent domain transfer methods from machine learning, including some that are novel, and evaluate them on genomic sequence data from model organisms of varying evolutionary distance. We find that in cases where the organisms are not closely related, the use of domain adaptation methods can help improve classification performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether supervised learning for mRNA splicing can benefit from transferring information between organisms. The central issue is domain transfer: a classification method must make use of information associated with one organism in a setting associated with another. The authors examine that issue using genomic sequence data rather than treating transfer as an abstract learning problem.

The study evaluates several domain adaptation approaches, including recent methods and some novel ones. It considers model organisms separated by different evolutionary distances. This makes relatedness an explicit part of the empirical comparison and lets the analysis examine transfer across biological settings that differ in how closely their organisms are related.

The reported finding is conditional: domain adaptation can improve classification when the organisms are not closely related. This supports its usefulness in those evaluated transfer settings without asserting that every adaptation method helps every organism pair. The contribution is empirical evidence connecting adaptation methods, evolutionary relatedness, and performance on a specific genomic classification task.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that domain adaptation can improve mRNA-splicing classification when transferring between organisms that are not closely related.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Domain Adaptation Algorithms for Genomic Sequence Analysis

abstract: Determining whether someone is talking has applications in many areas such as speech recognition, speaker diarization, social robotics, facial expression recognition, and human computer interaction. One popular approach to this problem is audio-visual synchrony detection. A candidate speaker is deemed to be talking if the visual signal around that speaker correlates with the auditory signal. Here we show that with the proper visual features (in this case movements of various facial muscle groups), a very accurate detector of speech can be created that does not use the audio signal at all. Further we show that this person independent visual-only detector can be used to train very accurate audio-based person dependent voice models. The voice model has the advantage of being able to identify when a particular person is speaking even when they are not visible to the camera (e.g. in the case of a mobile robot). Moreover, we show that a simple sensory fusion scheme between the auditory and visual models improves performance on the task of talking detection. The work here provides dramatic evidence about the efficacy of two very different approaches to multimodal speech detection on a challenging database.

paragraphs: Detecting whether a person is speaking often relies on matching visible movements with an audio signal. This paper investigates a different starting point: movements of facial muscle groups can themselves provide enough information for accurate speech detection. The resulting visual detector works across people and does not require audio to decide whether someone is talking.

The visual detector also supplies information for training audio models associated with particular people. This connects a person-independent visual capability to person-dependent voice recognition. Once trained, the voice model can identify when its person is speaking even if that person is outside the camera’s view, an ability relevant to settings such as mobile robotics.

The authors also combine the visual and auditory models through a simple sensory fusion scheme and report improved talking detection. Experiments on a challenging database support both the visual-only approach and the subsequent use of audio. The findings show how one sensing modality can help train another while their combination provides an additional performance benefit.
summary.tldr: Facial movements support accurate visual speech detection and can train person-specific voice models that also work when the speaker is unseen.

title: An Alternative to Low-level-Sychrony-Based Methods for Speech Detection

abstract: We consider the tree structured group Lasso where the structure over the features can be represented as a tree with leaf nodes as features and internal nodes as clusters of the features. The structured regularization with a pre-defined tree structure is based on a group-Lasso penalty, where one group is defined for each node in the tree. Such a regularization can help uncover the structured sparsity, which is desirable for applications with some meaningful tree structures on the features. However, the tree structured group Lasso is challenging to solve due to the complex regularization. In this paper, we develop an efficient algorithm for the tree structured group Lasso. One of the key steps in the proposed algorithm is to solve the Moreau-Yosida regularization associated with the grouped tree structure. The main technical contributions of this paper include (1) we show that the associated Moreau-Yosida regularization admits an analytical solution, and (2) we develop an efficient algorithm for determining the effective interval for the regularization parameter. Our experimental results on the AR and JAFFE face data sets demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Features sometimes come with a meaningful hierarchy: individual features form the leaves of a tree, and internal nodes represent clusters. Tree-structured group Lasso uses this hierarchy to encourage structured sparsity, assigning a group penalty to every node. The hierarchy is predefined, and the optimization seeks a sparse solution that reflects those feature groupings.

Although this penalty captures useful structure, it makes the learning problem difficult to solve. The paper develops an efficient algorithm whose key step involves the Moreau-Yosida regularization associated with the grouped tree. The authors show that this component has an analytical solution, providing a direct way to handle a central part of the structured regularization.

A second contribution is an efficient procedure for determining the effective interval of the regularization parameter. Experiments on the AR and JAFFE face datasets demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution makes an existing hierarchical sparsity formulation easier to optimize, helping turn meaningful feature trees into a usable learning constraint.
summary.tldr: An analytical Moreau-Yosida solution and efficient parameter-interval procedure make tree-structured group Lasso more practical to optimize.

title: Moreau-Yosida Regularization for Grouped Tree Structure Learning

abstract: This paper proposes a parsing algorithm for scene understanding which includes four aspects: computing 3D scene layout, detecting 3D objects (e.g. furniture), detecting 2D faces (windows, doors etc.), and segmenting background. In contrast to previous scene labeling work that applied discriminative classifiers to pixels (or super-pixels), we use a generative Stochastic Scene Grammar (SSG). This grammar represents the compositional structures of visual entities from scene categories, 3D foreground/background, 2D faces, to 1D lines. The grammar includes three types of production rules and two types of contextual relations. Production rules: (i) AND rules represent the decomposition of an entity into sub-parts; (ii) OR rules represent the switching among sub-types of an entity; (iii) SET rules rep- resent an ensemble of visual entities. Contextual relations: (i) Cooperative “+” relations represent positive links between binding entities, such as hinged faces of a object or aligned boxes; (ii) Competitive “-” relations represents negative links between competing entities, such as mutually exclusive boxes. We design an efficient MCMC inference algorithm, namely Hierarchical cluster sampling, to search in the large solution space of scene configurations. The algorithm has two stages: (i) Clustering: It forms all possible higher-level structures (clusters) from lower-level entities by production rules and contextual relations. (ii) Sampling: It jumps between alternative structures (clusters) in each layer of the hierarchy to find the most probable configuration (represented by a parse tree). In our experiment, we demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm over existing methods on public dataset. In addition, our approach achieves richer structures in the parse tree.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene involves more than assigning labels to pixels. This paper jointly addresses three-dimensional layout, three-dimensional objects, two-dimensional faces such as doors and windows, and background segmentation. It represents these elements through a generative stochastic scene grammar that connects scene categories to objects, faces, and lines in a hierarchy.

The grammar uses AND rules to describe parts, OR rules to choose among subtypes, and SET rules to represent collections of entities. Contextual relations express either cooperation, such as alignment or connected faces, or competition, such as mutually exclusive boxes. These structures let the model describe how candidate visual elements can fit together into a scene.

To search the possible configurations, the authors introduce hierarchical cluster sampling, an MCMC inference algorithm. It builds higher-level candidate structures from lower-level elements, then samples alternative structures across the hierarchy to seek the most probable parse tree. The reported public-dataset experiment shows better performance than existing methods, while the resulting parse trees provide richer structural descriptions of the scene.
summary.tldr: A stochastic scene grammar and hierarchical sampling jointly infer scene layout, objects, faces, and background as a structured parse tree.

title: Image Parsing with Stochastic Scene Grammar

abstract: Classical Boosting algorithms, such as AdaBoost, build a strong classifier without concern about the computational cost. Some applications, in particular in computer vision, may involve up to millions of training examples and features. In such contexts, the training time may become prohibitive. Several methods exist to accelerate training, typically either by sampling the features, or the examples, used to train the weak learners. Even if those methods can precisely quantify the speed improvement they deliver, they offer no guarantee of being more efficient than any other, given the same amount of time. This paper aims at shading some light on this problem, i.e. given a fixed amount of time, for a particular problem, which strategy is optimal in order to reduce the training loss the most. We apply this analysis to the design of new algorithms which estimate on the fly at every iteration the optimal trade-off between the number of samples and the number of features to look at in order to maximize the expected loss reduction. Experiments in object recognition with two standard computer vision data-sets show that the adaptive methods we propose outperform basic sampling and state-of-the-art bandit methods.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak learners into a strong classifier, but training can become expensive when there are very many examples and features. Sampling either examples or features can reduce computation. The paper asks a more specific question: given a fixed time budget, how should that computation be allocated to reduce training loss most effectively?

The authors analyze the trade-off between inspecting more examples and considering more features. They use that analysis to design algorithms that estimate a suitable allocation during every boosting iteration. The target is the greatest expected reduction in loss, so the sampling decision responds to the current learning problem rather than following one fixed allocation throughout training.

Experiments on object recognition using two standard computer-vision datasets show the proposed adaptive methods outperforming basic sampling approaches and state-of-the-art bandit methods. The contribution connects computational savings to learning progress: a faster iteration is useful insofar as it helps improve the classifier within the available time. The algorithms estimate the best trade-off as training proceeds; the reported empirical comparisons support their effectiveness on the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: Adaptive boosting algorithms choose how many examples and features to inspect at each iteration to maximize expected loss reduction within a time budget.

title: Boosting with Maximum Adaptive Sampling

abstract: The empirical success of the belief propagation approximate inference algorithm has inspired numerous theoretical and algorithmic advances. Yet, for continuous non-Gaussian domains performing belief propagation remains a challenging task: recent innovations such as nonparametric or kernel belief propagation, while useful, come with a substantial computational cost and offer little theoretical guarantees, even for tree structured models. In this work we present Nonparanormal BP for performing efficient inference on distributions parameterized by a Gaussian copulas network and any univariate marginals. For tree structured networks, our approach is guaranteed to be exact for this powerful class of non-Gaussian models. Importantly, the method is as efficient as standard Gaussian BP, and its convergence properties do not depend on the complexity of the univariate marginals, even when a nonparametric representation is used.

paragraphs: Belief propagation performs inference by passing information through a graphical model. Continuous variables with non-Gaussian distributions make this difficult: flexible approaches can be computationally expensive and may lack strong guarantees. This paper introduces Nonparanormal Belief Propagation for a model class that combines flexible individual-variable distributions with a structured dependence model.

Specifically, the joint distributions use a Gaussian copula network together with arbitrary univariate marginals. This separates the description of each variable's distribution from the way variables depend on one another. The method can therefore handle non-Gaussian marginal behavior while exploiting the computational structure associated with Gaussian belief propagation.

For tree-structured networks in this model class, the method is guaranteed to give exact inference. It is as efficient as standard Gaussian belief propagation, and its convergence properties do not depend on the complexity of the individual marginals, even with nonparametric representations. The exactness claim is tied to trees and the specified distribution class. Within that scope, the result combines substantial distributional flexibility with strong computational and theoretical properties.
summary.tldr: Nonparanormal belief propagation supports arbitrary marginals with Gaussian-BP efficiency and guarantees exact inference on trees in its model class.

title: Nonparanormal Belief Propagation (NPNBP)

abstract: Natural actor-critics are a popular class of policy search algorithms for finding locally optimal policies for Markov decision processes. In this paper we address a drawback of natural actor-critics that limits their real-world applicability - their lack of safety guarantees. We present a principled algorithm for performing natural gradient descent over a constrained domain. In the context of reinforcement learning, this allows for natural actor-critic algorithms that are guaranteed to remain within a known safe region of policy space. While deriving our class of constrained natural actor-critic algorithms, which we call Projected Natural Actor-Critics (PNACs), we also elucidate the relationship between natural gradient descent and mirror descent.

paragraphs: Natural actor-critic algorithms search for locally optimal policies in Markov decision processes. Their usefulness in real applications is limited when learning updates lack safety guarantees. This paper addresses that issue by developing a principled way to perform natural-gradient optimization while restricting the allowable domain.

Applied to reinforcement learning, the construction produces Projected Natural Actor-Critics. These algorithms are guaranteed to keep policies inside a known safe region of policy space. The guarantee concerns remaining within that specified region throughout the optimization process. Knowledge of a safe region is therefore central to the formulation: the result uses that region as a constraint on policy search.

The derivation also clarifies the relationship between natural gradient descent and mirror descent, connecting the constrained method to a broader optimization perspective. The main contribution is a class of policy-search algorithms with a stated region-preservation guarantee. It addresses how learning can proceed within established policy constraints, while retaining the local-optimization setting that motivates natural actor-critic methods.
summary.tldr: Projected Natural Actor-Critics constrain natural-gradient policy search to remain within a known safe region.

title: Projected Natural Actor-Critic

abstract: Parameter-specific adaptive learning rate methods are computationally efficient ways to reduce the ill-conditioning problems encountered when training large deep networks. Following recent work that strongly suggests that most of thecritical points encountered when training such networks are saddle points, we find how considering the presence of negative eigenvalues of the Hessian could help us design better suited adaptive learning rate schemes. We show that the popular Jacobi preconditioner has undesirable behavior in the presence of both positive and negative curvature, and present theoretical and empirical evidence that the so-called equilibration preconditioner is comparatively better suited to non-convex problems. We introduce a novel adaptive learning rate scheme, called ESGD, based on the equilibration preconditioner. Our experiments demonstrate that both schemes yield very similar step directions but that ESGD sometimes surpasses RMSProp in terms of convergence speed, always clearly improving over plain stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Adaptive learning rates adjust update sizes separately for different parameters, helping address ill-conditioning in large neural networks. This paper asks how those adjustments should account for nonconvex curvature. Its motivation comes from research suggesting that many critical points encountered during network training are saddle points, where curvature can have both positive and negative directions.

The authors show that the Jacobi preconditioner can behave undesirably when those curvature signs coexist. They present theoretical and empirical evidence favoring an equilibration preconditioner for nonconvex problems. They then use that preconditioner to develop ESGD, a new scheme for adapting learning rates.

In the reported experiments, ESGD and RMSProp produce very similar update directions, while ESGD sometimes converges faster. ESGD also clearly improves on plain stochastic gradient descent throughout those experiments. The findings support accounting for mixed-sign curvature when designing adaptive updates, with the speed advantage over RMSProp remaining an empirical result that occurs in some evaluated cases.
summary.tldr: ESGD adapts learning rates through equilibration, with evidence that this handles nonconvex curvature better than Jacobi preconditioning.

title: Equilibrated adaptive learning rates for non-convex optimization

abstract: We investigate the robust PCA problem of decomposing an observed matrix into the sum of a low-rank and a sparse error matrices via convex programming Principal Component Pursuit (PCP). In contrast to previous studies that assume the support of the error matrix is generated by uniform Bernoulli sampling, we allow non-uniform sampling, i.e., entries of the low-rank matrix are corrupted by errors with unequal probabilities. We characterize conditions on error corruption of each individual entry based on the local incoherence of the low-rank matrix, under which correct matrix decomposition by PCP is guaranteed. Such a refined analysis of robust PCA captures how robust each entry of the low rank matrix combats error corruption. In order to deal with non-uniform error corruption, our technical proof introduces a new weighted norm and develops/exploits the concentration properties that such a norm satisfies.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis seeks to separate an observed matrix into a low-rank component and a sparse matrix of errors. This paper studies when Principal Component Pursuit, a convex optimization approach to that separation, can recover the correct components. Its focus is on how the locations of errors affect recovery.

Earlier analyses assumed that entries were corrupted through uniform Bernoulli sampling, giving each entry the same corruption probability. The authors allow those probabilities to differ. They derive conditions for individual entries using the low-rank matrix’s local incoherence, relating the tolerated corruption pattern to the matrix’s structure at each location.

The resulting guarantee is conditional: Principal Component Pursuit correctly separates the matrices when the specified entry-level corruption conditions hold. This provides a more detailed account of robustness than a uniform corruption model. To establish it, the proof introduces a weighted norm and develops its concentration properties, supplying mathematical tools for analyzing unequal corruption probabilities.
summary.tldr: An entry-level analysis gives recovery guarantees for robust PCA when matrix entries have unequal probabilities of corruption.

title: Analysis of Robust PCA via Local Incoherence

abstract: Interactive submodular set cover is an interactive variant of submodular set cover over a hypothesis class of submodular functions, where the goal is to satisfy all sufficiently plausible submodular functions to a target threshold using as few (cost-weighted) actions as possible. It models settings where there is uncertainty regarding which submodular function to optimize. In this paper, we propose a new extension, which we call smooth interactive submodular set cover, that allows the target threshold to vary depending on the plausibility of each hypothesis. We present the first algorithm for this more general setting with theoretical guarantees on optimality. We further show how to extend our approach to deal with real-valued functions, which yields new theoretical results for real-valued submodular set cover for both the interactive and non-interactive settings.

paragraphs: Interactive submodular set cover studies how to choose inexpensive actions when the function to be satisfied is uncertain. The learner considers several hypotheses and seeks to bring all sufficiently plausible functions to a target value. Action costs matter, so the objective is to achieve coverage with as little cost-weighted action as possible.

The paper generalizes this setup by allowing each hypothesis to have a target determined by its plausibility. This smooth formulation makes the required level of satisfaction depend on the uncertainty attached to the hypothesis. It therefore extends the common-threshold version of the problem while retaining the action-selection objective.

The authors give the first algorithm for this generalized setting with theoretical optimality guarantees. They also extend the approach to real-valued functions, obtaining new theoretical results for both interactive and non-interactive submodular set cover. The contribution broadens how uncertainty and coverage requirements can be represented while preserving a framework for analyzing the quality of action choices.
summary.tldr: Smooth interactive submodular set cover lets coverage targets depend on hypothesis plausibility and provides algorithms with theoretical guarantees.

title: Smooth Interactive Submodular Set Cover

abstract: We develop a classification algorithm for estimating posterior distributions from positive-unlabeled data, that is robust to noise in the positive labels and effective for high-dimensional data. In recent years, several algorithms have been proposed to learn from positive-unlabeled data; however, many of these contributions remain theoretical, performing poorly on real high-dimensional data that is typically contaminated with noise. We build on this previous work to develop two practical classification algorithms that explicitly model the noise in the positive labels and utilize univariate transforms built on discriminative classifiers. We prove that these univariate transforms preserve the class prior, enabling estimation in the univariate space and avoiding kernel density estimation for high-dimensional data. The theoretical development and parametric and nonparametric algorithms proposed here constitute an important step towards wide-spread use of robust classification algorithms for positive-unlabeled data.

In recent years, several algorithms have been proposed to learn from positive-unlabeled data; however, many of these contributions remain theoretical, performing poorly on real high-dimensional data that is typically contaminated with noise. We build on this previous work to develop two practical classification algorithms that explicitly model the noise in the positive labels and utilize univariate transforms built on discriminative classifiers. We prove that these univariate transforms preserve the class prior, enabling estimation in the univariate space and avoiding kernel density estimation for high-dimensional data. The theoretical development and parametric and nonparametric algorithms proposed here constitute an important step towards wide-spread use of robust classification algorithms for positive-unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning uses examples labeled positive together with examples whose class is unknown. The paper addresses the additional complication that some positive labels are wrong. Its goal is to estimate class probabilities in a way that remains useful for noisy, high-dimensional data, where earlier theoretical methods can perform poorly.

The authors develop two practical algorithms that explicitly represent noise in the positive labels. Both use discriminative classifiers to construct one-dimensional transformations of the data. They prove that these transformations preserve the class prior, the overall proportion belonging to a class. This property lets the relevant estimation move into a one-dimensional space without losing that population quantity.

The reduction avoids kernel density estimation in the original high-dimensional space, directly addressing a difficulty identified by the paper. The resulting methods include parametric and nonparametric approaches for estimating the prior and posterior probabilities. Their significance lies in connecting an explicit label-noise model with a proven preservation property, making positive-unlabeled classification more practical in the setting considered.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms estimate class probabilities from noisy positives and unlabeled data using one-dimensional transformations that provably preserve the class prior.

title: Estimating the class prior and posterior from noisy positives and unlabeled data

abstract: Faced with saturation of Moore's law and increasing size and dimension of data, system designers have increasingly resorted to parallel and distributed computing to reduce computation time of machine-learning algorithms. However, distributed computing is often bottle necked by a small fraction of slow processors called "stragglers" that reduce the speed of computation because the fusion node has to wait for all processors to complete their processing. To combat the effect of stragglers, recent literature proposes introducing redundancy in computations across processors, e.g., using repetition-based strategies or erasure codes. The fusion node can exploit this redundancy by completing the computation using outputs from only a subset of the processors, ignoring the stragglers. In this paper, we propose a novel technique - that we call "Short-Dot" - to introduce redundant computations in a coding theory inspired fashion, for computing linear transforms of long vectors. Instead of computing long dot products as required in the original linear transform, we construct a larger number of redundant and short dot products that can be computed more efficiently at individual processors. Further, only a subset of these short dot products are required at the fusion node to finish the computation successfully. We demonstrate through probabilistic analysis as well as experiments on computing clusters that Short-Dot offers significant speed-up compared to existing techniques. We also derive trade-offs between the length of the dot-products and the resilience to stragglers (number of processors required to finish), for any such strategy and compare it to that achieved by our strategy.

Redundant computation helps because the final result can sometimes be reconstructed from only a subset of workers. This paper applies that idea to large linear transformations, where individual tasks would ordinarily involve dot products with long vectors.

Short-Dot replaces those long dot products with a larger collection of redundant, shorter dot products constructed using coding-inspired methods. Comparing Short-Dot with those trade-offs clarifies the balance its construction achieves between local work and the amount of redundancy needed to complete the overall computation.
summary.tldr: Short-Dot distributes redundant short dot products so large linear transforms can finish without waiting for every processor.

title: Short-Dot: Computing Large Linear Transforms Distributedly Using Coded Short Dot Products

abstract: This work constructs a hypothesis test for detecting whether an data-generating function $h: \real^p \rightarrow \real$ belongs to a specific reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_0$, where the structure of $\mathcal{H}_0$ is only partially known. Utilizing the theory of reproducing kernels, we reduce this hypothesis to a simple one-sided score test for a scalar parameter, develop a testing procedure that is robust against the mis-specification of kernel functions, and also propose an ensemble-based estimator for the null model to guarantee test performance in small samples. To demonstrate the utility of the proposed method, we apply our test to the problem of detecting nonlinear interaction between groups of continuous features. We evaluate the finite-sample performance of our test under different data-generating functions and estimation strategies for the null model. Our results revealed interesting connection between notions in machine learning (model underfit/overfit) and those in statistical inference (i.e. Type I error/power of hypothesis test), and also highlighted unexpected consequences of common model estimating strategies (e.g. estimating kernel hyperparameters using maximum likelihood estimation) on model inference.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hypothesis test for whether a data-generating function belongs to a specified reproducing kernel Hilbert space whose structure is only partly known. This offers a way to test properties of an unknown relationship while allowing considerable flexibility in the functions used to describe it.

Using reproducing-kernel theory, the authors reduce the original question to a one-sided score test involving a single scalar parameter. They develop robustness to kernel misspecification and introduce an ensemble estimator for the null model to support test performance in small samples. The construction makes the quality of null-model estimation an explicit part of the testing procedure.

The results connect underfitting and overfitting with false-positive behavior and statistical power, and reveal unexpected inferential consequences of common estimation choices, including maximum-likelihood kernel tuning. This shows why fitting a model and using it for a hypothesis test require closely coordinated choices.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based hypothesis test detects nonlinear effects while addressing kernel misspecification and the influence of null-model estimation on inference.

title: Robust Hypothesis Test for Nonlinear Effect with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a practical tension: a model can make accurate predictions while remaining difficult to understand. Existing explanation methods offer different ways to assign importance to input features, but their relationships and relative advantages are often unclear. SHAP provides a shared framework for understanding these methods and explaining individual predictions.

The framework assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its central theoretical contribution is to identify a class of additive feature importance measures and show that exactly one solution within that class satisfies a specified set of desirable properties. The uniqueness result is therefore tied to that class and those properties.

This perspective brings six existing methods into one framework and reveals that several lack the proposed properties. The authors also develop explanation methods informed by this analysis. These show improved computational performance, better agreement with human intuition, or both. The contribution combines a clearer basis for comparing explanations with practical methods for computing them.
summary.tldr: SHAP unifies feature-attribution methods and identifies a unique additive explanation satisfying a specified set of desirable properties.

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions

abstract: We introduce associative embedding, a novel method for supervising convolutional neural networks for the task of detection and grouping. A number of computer vision problems can be framed in this manner including multi-person pose estimation, instance segmentation, and multi-object tracking. Usually the grouping of detections is achieved with multi-stage pipelines, instead we propose an approach that teaches a network to simultaneously output detections and group assignments. This technique can be easily integrated into any state-of-the-art network architecture that produces pixel-wise predictions. We show how to apply this method to multi-person pose estimation and report state-of-the-art performance on the MPII and MS-COCO datasets.

paragraphs: Many vision tasks require both finding individual elements and deciding which ones belong together. In multi-person pose estimation, detecting body parts is only part of the problem; the detections must also be assigned to people. Instance segmentation and tracking multiple objects have a related structure, combining detection with decisions about membership.

Associative embedding provides a way to supervise a convolutional network so that it outputs detections and group assignments together. This brings grouping into the learned prediction process, which is commonly handled through a pipeline with several stages. The method is designed to integrate into network architectures that make predictions at individual pixels.

The paper demonstrates the approach on multi-person pose estimation and reports state-of-the-art results on MPII and MS-COCO. These findings support joint detection and grouping as an effective approach for that application. Its broader relevance comes from the shared structure of several vision problems, while the reported performance evidence specifically concerns pose estimation on the two named datasets.
summary.tldr: Associative embedding teaches a network to detect elements and predict their group assignments together, with strong multi-person pose results.

title: Associative Embedding: End-to-End Learning for Joint Detection and Grouping

abstract: Regularized empirical risk minimization problem with linear predictor appears frequently in machine learning. In this paper, we propose a new stochastic primal-dual method to solve this class of problems. Different from existing methods, our proposed methods only require O(1) operations in each iteration. We also develop a variance-reduction variant of the algorithm that converges linearly. Numerical experiments suggest that our methods are faster than existing ones such as proximal SGD, SVRG and SAGA on high-dimensional problems.

Numerical experiments suggest that our methods are faster than existing ones such as proximal SGD, SVRG and SAGA on high-dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Regularized empirical risk minimization trains a model by balancing fit to observed data with a regularization term. This paper considers that common learning objective for linear predictors. Its focus is the computational expense of optimization, especially when the prediction problem has many dimensions and repeated updates can become costly.

The authors propose a stochastic primal-dual method requiring O(1) operations per iteration. The central computational claim is therefore about the cost of an individual update. They also develop a variance-reduction variant with linear convergence, adding a convergence-rate result to the inexpensive-update design. These are complementary aspects of the method's optimization behavior.

Numerical experiments suggest that the proposed methods are faster than proximal SGD, SVRG, and SAGA on high-dimensional problems. That comparison provides empirical support for the approach's practical speed in the studied setting. The paper's contribution combines constant-cost iterations with a linearly convergent variant, while the reported experiments connect those algorithmic properties to observed runtime advantages for regularized linear prediction.
summary.tldr: A stochastic primal-dual optimizer uses constant-cost iterations, with a linearly convergent variance-reduction variant and promising high-dimensional runtime results.

title: Stochastic Primal-Dual Method for Empirical Risk Minimization with O(1) Per-Iteration Complexity

abstract: Machine understanding of complex images is a key goal of artificial intelligence. One challenge underlying this task is that visual scenes contain multiple inter-related objects, and that global context plays an important role in interpreting the scene. A natural modeling framework for capturing such effects is structured prediction, which optimizes over complex labels, while modeling within-label interactions. However, it is unclear what principles should guide the design of a structured prediction model that utilizes the power of deep learning components. Here we propose a design principle for such architectures that follows from a natural requirement of permutation invariance. We prove a necessary and sufficient characterization for architectures that follow this invariance, and discuss its implication on model design. Finally, we show that the resulting model achieves new state of the art results on the Visual Genome scene graph labeling benchmark, outperforming all recent approaches.
