paragraphs: Understanding a complex image involves identifying objects and interpreting their relationships. Because the objects influence how the whole scene is understood, predicting each label independently can miss relevant context. This paper uses structured prediction, which treats the output as an interconnected collection of labels and explicitly models interactions within that collection.

The authors propose permutation invariance as a principle for designing deep structured-prediction architectures. The ordering used to represent a scene's elements should not change the underlying interpretation. They prove a necessary and sufficient characterization of architectures satisfying the relevant invariance requirement, then discuss how that result guides model design.

The resulting model achieves a new state of the art on the Visual Genome scene graph labeling benchmark, outperforming the recent approaches included in the comparison. The paper therefore connects an architectural principle to both a mathematical characterization and an evaluated model. Its significance is that a natural structural requirement can provide concrete guidance for combining deep learning components, rather than leaving their organization entirely to experimentation.
summary.tldr: A permutation-invariance characterization guides a scene-graph architecture that achieves state-of-the-art results on the reported Visual Genome benchmark.

title: Mapping Images to Scene Graphs with Permutation-Invariant Structured Prediction

abstract: Modern deep transfer learning approaches have mainly focused on learning generic feature vectors from one task that are transferable to other tasks, such as word embeddings in language and pretrained convolutional features in vision. However, these approaches usually transfer unary features and largely ignore more structured graphical representations. This work explores the possibility of learning generic latent relational graphs that capture dependencies between pairs of data units (e.g., words or pixels) from large-scale unlabeled data and transferring the graphs to downstream tasks. Our proposed transfer learning framework improves performance on various tasks including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. We also show that the learned graphs are generic enough to be transferred to different embeddings on which the graphs have not been trained (including GloVe embeddings, ELMo embeddings, and task-specific RNN hidden units), or embedding-free units such as image pixels.

Our proposed transfer learning framework improves performance on various tasks including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. We also show that the learned graphs are generic enough to be transferred to different embeddings on which the graphs have not been trained (including GloVe embeddings, ELMo embeddings, and task-specific RNN hidden units), or embedding-free units such as image pixels.

paragraphs: Transfer learning commonly reuses feature vectors that describe individual units, such as words or image features. GLoMo explores transferring a different kind of knowledge: graphs describing relationships between pairs of units. The goal is to learn dependencies from large amounts of unlabeled data and reuse them in downstream tasks.

These latent relational graphs represent structure connecting units such as words or pixels. Transferring such structure can provide downstream models with information about how units depend on one another, alongside whatever individual representations those models use. The framework therefore makes relationships themselves a transferable product of unsupervised learning.

The authors report improved performance on question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. They also show that learned graphs transfer to representations on which the graphs were not trained, including GloVe, ELMo, and task-specific recurrent-network states, as well as units without embeddings such as pixels. These results support the possibility that useful relational structure can be reused across different representation choices, rather than remaining tied to its original feature space.
summary.tldr: GLoMo learns relational graphs from unlabeled data and transfers their dependency structure across tasks and different input representations.

title: GLoMo: Unsupervised Learning of Transferable Relational Graphs

abstract: Convolutional neural networks have achieved great success in various vision tasks; however, they incur heavy resource costs. By using deeper and wider networks, network accuracy can be improved rapidly. However, in an environment with limited resources (e.g., mobile applications), heavy networks may not be usable. This study shows that naive convolution can be deconstructed into a shift operation and pointwise convolution. To cope with various convolutions, we propose a new shift operation called active shift layer (ASL) that formulates the amount of shift as a learnable function with shift parameters. This new layer can be optimized end-to-end through backpropagation and it can provide optimal shift values. Finally, we apply this layer to a light and fast network that surpasses existing state-of-the-art networks.

This study shows that naive convolution can be deconstructed into a shift operation and pointwise convolution. To cope with various convolutions, we propose a new shift operation called active shift layer (ASL) that formulates the amount of shift as a learnable function with shift parameters. paragraphs: Convolutional networks can improve accuracy by becoming deeper and wider, but their resource demands make deployment difficult in settings such as mobile applications. This paper examines the convolution operation itself as a place to reduce those demands. The authors show that a standard convolution can be decomposed into a spatial shift operation and a pointwise convolution.

To make that decomposition adaptable, they introduce the active shift layer. Its shift amounts are expressed through learnable parameters, allowing the network to adjust the movement of features during training. These parameters can be optimized through backpropagation as part of the full network, and the authors describe the layer as capable of providing optimal shift values.

The layer is incorporated into a lightweight, fast network that the authors report surpasses existing state-of-the-art networks. The significance is the connection between an operational decomposition and a trainable architecture: spatial shifting becomes something the model can learn alongside its other parameters. This gives the proposed efficient network a mechanism for adapting its convolution-like processing to the task.
summary.tldr: A learnable spatial-shift layer helps turn decomposed convolutions into a lightweight network with strong reported performance.

title: Constructing Fast Network through Deconstruction of Convolution

abstract: Variational approximation has been widely used in large-scale Bayesian inference recently, the simplest kind of which involves imposing a mean field assumption to approximate complicated latent structures. Despite the computational scalability of mean field, theoretical studies of its loss function surface and the convergence behavior of iterative updates for optimizing the loss are far from complete. In this paper, we focus on the problem of community detection for a simple two-class Stochastic Blockmodel (SBM). Using batch co-ordinate ascent (BCAVI) for updates, we give a complete characterization of all the critical points and show different convergence behaviors with respect to initializations. When the parameters are known, we show a significant proportion of random initializations will converge to ground truth. On the other hand, when the parameters themselves need to be estimated, a random initialization will converge to an uninformative local optimum.

In this paper, we focus on the problem of community detection for a simple two-class Stochastic Blockmodel (SBM). paragraphs: Mean-field variational inference simplifies complicated latent-variable models to make Bayesian computation more scalable. Yet computational convenience does not by itself explain where iterative optimization will end up. This paper examines that issue for community detection in a simple stochastic blockmodel with two classes, focusing on the loss landscape and the role of initialization.

Using batch coordinate ascent variational inference, the authors characterize all critical points and describe how convergence changes with the starting point. This connects the geometry of the objective to the behavior of the actual update procedure. The analysis is specific enough to distinguish successful recovery of the underlying communities from convergence to a solution that reveals no useful community information.

When the model parameters are known, a significant proportion of random initializations converge to the ground truth. When those parameters must also be estimated, random initialization instead converges to an uninformative local optimum in the studied setting. The result shows that jointly estimating parameters can substantially change optimization behavior, even within this simple community-detection model.
summary.tldr: For a two-class stochastic blockmodel, mean-field convergence depends sharply on initialization and whether model parameters are known or estimated.

title: Mean Field for the Stochastic Blockmodel: Optimization Landscape and Convergence Issues

abstract: We study the problem of multiset prediction. The goal of multiset prediction is to train a predictor that maps an input to a multiset consisting of multiple items. Unlike existing problems in supervised learning, such as classification, ranking and sequence generation, there is no known order among items in a target multiset, and each item in the multiset may appear more than once, making this problem extremely challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel multiset loss function by viewing this problem from the perspective of sequential decision making. The proposed multiset loss function is empirically evaluated on two families of datasets, one synthetic and the other real, with varying levels of difficulty, against various baseline loss functions including reinforcement learning, sequence, and aggregated distribution matching loss functions. The experiments reveal the effectiveness of the proposed loss function over the others.

paragraphs: Multiset prediction maps an input to a collection of items in which order is unspecified and repeated items are allowed. Both features matter: the predictor must handle which items occur and their multiplicities without assuming a known target ordering. This makes the task different from ordinary classification, ranking, and sequence generation.

The authors propose a loss function by viewing multiset prediction as sequential decision making. This perspective provides a way to organize the prediction process even though the target collection has no known order. The central contribution is the training objective, designed around the structure of a multiset rather than simply adopting an objective from a neighboring prediction task.

The loss is evaluated on synthetic and real dataset families with varying difficulty. Comparisons include objectives based on reinforcement learning, sequence prediction, and aggregated distribution matching. The experiments favor the proposed loss over these alternatives. These findings support treating unordered collections with repetitions as a distinct learning problem and designing the loss accordingly, with the reported effectiveness established through the evaluated datasets and comparisons.
summary.tldr: A sequential-decision-based loss improves multiset prediction in experiments involving unordered outputs with repeated items.

title: Loss Functions for Multiset Prediction

abstract: Learning generative models that span multiple data modalities, such as vision and language, is often motivated by the desire to learn more useful, generalisable representations that faithfully capture common underlying factors between the modalities. In this work, we characterise successful learning of such models as the fulfilment of four criteria: i) implicit latent decomposition into shared and private subspaces, ii) coherent joint generation over all modalities, iii) coherent cross-generation across individual modalities, and iv) improved model learning for individual modalities through multi-modal integration. Here, we propose a mixture-of-experts multi-modal variational autoencoder (MMVAE) for learning of generative models on different sets of modalities, including a challenging image <-> language dataset, and demonstrate its ability to satisfy all four criteria, both qualitatively and quantitatively.
originalAbstract: Learning generative models that span multiple data modalities, such as vision and language, is often motivated by the desire to learn more useful, generalisable representations that faithfully capture common underlying factors between the modalities. In this work, we characterise successful learning of such models as the fulfilment of four criteria: i) implicit latent decomposition into shared and private subspaces, ii) coherent joint generation over all modalities, iii) coherent cross-generation across individual modalities, and iv) improved model learning for individual modalities through multi-modal integration. Here, we propose a mixture-of-experts multi-modal variational autoencoder (MMVAE) for learning of generative models on different sets of modalities, including a challenging image <-> language dataset, and demonstrate its ability to satisfy all four criteria, both qualitatively and quantitatively.

paragraphs: A model trained across modalities such as images and language should capture what they share while retaining information specific to each. This paper turns that broad ambition into four criteria for successful multimodal generative learning. It then proposes a mixture-of-experts multimodal variational autoencoder, MMVAE, and evaluates it against those criteria.

The first criterion is an implicit separation of shared and private information in the latent representation. The next two concern generation: samples produced jointly across modalities should agree, and generation of one modality from another should also be coherent. The fourth asks whether combining modalities improves learning for the individual modalities themselves.

The authors study different modality combinations, including a challenging image-language dataset, and report qualitative and quantitative evidence that MMVAE meets all four criteria. This gives the evaluation several complementary targets: representation structure, agreement in jointly generated outputs, cross-modal generation, and benefits to individual modalities. The findings support the proposed model across those aspects in the settings examined.
summary.tldr: MMVAE meets four proposed criteria for multimodal learning, spanning shared representations, coherent generation, and improved individual-modality learning.

title: Variational Mixture-of-Experts Autoencoders for Multi-Modal Deep Generative Models

abstract: Quantum information is a promising new paradigm for fast computations that can provide substantial speedups for many algorithms we use today. Among them, quantum machine learning is one of the most exciting applications of quantum computers. In this paper, we introduce q-means, a new quantum algorithm for clustering. It is a quantum version of a robust k-means algorithm, with similar convergence and precision guarantees. We also design a method to pick the initial centroids equivalent to the classical k-means++ method. Our algorithm provides currently an exponential speedup in the number of points of the dataset, compared to the classical k-means algorithm. We also detail the running time of q-means when applied to well-clusterable datasets. We provide a detailed runtime analysis and numerical simulations for specific datasets. Along with the algorithm, the theorems and tools introduced in this paper can be reused for various applications in quantum machine learning.

Among them, quantum machine learning is one of the most exciting applications of quantum computers. In this paper, we introduce q-means, a new quantum algorithm for clustering. Our algorithm provides currently an exponential speedup in the number of points of the dataset, compared to the classical k-means algorithm. We also detail the running time of q-means when applied to well-clusterable datasets. We provide a detailed runtime analysis and numerical simulations for specific datasets. Along with the algorithm, the theorems and tools introduced in this paper can be reused for various applications in quantum machine learning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces q-means, a quantum clustering algorithm based on a robust version of k-means. It aims to accelerate clustering while retaining convergence and precision guarantees similar to that robust classical procedure. The authors also design a method for selecting initial cluster centroids equivalent to classical k-means++ initialization.

The stated speedup is exponential in the number of data points compared with classical k-means. This identifies the particular aspect of dataset size in which the runtime improves. The paper provides a detailed runtime analysis and separately describes the running time for well-clusterable datasets, connecting the computational analysis to the structure of the clustering problem.

Numerical simulations on specific datasets accompany the algorithm and theoretical results. Together, these components examine its behavior as well as its computational guarantees. Beyond the clustering method itself, the authors present theorems and tools intended for reuse in other quantum machine learning applications. The central contribution combines quantum acceleration with attention to initialization, convergence, and precision.
summary.tldr: Q-means offers quantum clustering with an exponential speedup in dataset size and guarantees similar to robust k-means.

title: q-means: A quantum algorithm for unsupervised machine learning

abstract: We consider a stochastic linear bandit model in which the available actions correspond to arbitrary context vectors whose associated rewards follow a non-stationary linear regression model. In this setting, the unknown regression parameter is allowed to vary in time. To address this problem, we propose D-LinUCB, a novel optimistic algorithm based on discounted linear regression, where exponential weights are used to smoothly forget the past. This involves studying the deviations of the sequential weighted least-squares estimator under generic assumptions. As a by-product, we obtain novel deviation results that can be used beyond non-stationary environments. We provide theoretical guarantees on the behavior of D-LinUCB in both slowly-varying and abruptly-changing environments. We obtain an upper bound on the dynamic regret that is of order d B T^{1/3}T^{2/3}, where B T is a measure of non-stationarity (d and T being, respectively, dimension and horizon). This rate is known to be optimal. We also illustrate the empirical performance of D-LinUCB and compare it with recently proposed alternatives in simulated environments.

paragraphs: In a linear bandit problem, actions have contextual features and rewards depend on an unknown linear relationship. This paper allows that relationship to change over time. Consequently, observations collected long ago may describe a different reward environment, creating a need to adapt learning without discarding useful experience too abruptly.

The proposed algorithm, D-LinUCB, combines optimism with discounted linear regression. Exponential weights gradually reduce the influence of older observations, allowing the reward estimate to respond to change. The analysis develops deviation results for sequential weighted least-squares estimators under generic assumptions. These statistical results also have potential uses outside the nonstationary setting motivating the algorithm.

The authors give theoretical guarantees for both slowly varying environments and environments with abrupt changes. Their dynamic-regret bound depends on feature dimension, interaction horizon, and a measure of nonstationarity, and they identify the resulting rate as optimal. Simulated experiments compare D-LinUCB with recently proposed alternatives, illustrating how gradual forgetting performs when the underlying reward relationship evolves.
summary.tldr: D-LinUCB uses exponentially discounted regression to track changing rewards, with theoretical guarantees for gradual and abrupt environmental changes.

title: Weighted Linear Bandits for Non-Stationary Environments

abstract: Topic models are becoming increasingly relevant probabilistic models for dimensionality reduction of text data, inferring topics that capture meaningful themes of frequently co-occurring terms. We formulate topic modelling as an information retrieval task, where the goal is, based on the latent topic representation, to capture relevant term co-occurrence patterns. We evaluate performance for this task rigorously with regard to two types of errors, false negatives and positives, based on the well-known precision-recall trade-off and provide a statistical model that allows the user to balance between the contributions of the different error types. When the user focuses solely on the contribution of false negatives ignoring false positives altogether our proposed model reduces to a standard topic model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the proposed approach is effective and infers more coherent topics than existing related approaches.

paragraphs: Topic models compress text into latent themes built from words that frequently occur together. This paper reframes their job as an information retrieval task: the topic representation should recover relevant patterns of term co-occurrence. That perspective makes it possible to distinguish two different kinds of mistakes in the representation.

A false negative misses a relevant co-occurrence pattern, while a false positive retrieves an irrelevant one. The authors evaluate these errors through the precision–recall trade-off and develop a statistical model that lets users control their relative contributions. This gives topic modeling an explicit way to balance recovering relevant patterns against introducing unwanted ones.

The model reduces to a standard topic model when the user considers only false negatives and ignores false positives. This relationship explains how the proposed formulation extends an existing approach through a broader treatment of errors. Extensive experiments find that the method is effective and produces more coherent topics than related methods, supporting the value of considering both sides of the retrieval trade-off.
summary.tldr: Treating topic modeling as retrieval enables explicit precision–recall control and yields more coherent topics in the reported experiments.

title: Precision-Recall Balanced Topic Modelling

abstract: In deep neural nets, lower level embedding layers account for a large portion of the total number of parameters. Tikhonov regularization, graph-based regularization, and hard parameter sharing are approaches that introduce explicit biases into training in a hope to reduce statistical complexity. Alternatively, we propose stochastically shared embeddings (SSE), a data-driven approach to regularizing embedding layers, which stochastically transitions between embeddings during stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Because SSE integrates seamlessly with existing SGD algorithms, it can be used with only minor modifications when training large scale neural networks. We develop two versions of SSE: SSE-Graph using knowledge graphs of embeddings; SSE-SE using no prior information. We provide theoretical guarantees for our method and show its empirical effectiveness on 6 distinct tasks, from simple neural networks with one hidden layer in recommender systems, to the transformer and BERT in natural languages. We find that when used along with widely-used regularization methods such as weight decay and dropout, our proposed SSE can further reduce overfitting, which often leads to more favorable generalization results.

paragraphs: Embedding layers can contain a large share of a neural network's parameters, making them an important target for regularization. This paper proposes stochastically shared embeddings, or SSE, as a data-driven way to constrain their learning. The method randomly transitions between embeddings during stochastic gradient descent.

The authors develop two versions. SSE-Graph uses a knowledge graph relating embeddings, while SSE-SE requires no prior information. This makes the approach applicable within large neural-network training procedures without requiring an entirely separate optimization method.

The paper supplies theoretical guarantees and evaluates SSE on six tasks, ranging from recommender systems with simple networks to language models using transformers and BERT. The authors find that SSE can reduce overfitting further when combined with weight decay and dropout, often improving generalization. The empirical message is that regularizing how embeddings are used during training can complement established regularizers across the tested tasks and architectures.
summary.tldr: Stochastically shared embeddings regularize embedding layers through random transitions during training and can complement dropout and weight decay.

title: Stochastic Shared Embeddings: Data-driven Regularization of Embedding Layers

abstract: In Stackelberg security games when information about the attacker's payoffs is uncertain, algorithms have been proposed to learn the optimal defender commitment by interacting with the attacker and observing their best responses. In this paper, we show that, however, these algorithms can be easily manipulated if the attacker responds untruthfully. As a key finding, attacker manipulation normally leads to the defender learning a maximin strategy, which effectively renders the learning attempt meaningless as to compute a maximin strategy requires no additional information about the other player at all. We then apply a game-theoretic framework at a higher level to counteract such manipulation, in which the defender commits to a policy that specifies her strategy commitment according to the learned information. We provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute the optimal such policy, and in addition, a heuristic approach that applies even when the attacker's payoff space is infinite or completely unknown. Empirical evaluation shows that our approaches can improve the defender's utility significantly as compared to the situation when attacker manipulation is ignored.

paragraphs: In Stackelberg security games, a defender may learn about an attacker's unknown payoffs by observing responses to defensive commitments. This paper shows that such learning algorithms can be manipulated when the attacker responds untruthfully. The observations used for learning are themselves choices made by a strategic participant.

The authors find that manipulation normally leads the defender to learn a maximin strategy. Such a strategy can be computed without additional information about the attacker, so this outcome undermines the purpose of learning. The finding motivates explicitly accounting for how attackers may influence the information a defender receives.

The proposed response moves commitment to a higher level: the defender commits to a policy specifying how learned information determines the eventual strategy. The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm for the optimal policy and a heuristic applicable even to infinite or completely unknown attacker payoff spaces. Empirical evaluation shows significant utility improvements compared with ignoring manipulation, supporting the value of designing the learning process around strategic responses.
summary.tldr: A defender can counter strategic manipulation of learning by committing to a policy governing how learned information changes its strategy.

title: Manipulating a Learning Defender and Ways to Counteract

abstract: With latent variables, stochastic recurrent models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in modeling sound-wave sequence. However, opposite results are also observed in other domains, where standard recurrent networks often outperform stochastic models. To better understand this discrepancy, we re-examine the roles of latent variables in stochastic recurrent models for speech density estimation. Our analysis reveals that under the restriction of fully factorized output distribution in previous evaluations, the stochastic variants were implicitly leveraging intra-step correlation but the deterministic recurrent baselines were prohibited to do so, resulting in an unfair comparison. To correct the unfairness, we remove such restriction in our re-examination, where all the models can explicitly leverage intra-step correlation with an auto-regressive structure. Over a diverse set of univariate and multivariate sequential data, including human speech, MIDI music, handwriting trajectory, and frame-permuted speech, our results show that stochastic recurrent models fail to deliver the performance advantage claimed in previous work. %exhibit any practical advantage despite the claimed theoretical superiority. In contrast, standard recurrent models equipped with an auto-regressive output distribution consistently perform better, dramatically advancing the state-of-the-art results on three speech datasets.

paragraphs: Stochastic recurrent models with latent variables had shown strong results for sound-wave sequences, while ordinary recurrent networks often performed better elsewhere. This paper re-examines that discrepancy by looking at how earlier speech density-estimation comparisons represented dependencies within a single time step.

The authors find that a fully factorized output distribution imposed an unequal restriction. Stochastic models could implicitly exploit correlations among values within a step through their latent variables, while deterministic baselines could not. They revise the comparison so that every model can explicitly represent those correlations using an autoregressive output structure.

Across data including speech, MIDI music, handwriting trajectories, and frame-permuted speech, stochastic recurrent models no longer deliver the previously claimed advantage. Standard recurrent models with autoregressive outputs consistently perform better in the reported evaluation and substantially advance results on three speech datasets. The findings attribute the earlier comparison’s imbalance to unequal access to within-step correlations, changing how the observed benefit of latent variables should be interpreted.
summary.tldr: Allowing all models to represent within-step correlations removes the reported stochastic-model advantage and favors standard recurrent models in the evaluated tasks.

title: Re-examination of the Role of Latent Variables in Sequence Modeling

abstract: We unify the theory of optimal control of transport equations with the practice of training and testing of ResNets. Based on this unified viewpoint, we propose a simple yet effective ResNets ensemble algorithm to boost the accuracy of the robustly trained model on both clean and adversarial images. The proposed algorithm consists of two components: First, we modify the base ResNets by injecting a variance specified Gaussian noise to the output of each residual mapping. Second, we average over the production of multiple jointly trained modified ResNets to get the final prediction. These two steps give an approximation to the Feynman-Kac formula for representing the solution of a convection-diffusion equation. For the CIFAR10 benchmark, this simple algorithm leads to a robust model with a natural accuracy of {\bf 85.62}\% on clean images and a robust accuracy of ${\bf 57.94 \%}$ under the 20 iterations of the IFGSM attack, which outperforms the current state-of-the-art in defending against IFGSM attack on the CIFAR10.

paragraphs: The paper connects the training and testing of residual networks with optimal control of transport equations. It uses this mathematical viewpoint to design an ensemble intended to improve a robustly trained model on both ordinary images and adversarially modified images. The theory motivates concrete changes to the networks and their predictions.

First, each residual mapping has Gaussian noise with a specified variance added to its output. Second, multiple modified ResNets are trained jointly, and their outputs are averaged to produce the final prediction. Together, these operations approximate the Feynman-Kac representation of a convection-diffusion equation's solution, linking noisy network computation and averaging to the underlying mathematical formulation.

On CIFAR10, the method reaches 85.62% accuracy on clean images and 57.94% robust accuracy under a 20-iteration IFGSM attack. The authors report that this exceeds the existing state of the art for defending against IFGSM on that benchmark. The evidence therefore supports improved clean and attack-specific performance for the evaluated ensemble.
summary.tldr: A mathematically motivated ensemble of noisy ResNets improves clean-image and IFGSM-attack accuracy on CIFAR10.

title: ResNets Ensemble via the Feynman-Kac Formalism to Improve Natural and Robust Accuracies

abstract: Matrix factorization (MF) is a versatile learning method that has found wide applications in various data-driven disciplines. Still, many MF algorithms do not adequately scale with the size of available datasets and/or lack interpretability. To improve the computational efficiency of the method, an online (streaming) MF algorithm was proposed in Mairal et al., 2010. To enable data interpretability, a constrained version of MF, termed convex MF, was introduced in Ding et al., 2010. In the latter work, the basis vectors are required to lie in the convex hull of the data samples, thereby ensuring that every basis can be interpreted as a weighted combination of data samples. No current algorithmic solutions for online convex MF are known as it is challenging to find adequate convex bases without having access to the complete dataset. We address both problems by proposing the first online convex MF algorithm that maintains a collection of constant-size sets of representative data samples needed for interpreting each of the basis (Ding et al., 2010) and has the same almost sure convergence guarantees as the online learning algorithm of Mairal et al., 2010. Our proof techniques combine random coordinate descent algorithms with specialized quasi-martingale convergence analysis. Experiments on synthetic and real world datasets show significant computational savings of the proposed online convex MF method compared to classical convex MF. Since the proposed method maintains small representative sets of data samples needed for convex interpretations, it is related to a body of work in theoretical computer science, pertaining to generating point sets (Blum et al., 2016), and in computer vision, pertaining to archetypal analysis (Mei et al., 2018). Nevertheless, it differs from these lines of work both in terms of the objective and algorithmic implementations.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization represents data using learned basis vectors, but scalability and interpretability can pull in different directions. Convex matrix factorization makes each basis a weighted combination of observed samples, giving it a direct connection to the data. Maintaining that property in a streaming algorithm is difficult without access to the complete dataset.

This paper proposes an online convex factorization method that keeps constant-size collections of representative samples for interpreting each basis. These small collections preserve the connection between basis vectors and actual observations while supporting online updates. The method combines the streaming goal of online matrix factorization with the sample-based interpretation of convex factorization.

The authors establish the same almost-sure convergence guarantees as the earlier online learning algorithm they build upon, using random coordinate descent and specialized quasi-martingale analysis. Synthetic and real-data experiments show significant computational savings compared with classical convex matrix factorization. The representative collections are therefore both an interpretability device and a practical part of making convex factorization work with data arriving over time.
summary.tldr: An online convex matrix factorization method maintains small representative sample sets to combine streaming computation with interpretable basis vectors.

title: Online Convex Matrix Factorization with Representative Regions

abstract: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) forms a fundamental building block in many applications for learning over sensitive data. Two standard approaches, privacy amplification by subsampling, and privacy amplification by shuffling, permit adding lower noise in DP-SGD than via na\"{\i}ve schemes. A key assumption in both these approaches is that the elements in the data set can be uniformly sampled, or be uniformly permuted --- constraints that may become prohibitive when the data is processed in a decentralized or distributed fashion. In this paper, we focus on conducting iterative methods like DP-SGD in the setting of federated learning (FL) wherein the data is distributed among many devices (clients). Our main contribution is the \emph{random check-in} distributed protocol, which crucially relies only on randomized participation decisions made locally and independently by each client. It has privacy/accuracy trade-offs similar to privacy amplification by subsampling/shuffling. However, our method does not require server-initiated communication, or even knowledge of the population size. To our knowledge, this is the first privacy amplification tailored for a distributed learning framework, and it may have broader applicability beyond FL. Along the way, we improve the privacy guarantees of amplification by shuffling and show that, in practical regimes, this improvement allows for similar privacy and utility using data from an order of magnitude fewer users.

paragraphs: Differentially private training can benefit from random sampling or shuffling, which permits less noise for a privacy guarantee. Those approaches rely on uniform sampling or permutation of data, requirements that may be difficult when data is distributed across devices. This paper develops a participation protocol suited to that distributed setting.

In random check-ins, clients independently make local randomized decisions about whether to participate. The protocol achieves privacy–accuracy trade-offs similar to amplification through subsampling or shuffling. It does not require communication initiated by the server or knowledge of the population size, making the participation mechanism compatible with the federated setting considered by the authors.

The paper separately strengthens privacy guarantees for amplification by shuffling. In practical regimes, the improved analysis allows similar privacy and utility using an order of magnitude fewer users. Together, these contributions address both how distributed participation can be organized and how existing shuffling guarantees can be sharpened. The authors also suggest that random check-ins may have applications beyond federated learning.
summary.tldr: Independent random client check-ins provide privacy amplification for distributed learning without server-initiated communication or a known population size.

title: Privacy Amplification via Random Check-Ins

abstract: A finite-state machine (FSM) is a computation model to process binary strings in sequential circuits. Hence, a single-input linear FSM is conventionally used to implement complex single-input functions , such as tanh and exponentiation functions, in stochastic computing (SC) domain where continuous values are represented by sequences of random bits. In this paper, we introduce a method that can train a multi-layer FSM-based network where FSMs are connected to every FSM in the previous and the next layer. We show that the proposed FSM-based network can synthesize multi-input complex functions such as 2D Gabor filters and can perform non-sequential tasks such as image classifications on stochastic streams with no multiplication since FSMs are implemented by look-up tables only. Inspired by the capability of FSMs in processing binary streams, we then propose an FSM-based model that can process time series data when performing temporal tasks such as character-level language modeling. Unlike long short-term memories (LSTMs) that unroll the network for each input time step and perform back-propagation on the unrolled network, our FSM-based model requires to backpropagate gradients only for the current input time step while it is still capable of learning long-term dependencies. Therefore, our FSM-based model can learn extremely long-term dependencies as it requires 1/l memory storage during training compared to LSTMs, where l is the number of time steps. Moreover, our FSM-based model reduces the power consumption of training on a GPU by 33% compared to an LSTM model of the same size.

paragraphs: Finite-state machines process sequences of bits, and stochastic computing represents continuous values through random bit streams. This paper introduces a way to train multilayer networks of connected finite-state machines. The approach extends their use from single-input functions to more complex computations involving multiple inputs.

The authors show that these networks can synthesize functions such as two-dimensional Gabor filters and perform image classification on stochastic streams. These findings connect the model's training procedure to reduced memory and power requirements.
summary.tldr: Trainable finite-state-machine networks support multiplication-free stochastic computation and temporal learning with reported memory and power savings over LSTMs.

title: Training Linear Finite-State Machines

abstract: In this paper, we revisit and improve the convergence of policy gradient (PG), natural PG (NPG) methods, and their variance-reduced variants, under general smooth policy parametrizations. More specifically, with the Fisher information matrix of the policy being positive definite: i) we show that a state-of-the-art variance-reduced PG method, which has only been shown to converge to stationary points, converges to the globally optimal value up to some inherent function approximation error due to policy parametrization; ii) we show that NPG enjoys a lower sample complexity; iii) we propose SRVR-NPG, which incorporates variance-reduction into the NPG update. Our improvements follow from an observation that the convergence of (variance-reduced) PG and NPG methods can improve each other: the stationary convergence analysis of PG can be applied on NPG as well, and the global convergence analysis of NPG can help to establish the global convergence of (variance-reduced) PG methods. Our analysis carefully integrates the advantages of these two lines of works. Thanks to this improvement, we have also made variance-reduction for NPG possible for the first time, with both global convergence and an efficient finite-sample complexity.

paragraphs: This paper strengthens theoretical guarantees for policy gradient and natural policy gradient methods, including versions that reduce sampling variability. The central question is whether these methods merely reach a point where local improvement stalls, or can approach the best achievable reward. The analysis considers general smooth policy parameterizations and assumes that the policy’s Fisher information matrix is positive definite.

The key move is to combine two previously separate lines of reasoning. Arguments about reaching stationary points with policy gradients also help analyze natural policy gradients. Conversely, arguments about global convergence for natural policy gradients help establish stronger guarantees for variance-reduced policy gradients. This connection upgrades an existing method’s guarantee to global optimality up to an inherent policy-approximation error.

The authors also establish a lower sample complexity for natural policy gradients and introduce SRVR-NPG, which adds variance reduction to their updates. Its analysis provides global convergence and efficient finite-sample complexity. These findings strengthen what the methods can be guaranteed to achieve under the stated assumptions, while retaining the error associated with the chosen policy representation.
summary.tldr: Combining policy-gradient analyses yields stronger conditional convergence guarantees and a variance-reduced natural policy-gradient method.

title: An Improved Analysis of (Variance-Reduced) Policy Gradient and Natural Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: Over-parameterized models, such as DeepNets and ConvNets, form a class of models that are routinely adopted in a wide variety of applications, and for which Bayesian inference is desirable but extremely challenging. Variational inference offers the tools to tackle this challenge in a scalable way and with some degree of flexibility on the approximation, but for overparameterized models this is challenging due to the over-regularization property of the variational objective. Inspired by the literature on kernel methods, and in particular on structured approximations of distributions of random matrices, this paper proposes Walsh-Hadamard Variational Inference (WHVI), which uses Walsh-Hadamardbased factorization strategies to reduce the parameterization and accelerate computations, thus avoiding over-regularization issues with the variational objective. Extensive theoretical and empirical analyses demonstrate that WHVI yields considerable speedups and model reductions compared to other techniques to carry out approximate inference for over-parameterized models, and ultimately show how advances in kernel methods can be translated into advances in approximate Bayesian inference for Deep Learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference is appealing for large neural networks but difficult to perform efficiently. Variational inference offers scalable approximations, yet its objective can over-regularize over-parameterized models. This paper addresses that problem by changing how the approximation is represented, drawing inspiration from structured random-matrix methods developed for kernels.

Walsh-Hadamard Variational Inference, or WHVI, uses Walsh-Hadamard-based factorizations to reduce the number of parameters and accelerate computation. The structured representation is intended to avoid the over-regularization issues of the variational objective. Its design links the size and computational organization of the approximation to the behavior of Bayesian learning.

The authors provide extensive theoretical and empirical analyses, reporting substantial speedups and model reductions compared with other approximate-inference techniques for over-parameterized models. The contribution therefore concerns both the cost of inference and the suitability of its parameterization. More broadly, it demonstrates a concrete route by which advances in kernel methods can improve approximate Bayesian inference for deep and convolutional neural networks.
summary.tldr: WHVI uses structured Walsh-Hadamard factorizations to reduce Bayesian neural-network inference costs and address variational over-regularization.

title: Walsh-Hadamard Variational Inference for Bayesian Deep Learning

abstract: Learning from spatio-temporal data has numerous applications such as human-behavior analysis, object tracking, video compression, and physics simulation. However, existing methods still perform poorly on challenging video tasks such as long-term forecasting. This is because these kinds of challenging tasks require learning long-term spatio-temporal correlations in the video sequence. In this paper, we propose a higher-order convolutional LSTM model that can efficiently learn these correlations, along with a succinct representations of the history. This is accomplished through a novel tensor train module that performs prediction by combining convolutional features across time. To make this feasible in terms of computation and memory requirements, we propose a novel convolutional tensor-train decomposition of the higher-order model. This decomposition reduces the model complexity by jointly approximating a sequence of convolutional kernels as a low-rank tensor-train factorization. As a result, our model outperforms existing approaches, but uses only a fraction of parameters, including the baseline models. Our results achieve state-of-the-art performance in a wide range of applications and datasets, including the multi-steps video prediction on the Moving-MNIST-2 and KTH action datasets as well as early activity recognition on the Something-Something V2 dataset.

paragraphs: Predicting a video far into the future requires learning relationships that extend across both space and time. The paper addresses this challenge with a higher-order convolutional LSTM that combines information from a history of convolutional features. Its aim is to capture longer-term correlations while keeping the representation of that history compact.

The key component is a tensor-train module that combines features across time for prediction. A direct higher-order model would impose substantial computation and memory demands, so the authors introduce a convolutional tensor-train decomposition. It jointly approximates a sequence of convolutional kernels through a low-rank factorization, reducing the complexity of modeling those temporal relationships.

The authors report stronger performance than existing approaches while using only a fraction of their parameters, including those of baseline models. They report state-of-the-art results for multistep video prediction on Moving-MNIST-2 and KTH, and early activity recognition on Something-Something V2. These findings support the idea that a compact factorization can make richer temporal modeling practical, improving the evaluated tasks without requiring a correspondingly large parameter count.
summary.tldr: A tensor-train convolutional LSTM captures longer-term video relationships with fewer parameters and reports strong prediction and early-recognition results.

title: Convolutional Tensor-Train LSTM for Spatio-Temporal Learning

abstract: The present contribution deals with decentralized policy evaluation in multi-agent Markov decision processes using temporal-difference (TD) methods with linear function approximation for scalability. The agents cooperate to estimate the value function of such a process by observing continual state transitions of a shared environment over the graph of interconnected nodes (agents), along with locally private rewards. Different from existing consensus-type TD algorithms, the approach here develops a simple decentralized TD tracker by wedding TD learning with gradient tracking techniques. The non-asymptotic properties of the novel TD tracker are established for both independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) as well as Markovian transitions through a unifying multistep Lyapunov analysis. In contrast to the prior art, the novel algorithm forgoes the limiting error bounds on the number of agents, which endows it with performance comparable to that of centralized TD methods that are the sharpest known to date.

paragraphs: The paper studies policy evaluation by a network of cooperating agents. Each agent observes transitions in a shared environment but has locally private rewards. Together, the agents seek to estimate the policy's value function. Linear function approximation makes this estimation scalable by representing values through a limited collection of features.

The proposed algorithm combines temporal-difference learning with gradient tracking. This produces a decentralized TD tracker that goes beyond the consensus-style approaches discussed in the abstract. The central design issue is how agents can coordinate their learning across the communication graph while working with rewards that are observed locally.

The authors establish finite-time properties through a unified multistep Lyapunov analysis, covering both independent transitions and transitions with Markovian dependence. Their analysis avoids the limiting dependence on the number of agents present in earlier error bounds and yields performance comparable to the sharpest centralized TD results described in the abstract. This is significant because it gives a theoretical account of decentralized evaluation after finite amounts of learning, including when successive observations are dependent.
summary.tldr: Combining TD learning with gradient tracking gives decentralized policy evaluation finite-time guarantees comparable to strong centralized results.

title: Decentralized TD Tracking with Linear Function Approximation and its Finite-Time Analysis

abstract: Estimating counterfactual outcome of different treatments from observational data is an important problem to assist decision making in a variety of fields. Among the various forms of treatment specification, bundle treatment has been widely adopted in many scenarios, such as recommendation systems and online marketing. The bundle treatment usually can be abstracted as a high dimensional binary vector, which makes it more challenging for researchers to remove the confounding bias in observational data. In this work, we assume the existence of low dimensional latent structure underlying bundle treatment. Via the learned latent representations of treatments, we propose a novel variational sample re-weighting (VSR) method to eliminate confounding bias by decorrelating the treatments and confounders. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that the predictive model trained on this re-weighted dataset can achieve more accurate counterfactual outcome prediction.

paragraphs: Counterfactual prediction asks what outcome would occur under a different treatment than the one observed. This paper studies treatments made up of bundles, such as combinations used in recommendation or online marketing. A bundle can be represented by many binary choices, making it difficult to separate treatment effects from confounding patterns in observational data.

The approach assumes that these high-dimensional bundles have an underlying low-dimensional structure. It learns latent treatment representations and uses them in a variational sample re-weighting method called VSR. The re-weighting is designed to remove confounding bias by decorrelating treatments and confounders, changing how much each observed example contributes to subsequent learning.

A predictive model is then trained on the re-weighted dataset. The authors report extensive experiments showing more accurate counterfactual outcome prediction. The central idea is to make bundle adjustment manageable through a compact treatment representation, rather than treating every component combination independently. The assumed latent structure is therefore an explicit part of the method's formulation and of how it addresses the high-dimensional treatment problem.
summary.tldr: Assuming low-dimensional structure in treatment bundles, VSR reweights observational samples to decorrelate treatments and confounders and improve counterfactual prediction.

title: Counterfactual Prediction for Bundle Treatment

abstract: Robustness against adversarial attacks has recently been at the forefront of algorithmic design for machine learning tasks. In the adversarial streaming model, an adversary gives an algorithm a sequence of adaptively chosen updates $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ as a data stream. The goal of the algorithm is to compute or approximate some predetermined function for every prefix of the adversarial stream, but the adversary may generate future updates based on previous outputs of the algorithm. In particular, the adversary may gradually learn the random bits internally used by an algorithm to manipulate dependencies in the input. This is especially problematic as many important problems in the streaming model require randomized algorithms, as they are known to not admit any deterministic algorithms that use sublinear space. In this paper, we introduce adversarially robust streaming algorithms for central machine learning and algorithmic tasks, such as regression and clustering, as well as their more general counterparts, subspace embedding, low-rank approximation, and coreset construction. For regression and other numerical linear algebra related tasks, we consider the row arrival streaming model. Our results are based on a simple, but powerful, observation that many importance sampling-based algorithms give rise to adversarial robustness which is in contrast to sketching based algorithms, which are very prevalent in the streaming literature but suffer from adversarial attacks. In addition, we show that the well-known merge and reduce paradigm in streaming is adversarially robust. Since the merge and reduce paradigm allows coreset constructions in the streaming setting, we thus obtain robust algorithms for $k$-means, $k$-median, $k$-center, Bregman clustering, projective clustering, principal component analysis (PCA) and non-negative matrix factorization. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first adversarially robust results for these problems yet require no new algorithmic implementations. Finally, we empirically confirm the robustness of our algorithms on various adversarial attacks and demonstrate that by contrast, some common existing algorithms are not robust.

paragraphs: A streaming algorithm processes incoming data while retaining a limited summary. This becomes harder when an adversary chooses future inputs after observing earlier outputs. Those outputs can reveal information about the algorithm’s randomness, allowing the adversary to exploit dependencies that would not arise in a fixed, independently chosen stream.

The paper shows that many algorithms based on importance sampling remain reliable under this adaptive interaction. It develops robust methods for regression, clustering, and related numerical tasks, including low-rank approximation and subspace embedding. For regression and the other numerical linear algebra problems, the analysis uses a setting in which matrix rows arrive sequentially.

The authors also establish robustness of the merge-and-reduce strategy, extending the result to streaming coreset constructions for several clustering and matrix problems. These guarantees can apply without new algorithmic implementations. Experiments support robustness against the attacks studied and show failures of some common alternatives. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical explanation of existing methods’ resilience and a route to robust streaming algorithms.
summary.tldr: Importance sampling and merge-and-reduce provide adversarial robustness for a broad range of streaming learning algorithms.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Streaming Algorithms through Importance Sampling

abstract: To deal with ambiguities in partial multilabel learning (PML), state-of-the-art methods perform disambiguation by identifying ground-truth labels directly. However, there is an essential question:“Can the ground-truth labels be identified precisely?". If yes, “How can the ground-truth labels be found?". This paper provides affirmative answers to these questions. Instead of adopting hand-made heuristic strategy, we propose a novel Mutual Information Label Identification for Partial Multilabel Learning (MILI-PML), which is derived from a clear probabilistic formulation and could be easily interpreted theoretically from the mutual information perspective, as well as naturally incorporates the feature/label relevancy considerations. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets clearly demonstrate the superiorities of the proposed MILI-PML.

paragraphs: Partial multi-label learning involves ambiguity about which labels truly apply to an example. Existing methods try to resolve that ambiguity by directly identifying ground-truth labels. This paper examines the foundation of that process, asking whether precise identification is possible and how a method can carry it out.

The proposed approach, MILI-PML, derives label identification from a probabilistic formulation and interprets it through mutual information. It also incorporates the relevance between input features and labels. This connects the disambiguation decision to relationships present in the data, giving the procedure a theoretical interpretation instead of relying on a manually designed heuristic.

The authors present affirmative answers to their identification questions through this framework and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets. Their extensive experiments show advantages over the compared approaches. The significance is the combination of a principled account of label identification with empirical evidence for the resulting algorithm. Feature-label relevance becomes part of the formulation itself, providing a coherent basis for deciding which ambiguous labels to retain.
summary.tldr: MILI-PML uses a probabilistic, mutual-information-based formulation to identify true labels within ambiguous multi-label supervision.

title: Understanding Partial Multi-Label Learning via Mutual Information

abstract: This paper considers two fundamental sequential decision-making problems: the problem of prediction with expert advice and the multi-armed bandit problem. We focus on stochastic regimes in which an adversary may corrupt losses, and we investigate what level of robustness can be achieved against adversarial corruption. The main contribution of this paper is to show that optimal robustness can be expressed by a square-root dependency on the amount of corruption. More precisely, we show that two classes of algorithms, anytime Hedge with decreasing learning rate and algorithms with second-order regret bounds, achieve $O( \frac{\log N}{\Delta} + \sqrt{ \frac{C \log N }{\Delta} } )$-regret, where $N, \Delta$, and $C$ represent the number of experts, the gap parameter, and the corruption level, respectively. We further provide a matching lower bound, which means that this regret bound is tight up to a constant factor. For the multi-armed bandit problem, we also provide a nearly-tight lower bound up to a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: This paper asks how robust sequential decision-making can be when an adversary corrupts losses in an otherwise stochastic setting. It considers prediction with expert advice and multi-armed bandits. The objective is to characterize the unavoidable performance cost of corruption, rather than merely show that a particular algorithm tolerates some corrupted observations.

For expert prediction, the authors analyze anytime Hedge with decreasing learning rates and algorithms satisfying second-order regret bounds. Their regret guarantee combines an uncorrupted term depending on the number of experts and the gap parameter with an additional term growing as the square root of the corruption level. Thus, corruption enters the guarantee through a sublinear dependence.

A matching lower bound shows that the expert-prediction guarantee is tight up to a constant factor. This establishes that the square-root corruption dependence captures optimal robustness in the studied setting. For multi-armed bandits, the paper separately supplies a lower bound that is nearly tight, differing by a logarithmic factor. The two results have different precision, but both clarify fundamental limits on robustness.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal square-root corruption dependence for expert prediction and a nearly tight lower bound for corrupted stochastic bandits.

title: On Optimal Robustness to Adversarial Corruption in Online Decision Problems

abstract: BinaryConnect (BC) and its many variations have become the de facto standard for neural network quantization. However, our understanding of the inner workings of BC is still quite limited. We attempt to close this gap in four different aspects: (a) we show that existing quantization algorithms, including post-training quantization, are surprisingly similar to each other; (b) we argue for proximal maps as a natural family of quantizers that is both easy to design and analyze; (c) we refine the observation that BC is a special case of dual averaging, which itself is a special case of the generalized conditional gradient algorithm; (d) consequently, we propose ProxConnect (PC) as a generalization of BC and we prove its convergence properties by exploiting the established connections. We conduct experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, and verify that PC achieves competitive performance.

paragraphs: BinaryConnect is widely used as a foundation for neural-network quantization, yet its optimization behavior has been less well understood. This paper examines the mathematical relationships behind BinaryConnect and related methods. The authors show that algorithms often treated separately, including post-training quantization, have substantial similarities.

They argue that proximal maps provide a useful family of quantizers because they are comparatively straightforward to design and analyze. They also refine the connection between BinaryConnect and dual averaging, then place dual averaging within the broader generalized conditional-gradient framework. These links make established optimization ideas available for understanding quantized-network training.

Building on this analysis, the authors introduce ProxConnect as a generalization of BinaryConnect and prove convergence properties through the identified connections. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet find competitive performance. The contribution therefore combines a clearer account of existing methods with a new algorithm supported by theory and empirical evaluation. The experimental claim is competitiveness, while the mathematical contribution concerns how quantization methods can be organized and analyzed within shared optimization frameworks.
summary.tldr: ProxConnect generalizes BinaryConnect through proximal quantizers and established optimization connections, with convergence results and competitive experiments.

title: Demystifying and Generalizing BinaryConnect

abstract: In constrained multi-objective RL, the goal is to learn a policy that achieves the best performance specified by a multi-objective preference function under a constraint. We focus on the offline setting where the RL agent aims to learn the optimal policy from a given dataset. This scenario is common in real-world applications where interactions with the environment are expensive and the constraint violation is dangerous. For such a setting, we transform the original constrained problem into a primal-dual formulation, which is solved via dual gradient ascent. Moreover, we propose to combine such an approach with pessimism to overcome the uncertainty in offline data, which leads to our Pessimistic Dual Iteration (PEDI). We establish upper bounds on both the suboptimality and constraint violation for the policy learned by PEDI based on an arbitrary dataset, which proves that PEDI is provably sample efficient. We also specialize PEDI to the setting with linear function approximation. To the best of our knowledge, we propose the first provably efficient constrained multi-objective RL algorithm with offline data without any assumption on the coverage of the dataset.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a policy from a fixed dataset when performance involves multiple objectives and behavior must satisfy a constraint. A preference function determines how the objectives are combined. The offline setting matters when collecting new interactions is expensive or violating the constraint could be dangerous, so learning must work with the evidence already available.

The authors reformulate the constrained problem in primal-dual terms and solve it through dual gradient ascent. They combine this approach with pessimism to account for uncertainty in the offline data, producing Pessimistic Dual Iteration, or PEDI. Pessimism is central because uncertain estimates from a fixed dataset must be handled when assessing possible policies.

The analysis provides upper bounds on both performance suboptimality and constraint violation for the learned policy using an arbitrary dataset. The authors establish sample efficiency without assuming dataset coverage and also specialize the method to linear function approximation. These are guarantees that bound the two quantities; they do not claim that every dataset yields an exactly optimal policy with zero constraint violations.
summary.tldr: PEDI combines primal-dual optimization with pessimism to bound offline multi-objective policy suboptimality and constraint violation without a dataset coverage assumption.

title: Offline Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning via Pessimistic Dual Value Iteration

abstract: In the problems of image retrieval and few-shot classification, the mainstream approaches focus on learning a better feature representation. However, directly tackling the distance or similarity measure between images could also be efficient. To this end, we revisit the idea of re-ranking the top-k retrieved images in the context of image retrieval (e.g., the k-reciprocal nearest neighbors) and generalize this idea to transductive few-shot learning. We propose to meta-learn the re-ranking updates such that the similarity graph converges towards the target similarity graph induced by the image labels. Specifically, the re-ranking module takes as input an initial similarity graph between the query image and the contextual images using a pre-trained feature extractor, and predicts an improved similarity graph by leveraging the structure among the involved images. We show that our re-ranking approach can be applied to unseen images and can further boost existing approaches for both image retrieval and few-shot learning problems. Our approach operates either independently or in conjunction with classical re-ranking approaches, yielding clear and consistent improvements on image retrieval (CUB, Cars, SOP, rOxford5K and rParis6K) and transductive few-shot classification (Mini-ImageNet, tiered-ImageNet and CIFAR-FS) benchmarks. Our code is available at https://imagine.enpc.fr/~shenx/SSR/.

paragraphs: Image retrieval and few-shot classification often improve by learning stronger image representations. This paper instead focuses on refining similarities between images after an initial representation is available. It revisits re-ranking retrieved images and extends the idea to transductive few-shot classification, where relationships among the images being considered can inform predictions.

The method begins with a similarity graph built using a pretrained feature extractor. A learned re-ranking module examines the graph’s structure and predicts improved similarities. Its updates are meta-learned so that the graph moves toward a target similarity graph defined by image labels. This makes the relationships among contextual images part of the refinement process.

The authors show that the module applies to unseen images and can improve existing retrieval and few-shot methods. It works independently or alongside classical re-ranking techniques. Experiments report clear, consistent improvements across the listed image-retrieval and transductive classification benchmarks. The contribution demonstrates that learning how to revise image relationships can add value beyond the initial features used to construct them.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned re-ranking module refines image similarity graphs and improves retrieval and transductive few-shot classification.

title: Re-ranking for image retrieval and transductive few-shot classification

abstract: In overparametrized models, the noise in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly regularizes the optimization trajectory and determines which local minimum SGD converges to. Motivated by empirical studies that demonstrate that training with noisy labels improves generalization, we study the implicit regularization effect of SGD with label noise. We show that SGD with label noise converges to a stationary point of a regularized loss $L(\theta) +\lambda R(\theta)$, where $L(\theta)$ is the training loss, $\lambda$ is an effective regularization parameter depending on the step size, strength of the label noise, and the batch size, and $R(\theta)$ is an explicit regularizer that penalizes sharp minimizers. Our analysis uncovers an additional regularization effect of large learning rates beyond the linear scaling rule that penalizes large eigenvalues of the Hessian more than small ones. We also prove extensions to classification with general loss functions, significantly strengthening the prior work of Blanc et al. to global convergence and large learning rates and of HaoChen et al. to general models.

paragraphs: Noise in stochastic gradient descent can influence which solution an overparameterized model reaches. Motivated by empirical observations that noisy-label training can improve generalization, this paper analyzes the optimization effect of label noise. It seeks an explicit mathematical account of the preference for flatter solutions, where the loss changes less sharply around a minimizer.

The authors show convergence to a stationary point of a regularized objective consisting of the training loss plus a penalty for sharp minimizers. The effective strength of that penalty depends on the learning rate, label-noise strength, and batch size. This connects training choices to a specific regularization effect rather than describing noise only as random disturbance.

The analysis also identifies an extra effect of large learning rates beyond the linear scaling rule: directions with larger Hessian eigenvalues receive stronger penalties. Extensions cover classification with general loss functions and strengthen previous results regarding global convergence, large learning rates, and model generality. The stated convergence target remains a stationary point of the regularized loss.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes label-noise SGD through an explicit sharpness penalty whose strength depends on learning rate, noise, and batch size.

title: Label Noise SGD Provably Prefers Flat Global Minimizers

abstract: While current vision algorithms excel at many challenging tasks, it is unclear how well they understand the physical dynamics of real-world environments. Here we introduce Physion, a dataset and benchmark for rigorously evaluating the ability to predict how physical scenarios will evolve over time. Our dataset features realistic simulations of a wide range of physical phenomena, including rigid and soft- body collisions, stable multi-object configurations, rolling, sliding, and projectile motion, thus providing a more comprehensive challenge than previous bench- marks. We used Physion to benchmark a suite of models varying in their architecture, learning objective, input-output structure, and training data. In parallel, we obtained precise measurements of human prediction behavior on the same set of scenarios, allowing us to directly evaluate how well any model could approximate human behavior. We found that vision algorithms that learn object-centric representations generally outperform those that do not, yet still fall far short of human performance. On the other hand, graph neural networks with direct access to physical state information both perform substantially better and make predictions that are more similar to those made by humans. These results suggest that extracting physical representations of scenes is the main bottleneck to achieving human-level and human-like physical understanding in vision algorithms. We have publicly released all data and code to facilitate the use of Physion to benchmark additional models in a fully reproducible manner, enabling systematic evaluation of progress towards vision algorithms that understand physical environments as robustly as people do.

title: Physion: Evaluating Physical Prediction from Vision in Humans and Machines

abstract: While deep learning has enabled tremendous progress on text and image datasets, its superiority on tabular data is not clear. We contribute extensive benchmarks of standard and novel deep learning methods as well as tree-based models such as XGBoost and Random Forests, across a large number of datasets and hyperparameter combinations. We define a standard set of 45 datasets from varied domains with clear characteristics of tabular data and a benchmarking methodology accounting for both fitting models and finding good hyperparameters. Results show that tree-based models remain state-of-the-art on medium-sized data ($\sim$10K samples) even without accounting for their superior speed. To understand this gap, we conduct an empirical investigation into the differing inductive biases of tree-based models and neural networks. This leads to a series of challenges which should guide researchers aiming to build tabular-specific neural network: 1) be robust to uninformative features, 2) preserve the orientation of the data, and 3) be able to easily learn irregular functions. To stimulate research on tabular architectures, we contribute a standard benchmark and raw data for baselines: every point of a 20\,000 compute hours hyperparameter search for each learner.
