The paper's conclusion concerns the studied tabular regime and supplies concrete architectural questions alongside the performance evidence.
summary.tldr: A 45-dataset benchmark finds trees ahead on medium-sized tabular data and identifies three learning challenges for tabular neural networks.

title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?

abstract: In recent centralized nonconvex distributed learning and federated learning, local methods are one of the promising approaches to reduce communication time. However, existing work has mainly focused on studying first-order optimality guarantees. On the other side, second-order optimality guaranteed algorithms, i.e., algorithms escaping saddle points, have been extensively studied in the non-distributed optimization literature. In this paper, we study a new local algorithm called Bias-Variance Reduced Local Perturbed SGD (BVR-L-PSGD), that combines the existing bias-variance reduced gradient estimator with parameter perturbation to find second-order optimal points in centralized nonconvex distributed optimization. BVR-L-PSGD enjoys second-order optimality with nearly the same communication complexity as the best known one of BVR-L-SGD to find first-order optimality. Particularly, the communication complexity is better than non-local methods when the local datasets heterogeneity is smaller than the smoothness of the local loss. In an extreme case, the communication complexity approaches to $\widetilde \Theta(1)$ when the local datasets heterogeneity goes to zero. Numerical results validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Local optimization methods reduce communication in distributed learning by allowing work between exchanges. Much previous analysis established first-order guarantees, which concern small gradients. This paper asks whether a local method can also escape saddle points and obtain second-order guarantees without losing the communication advantages that make local training attractive.

The proposed BVR-L-PSGD algorithm combines a bias-variance reduced gradient estimator with perturbations to the model parameters. The estimator supports the local optimization process, while perturbations enable the saddle-point escape objective. The authors analyze this combination for centralized nonconvex distributed optimization and prove second-order optimality with nearly the communication complexity of the corresponding first-order BVR-L-SGD method.

The communication advantage is qualified by how different the local datasets are. The bound improves over non-local methods when this heterogeneity is smaller than the smoothness of the local loss. As heterogeneity approaches zero, the communication complexity approaches a constant up to logarithmic factors. Numerical results support the theoretical findings, linking stronger optimization guarantees to favorable similarity among local datasets.
summary.tldr: BVR-L-PSGD adds saddle-point escape guarantees to local distributed optimization with nearly the communication cost of its first-order counterpart.

title: Escaping Saddle Points with Bias-Variance Reduced Local Perturbed SGD for Communication Efficient Nonconvex Distributed Learning

abstract: The conventional, widely used treatment of deep learning models as black boxes provides limited or no insights into the mechanisms that guide neural network decisions. Significant research effort has been dedicated to building interpretable models to address this issue. Most efforts either focus on the high-level features associated with the last layers, or attempt to interpret the output of a single layer. In this paper, we take a novel approach to enhance the transparency of the function of the whole network. We propose a neural network architecture for classification, in which the information that is relevant to each class flows through specific paths. These paths are designed in advance before training leveraging coding theory and without depending on the semantic similarities between classes. A key property is that each path can be used as an autonomous single-purpose model. This enables us to obtain, without any additional training and for any class, a lightweight binary classifier that has at least $60\%$ fewer parameters than the original network. Furthermore, our coding theory based approach allows the neural network to make early predictions at intermediate layers during inference, without requiring its full evaluation. Remarkably, the proposed architecture provides all the aforementioned properties while improving the overall accuracy. We demonstrate these properties on a slightly modified ResNeXt model tested on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k.

The contribution links transparency to practical reuse: class-specific paths provide a way to inspect how information is organized, extract smaller classifiers, and make intermediate predictions within the same trained network.
summary.tldr: Coded ResNeXt assigns classes predefined information paths that support smaller standalone classifiers and early predictions while improving reported accuracy.

title: Towards Disentangling Information Paths with Coded ResNeXt

abstract: Semantic code search is the task of retrieving a code snippet given a textual description of its functionality. Recent work has been focused on using similarity metrics between neural embeddings of text and code. However, current language models are known to struggle with longer, compositional sentences, and multi-step reasoning. To overcome this limitation, we propose supplementing the query sentence with a layout of its semantic structure. The semantic layout is used to break down the final reasoning decision into a series of lower-level decisions. We use a Neural Module Network architecture to implement this idea. We compare our model - $NS^3$ (Neuro-Symbolic Semantic Search) - to a number of baselines, including state-of-the-art semantic code retrieval methods, such as CodeBERT, CuBERT and GraphCodeBERT, and evaluate on two datasets - Code Search Net (CSN) and Code Search and Question Answering (CoSQA). On these datasets, we demonstrate that our approach results in higher performance. We also perform additional studies to show the effectiveness of our modular design when handling compositional queries.

paragraphs: Semantic code search retrieves code from a natural-language description of what it should do. Many methods compare learned representations of the query and code. The paper focuses on a weakness of this approach: longer descriptions can combine several requirements, and matching them may demand compositional or multi-step reasoning.

NS3 supplements the query with a layout of its semantic structure. That layout breaks the final matching decision into a sequence of smaller decisions, implemented through a Neural Module Network. The structure of the description therefore helps organize the reasoning used to assess code, rather than leaving the entire decision to a single comparison between representations.

The authors evaluate NS3 on Code Search Net and Code Search and Question Answering, comparing it with methods including CodeBERT, CuBERT, and GraphCodeBERT. They report higher performance on both datasets. Additional studies examine compositional queries and support the effectiveness of the modular design. The findings indicate that explicitly organizing query meaning can improve code retrieval in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: NS3 uses a query's semantic structure to organize modular reasoning and improve semantic code retrieval.

title: NS3: Neuro-symbolic Semantic Code Search

abstract: Causal discovery and causal reasoning are classically treated as separate and consecutive tasks: one first infers the causal graph, and then uses it to estimate causal effects of interventions. However, such a two-stage approach is uneconomical, especially in terms of actively collected interventional data, since the causal query of interest may not require a fully-specified causal model. From a Bayesian perspective, it is also unnatural, since a causal query (e.g., the causal graph or some causal effect) can be viewed as a latent quantity subject to posterior inference—quantities that are not of direct interest ought to be marginalized out in this process, thus contributing to our overall uncertainty. In this work, we propose Active Bayesian Causal Inference (ABCI), a fully-Bayesian active learning framework for integrated causal discovery and reasoning, i.e., for jointly inferring a posterior over causal models and queries of interest. In our approach to ABCI, we focus on the class of causally-sufficient nonlinear additive Gaussian noise models, which we model using Gaussian processes. To capture the space of causal graphs, we use a continuous latent graph representation, allowing our approach to scale to practically relevant problem sizes. We sequentially design experiments that are maximally informative about our target causal query, collect the corresponding interventional data, update our beliefs, and repeat. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our approach is more data-efficient than existing methods that only focus on learning the full causal graph. This allows us to accurately learn downstream causal queries from fewer samples, while providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates of the quantities of interest.

This paper combines those steps, choosing experiments around the particular causal question that needs answering.

Its implementation studies nonlinear additive Gaussian noise models with causal sufficiency, uses Gaussian processes to represent relationships, and represents graphs through continuous latent variables.

It also produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. The finding supports directing experimental effort toward the desired answer while retaining uncertainty about unresolved causal structure, within the model class studied.
summary.tldr: ABCI chooses interventions to answer specific causal questions, improving sample efficiency in simulations while maintaining calibrated uncertainty.

title: Active Bayesian Causal Inference

abstract: Optimal experimental design seeks to determine the most informative allocation of experiments to infer an unknown statistical quantity. In this work, we investigate optimal design of experiments for {\em estimation of linear functionals in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs)}. This problem has been extensively studied in the linear regression setting under an estimability condition, which allows estimating parameters without bias. We generalize this framework to RKHSs, and allow for the linear functional to be only approximately inferred, i.e., with a fixed bias. This scenario captures many important modern applications such as estimation of gradient maps, integrals and solutions to differential equations. We provide algorithms for constructing bias-aware designs for linear functionals. We derive non-asymptotic confidence sets for fixed and adaptive designs under sub-Gaussian noise, enabling us to certify estimation with bounded error with high probability.

paragraphs: Experimental design asks which measurements will be most informative about a quantity of interest. This paper studies that question for linear functionals of functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, or RKHSs. The target can be a quantity derived from a function, with applications including gradient maps, integrals, and solutions to differential equations.

Classical work in linear regression often assumes an estimability condition that permits unbiased estimation. The authors extend the framework to RKHSs and allow the desired functional to be inferred approximately with a fixed bias. Their algorithms construct designs that explicitly account for this bias, making approximation part of the design problem rather than requiring unbiased recovery.

The paper also derives finite-sample confidence sets for both fixed measurement designs and adaptive ones. These guarantees assume sub-Gaussian noise and certify bounded estimation error with high probability. Together, the design algorithms and confidence sets connect two decisions: where to collect information and how much confidence to place in the resulting approximate estimate.
summary.tldr: The paper designs informative measurements for RKHS functionals while accounting for fixed bias and providing high-probability error guarantees.

title: Experimental Design for Linear Functionals in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

abstract: Post-processing ensemble prediction systems can improve the reliability of weather forecasting, especially for extreme event prediction. In recent years, different machine learning models have been developed to improve the quality of weather post-processing. However, these models require a comprehensive dataset of weather simulations to produce high-accuracy results, which comes at a high computational cost to generate. This paper introduces the ENS-10 dataset, consisting of ten ensemble members spanning 20 years (1998--2017). The ensemble members are generated by perturbing numerical weather simulations to capture the chaotic behavior of the Earth. To represent the three-dimensional state of the atmosphere, ENS-10 provides the most relevant atmospheric variables at 11 distinct pressure levels and the surface at \ang{0.5} resolution for forecast lead times T=0, 24, and 48 hours (two data points per week). We propose the ENS-10 prediction correction task for improving the forecast quality at a 48-hour lead time through ensemble post-processing. We provide a set of baselines and compare their skill at correcting the predictions of three important atmospheric variables. Moreover, we measure the baselines' skill at improving predictions of extreme weather events using our dataset. The ENS-10 dataset is available under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

paragraphs: Ensemble weather forecasting uses multiple simulations to represent uncertainty in future conditions. Machine-learning post-processing can improve these forecasts, but generating the simulation data needed for training is computationally expensive. ENS-10 provides a shared dataset for studying that correction process, including its usefulness for extreme-weather prediction.

The dataset contains ten ensemble members covering 1998–2017. These members are produced by perturbing numerical weather simulations to capture the atmosphere's chaotic behavior. Atmospheric variables are provided at 11 pressure levels and at the surface, with 0.5-degree spatial resolution. Forecast lead times are 0, 24, and 48 hours, and the dataset supplies two data points per week.

The authors define a prediction-correction task focused on forecasts 48 hours ahead. They provide baselines and compare how well these correct three atmospheric variables, including their performance on extreme events. The contribution is a dataset and evaluation task for making post-processing methods comparable, with explicit attention to extreme-weather performance. ENS-10 is released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license.
summary.tldr: ENS-10 provides twenty years of ensemble weather data and a benchmark for correcting 48-hour forecasts, including extreme-event predictions.

title: ENS-10: A Dataset For Post-Processing Ensemble Weather Forecasts

abstract: Multi-fidelity modeling and learning is important in physical simulation related applications. It can leverage both low-fidelity and high-fidelity examples for training so as to reduce the cost of data generation yet still achieving good performance. While existing approaches only model finite, discrete fidelities, in practice, the feasible fidelity choice is often infinite, which can correspond to a continuous mesh spacing or finite element length. In this paper, we propose Infinite Fidelity Coregionalization (IFC). Given the data, our method can extract and exploit rich information within infinite, continuous fidelities to bolster the prediction accuracy. Our model can interpolate and/or extrapolate the predictions to novel fidelities that are not covered by the training data. Specifically, we introduce a low-dimensional latent output as a continuous function of the fidelity and input, and multiple it with a basis matrix to predict high-dimensional solution outputs. We model the latent output as a neural Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) to capture the complex relationships within and integrate information throughout the continuous fidelities. We then use Gaussian processes or another ODE to estimate the fidelity-varying bases. For efficient inference, we reorganize the bases as a tensor, and use a tensor-Gaussian variational posterior approximation to develop a scalable inference algorithm for massive outputs. We show the advantage of our method in several benchmark tasks in computational physics.

Combining cheaper low-fidelity examples with more detailed ones can reduce data generation costs. Infinite Fidelity Coregionalization models fidelity as a continuous quantity, allowing it to capture relationships beyond a fixed collection of discrete simulation levels.

It can interpolate or extrapolate to fidelity levels absent from training data. Results on computational physics benchmarks show advantages for the approach, supporting continuous fidelity modeling as a useful way to improve predictions from simulations of varying resolution.
summary.tldr: Infinite Fidelity Coregionalization learns across continuous simulation fidelities and predicts outputs at fidelity levels unseen during training.

title: Infinite-Fidelity Coregionalization for Physical Simulation

abstract: Chromatic Correlation Clustering (CCC) (introduced by Bonchi et al. [6]) is a natural generalization of the celebrated Correlation Clustering (CC) problem. It models objects with categorical pairwise relationships by an edge-colored graph, and has many applications in data mining, social networks and bioinformatics. We show that there exists a 2.5-approximation to the CCC problem based on a Linear Programming (LP) approach, thus improving the best-known approximation ratio of 3 achieved by Klodt et al. [25]. We also present an efficient heuristic algorithm for CCC leveraging a greedy clustering strategy, and conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Chromatic correlation clustering organizes objects whose pairwise relationships belong to different categories. The input is a graph in which objects are nodes and relationship categories are represented by edge colors. This extends ordinary correlation clustering to settings where the relationships carry more categorical information, with applications in data mining, social networks, and bioinformatics.

The paper improves the theoretical guarantee available for this problem using a linear programming approach. It establishes a 2.5-approximation, improving the previously best known factor of 3. The smaller approximation factor gives a tighter worst-case guarantee relative to an optimal solution; it is a statement about solution quality, rather than a claim that the algorithm always finds the optimum.

The authors also develop an efficient heuristic based on greedy clustering and evaluate its effectiveness and efficiency in extensive experiments. This supplies a practical algorithm alongside the theoretical advance. These are distinct contributions: the approximation result strengthens the formal understanding of the problem, while the heuristic experiments address how well the proposed practical strategy works.
summary.tldr: The paper improves chromatic correlation clustering's approximation guarantee from 3 to 2.5 and introduces an experimentally effective greedy heuristic.

title: Chromatic Correlation Clustering, Revisited

abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

This paper addresses that concern by training a student model to absorb knowledge from multiple teachers, each trained on an exemplar distribution. The objective is a lightweight model with broader routing competence.

Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation combines these sources of expertise through a shared student. Its adaptive strategy gives additional attention to distributions that the student finds difficult. That focus is intended to help the student absorb knowledge it has not yet mastered, rather than treating all distributions as equally easy throughout learning.

Experiments compare the approach with baseline neural methods on unseen instances from both familiar and different distributions. These include randomly generated problems and instances from TSPLIB and CVRPLIB. The student achieves competitive results across these settings while requiring fewer computational resources at inference. The findings support distillation as a way to combine distribution-specific expertise into a more general model with lower deployment cost.
summary.tldr: Adaptive distillation from multiple routing teachers produces a lightweight student with competitive performance across familiar and unfamiliar instance distributions.

title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Referred to as the third rung of the causal inference ladder, counterfactual queries typically ask the "What if ?" question retrospectively. The standard approach to estimate counterfactuals resides in using a structural equation model that accurately reflects the underlying data generating process. However, such models are seldom available in practice and one usually wishes to infer them from observational data alone. Unfortunately, the correct structural equation model is in general not identifiable from the observed factual distribution. Nevertheless, in this work, we show that under the assumption that the main latent contributors to the treatment responses are categorical, the counterfactuals can be still reliably predicted. Building upon this assumption, we introduce CounterFactual Query Prediction (\method), a novel method to infer counterfactuals from continuous observations when the background variables are categorical. We show that our method significantly outperforms previously available deep-learning-based counterfactual methods, both theoretically and empirically on time series and image data. Our code is available at https://github.com/edebrouwer/cfqp.

paragraphs: Counterfactual questions ask what would have happened to an observed case if its treatment had been different. Answering them usually depends on a structural equation model that correctly describes how the data were generated. Such a model is often unavailable, and observational data generally do not uniquely identify the correct one.

This paper investigates a specific assumption that makes reliable counterfactual prediction possible: the main unobserved contributors to treatment responses are categorical. The observations themselves can still be continuous. The distinction matters because the categorical structure is imposed on the hidden background variables, rather than requiring the measured data to fall into discrete categories.

Building on that assumption, the authors introduce CounterFactual Query Prediction, a method for inferring counterfactuals from continuous observations with categorical background variables. They report theoretical and empirical advantages over previously available deep-learning-based counterfactual methods, with experiments on time series and images. The contribution identifies a structured setting in which counterfactual prediction can succeed despite the general difficulty of recovering the underlying structural model from observations alone.
summary.tldr: Assuming categorical latent contributors to treatment responses enables a counterfactual prediction method with reported theoretical and empirical advantages.

title: Deep Counterfactual Estimation with Categorical Background Variables

abstract: We consider the pool-based active learning problem, where only a subset of the training data is labeled, and the goal is to query a batch of unlabeled samples to be labeled so as to maximally improve model performance. We formulate the problem using constrained learning, where a set of constraints bounds the performance of the model on labeled samples. Considering a primal-dual approach, we optimize the primal variables, corresponding to the model parameters, as well as the dual variables, corresponding to the constraints. As each dual variable indicates how significantly the perturbation of the respective constraint affects the optimal value of the objective function, we use it as a proxy of the informativeness of the corresponding training sample. Our approach, which we refer to as Active Learning via Lagrangian dualitY, or ALLY, leverages this fact to select a diverse set of unlabeled samples with the highest estimated dual variables as our query set. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach in a variety of classification and regression tasks and discuss its limitations depending on the capacity of the model used and the degree of redundancy in the dataset. We also examine the impact of the distribution shift induced by active sampling and show that ALLY can be used in a generative mode to create novel, maximally-informative samples.

paragraphs: Active learning asks which unlabeled examples should receive labels next to improve a model most effectively. This paper approaches that choice through constrained learning. It places bounds on model performance for labeled examples, then jointly optimizes the model parameters and additional variables associated with those constraints.

These additional, or dual, variables describe how strongly changing a constraint would affect the best achievable objective. ALLY uses this sensitivity as a proxy for how informative an example is. It estimates dual variables for unlabeled examples and selects a diverse batch with high estimated values, connecting sample selection to the optimization problem used to train the model.

Experiments demonstrate benefits across classification and regression tasks. The paper also examines limitations associated with model capacity and redundant data, as well as the distribution shift introduced by actively choosing samples. Finally, it shows that ALLY can operate generatively, creating new samples intended to be maximally informative rather than selecting only from an existing pool.
summary.tldr: ALLY uses the sensitivity of a constrained learning objective to identify informative examples for labeling or generation.

title: A Lagrangian Duality Approach to Active Learning

abstract: This paper presents \textit{PolyDiffuse}, a novel structured reconstruction algorithm that transforms visual sensor data into polygonal shapes with Diffusion Models (DM), an emerging machinery amid exploding generative AI, while formulating reconstruction as a generation process conditioned on sensor data. The task of structured reconstruction poses two fundamental challenges to DM: 1) A structured geometry is a ''set'' (e.g., a set of polygons for a floorplan geometry), where a sample of $N$ elements has $N!$ different but equivalent representations, making the denoising highly ambiguous; and 2) A ''reconstruction'' task has a single solution, where an initial noise needs to be chosen carefully, while any initial noise works for a generation task.Our technical contribution is the introduction of a Guided Set Diffusion Model where 1) the forward diffusion process learns \textit{guidance networks} to control noise injection so that one representation of a sample remains distinct from its other permutation variants, thus resolving denoising ambiguity; and 2) the reverse denoising process reconstructs polygonal shapes, initialized and directed by the guidance networks, as a conditional generation process subject to the sensor data.We have evaluated our approach for reconstructing two types of polygonal shapes: floorplan as a set of polygons and HD map for autonomous cars as a set of polylines.Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, we demonstrate that PolyDiffuse significantly advances the current state of the art and enables broader practical applications. The code and data are available on our project page: https://poly-diffuse.github.io.

paragraphs: PolyDiffuse reconstructs polygonal geometry from visual sensor data by treating reconstruction as conditional generation with a diffusion model. Structured geometry creates a special difficulty: a set of polygons or polylines can be listed in many equivalent orders. Those alternative representations make the denoising process ambiguous.

Reconstruction also needs noise initialization suited to recovering a particular solution from the observations. The proposed Guided Set Diffusion Model learns guidance networks during forward diffusion to control noise injection and keep permutation variants distinct. During reverse diffusion, those networks initialize and guide the reconstruction while conditioning it on sensor data.

The authors evaluate floorplan reconstruction, represented as sets of polygons, and autonomous-driving HD map reconstruction, represented as sets of polylines. Experiments on standard benchmarks report substantial advances over the state of the art. The contribution is a diffusion formulation that directly addresses both set-representation ambiguity and the need for observation-specific reconstruction, enabling the model to produce structured geometry from sensor inputs.
summary.tldr: PolyDiffuse guides noise injection and denoising to reconstruct polygonal floorplans and maps while resolving ambiguities caused by equivalent set orderings.

title: PolyDiffuse: Polygonal Shape Reconstruction via Guided Set Diffusion Models

abstract: Accessible high-quality data is the bread and butter of machine learning research, and the demand for data has exploded as larger and more advanced ML models are built across different domains. Yet, real data often contain sensitive information, are subject to various biases, and are costly to acquire, which compromise their quality and accessibility. Synthetic data have thus emerged as a complement to, sometimes even a replacement for, real data for ML training. However, the landscape of synthetic data research has been fragmented due to the diverse range of data modalities, such as tabular, time series, and images, and the wide array of use cases, including privacy preservation, fairness considerations, and data augmentation. This fragmentation poses practical challenges when comparing and selecting synthetic data generators in for different problem settings. To this end, we develop Synthcity, an open-source Python library that allows researchers and practitioners to perform one-click benchmarking of synthetic data generators across data modalities and use cases. Beyond benchmarking, Synthcity serves as a centralized toolkit for accessing cutting-edge data generators. In addition, Synthcity’s flexible plug-in style API makes it easy to incorporate additional data generators into the framework. Using examples of tabular data generation and data augmentation, we illustrate the general applicability of Synthcity, and the insight one can obtain.

paragraphs: Synthetic data can supplement real training data when access is constrained by sensitivity, bias, or acquisition cost. Choosing a generator is complicated because synthetic-data research spans different data types and goals, including privacy, fairness, and augmentation. Synthcity addresses the practical difficulty of comparing methods across this fragmented landscape.

The contribution is an open-source Python library for benchmarking synthetic-data generators across modalities and use cases. It also provides a centralized collection of generators, bringing evaluation and access into the same toolkit. A plug-in API allows additional generators to be incorporated, so the framework can accommodate methods beyond its existing collection.

The paper demonstrates the framework through examples involving tabular generation and data augmentation. These examples illustrate its applicability and the insights obtainable from comparative evaluation. The main value is shared infrastructure for selecting and studying generators in context: users can compare methods according to the task they need synthetic data to serve, rather than treating generation quality as a single, universal requirement.
summary.tldr: Synthcity provides an extensible library for accessing and benchmarking synthetic-data generators across data types and use cases.

title: Synthcity: a benchmark framework for diverse use cases of tabular synthetic data

abstract: When training a machine learning model with differential privacy, one sets a privacy budget. This uniform budget represents an overall maximal privacy violation that any user is willing to face by contributing their data to the training set. We argue that this approach is limited because different users may have different privacy expectations. Thus, setting a uniform privacy budget across all points may be overly conservative for some users or, conversely, not sufficiently protective for others. In this paper, we capture these preferences through individualized privacy budgets. To demonstrate their practicality, we introduce a variant of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) which supports such individualized budgets. DP-SGD is the canonical approach to training models with differential privacy. We modify its data sampling and gradient noising mechanisms to arrive at our approach, which we call Individualized DP-SGD (IDP-SGD). Because IDP-SGD provides privacy guarantees tailored to the preferences of individual users and their data points, we empirically find it to improve privacy-utility trade-offs.

paragraphs: Differentially private model training usually applies one privacy budget across the training data. That budget expresses the allowed privacy loss, but people may have different preferences about that allowance. A shared setting can therefore be more restrictive than some contributors want while failing to provide the level of protection others expect.

This paper introduces individualized privacy budgets and a training procedure that supports them. The method, Individualized DP-SGD, adapts the standard differentially private stochastic gradient descent algorithm. It changes both how training data are sampled and how noise is added to gradients, allowing privacy guarantees to reflect the preferences associated with individual users and their data points.

The authors empirically find improved privacy-utility trade-offs with this approach. The significance is that privacy preferences become part of the training design, rather than being compressed into a single common budget. The reported improvement concerns the balance between useful model behavior and tailored protection; it does not require every contributor to accept the same privacy allowance.
summary.tldr: Individualized DP-SGD adapts sampling and gradient noise to support different privacy budgets and empirically improve privacy-utility trade-offs.

title: Have it your way: Individualized Privacy Assignment for DP-SGD

abstract: Compressed videos offer a compelling alternative to raw videos, showing the possibility to significantly reduce the on-line computational and storage cost. However, current approaches to compressed video processing generally follow the resource-consuming pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm, which does not fully take advantage of such properties, making them not favorable enough for widespread applications. Inspired by recent successes of prompt tuning techniques in computer vision, this paper presents the first attempt to build a prompt based representation learning framework, which enables effective and efficient adaptation of pre-trained raw video models to compressed video understanding tasks. To this end, we propose a novel prompt tuning approach, namely Compressed Video Prompt Tuning (CVPT), emphatically dealing with the challenging issue caused by the inconsistency between pre-training and downstream data modalities. Specifically, CVPT replaces the learnable prompts with compressed modalities (\emph{e.g.} Motion Vectors and Residuals) by re-parameterizing them into conditional prompts followed by layer-wise refinement. The conditional prompts exhibit improved adaptability and generalizability to instances compared to conventional individual learnable ones, and the Residual prompts enhance the noisy motion cues in the Motion Vector prompts for further fusion with the visual cues from I-frames. Additionally, we design Selective Cross-modal Complementary Prompt (SCCP) blocks. After inserting them into the backbone, SCCP blocks leverage semantic relations across diverse levels and modalities to improve cross-modal interactions between prompts and input flows. Extensive evaluations on HMDB-51, UCF-101 and Something-Something v2 demonstrate that CVPT remarkably outperforms the state-of-the-art counterparts, delivering a much better balance between accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Compressed video offers opportunities to reduce online computation and storage, but adapting models through expensive pretraining and fine-tuning can weaken those advantages. This paper introduces Compressed Video Prompt Tuning, or CVPT, to adapt models pretrained on raw video to compressed-video understanding. Its central challenge is the mismatch between the data used in pretraining and the compressed inputs used downstream.

CVPT turns compressed modalities, including motion vectors and residuals, into conditional prompts and refines them across layers. These prompts depend on the input instance, giving them more flexibility than individually learned prompts. Residual prompts improve noisy motion information, which is then combined with visual information from I-frames.

The framework also inserts Selective Cross-modal Complementary Prompt blocks into the backbone. These blocks use semantic relationships across modalities and levels to improve interaction between prompts and input streams. Evaluations on HMDB-51, UCF-101, and Something-Something v2 report substantial gains over leading counterparts and a better balance between accuracy and efficiency, supporting compressed information as an effective basis for model adaptation.
summary.tldr: CVPT uses input-dependent prompts from compressed video to adapt raw-video models with a better evaluated accuracy–efficiency balance.

title: Compressed Video Prompt Tuning

abstract: We study the Combinatorial Group Testing (CGT) problem in a novel game-theoretic framework, with a solution concept of Adversarial Equilibrium (AE). In this new framework, we have $n$ selfish agents corresponding to the elements of the universe $[n] =\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ and a hidden set $K \subseteq [n]$ of active agents of size $|K| = k \ll n$. In each round of the game, each active agent decides if it is present in a query $Q \subseteq [n]$, and all agents receive feedback on $Q \cap K$. The goal of each active agent is to assure that its id could be learned from the feedback as early as possible. We present a comprehensive set of results in this new game, where we design and analyze adaptive algorithmic strategies of agents which are AE's. In particular, if $k$ is known to the agents, then we design adaptive AE strategies with provably near optimal learning time of $O(k \log(n/k))$. In the case of unknown $k$, we design an adaptive AE strategies with learning time of order $n^k$, and we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ on the learning time of any such algorithmic strategies. This shows a strong separations between the two models of known and unknown $k$, as well as between the classic CGT, i.e., without selfish agents, and our game theoretic CGT model.

paragraphs: Combinatorial group testing seeks to identify a small active subset within a larger population through queries involving groups. This paper changes the problem by making the elements selfish agents. Each active agent chooses whether to participate in a query and wants its own identity to become learnable from the feedback as early as possible.

The authors study adaptive strategies under a solution concept called Adversarial Equilibrium. The central distinction is whether agents know k, the number of active agents among n total agents. When k is known, they construct equilibrium strategies with learning time O(k log(n/k)), which they establish as nearly optimal. Thus, strategic participation can still permit efficient identification in this information setting.

When k is unknown, the authors construct strategies taking time on the order of n to the power k and prove a lower bound of order n for any such strategies. These bounds leave a gap, but establish a strong separation from the known-k case. The results show how agents' incentives and information change the difficulty of group testing relative to its classical formulation.
summary.tldr: Group testing with selfish agents admits nearly optimal equilibrium strategies when the active population size is known, but becomes substantially harder when it is unknown.

title: Combinatorial Group Testing with Selfish Agents

abstract: Self-training is a well-established technique in semi-supervised learning, which leverages unlabeled data by generating pseudo-labels and incorporating them with a limited labeled dataset for training. The effectiveness of self-training heavily relies on the accuracy of these pseudo-labels. In this paper, we introduce doubly-robust self-training, an innovative semi-supervised algorithm that provably balances between two extremes. When pseudo-labels are entirely incorrect, our method reduces to a training process solely using labeled data. Conversely, when pseudo-labels are completely accurate, our method transforms into a training process utilizing all pseudo-labeled data and labeled data, thus increasing the effective sample size. Through empirical evaluations on both the ImageNet dataset for image classification and the nuScenes autonomous driving dataset for 3D object detection, we demonstrate the superiority of the doubly-robust loss over the self-training baseline.

paragraphs: Self-training expands a small labeled dataset by assigning predicted labels to unlabeled examples and then learning from them. These predictions, called pseudo-labels, can make additional data useful, but their accuracy strongly affects the result. This paper introduces a loss designed to balance reliance on pseudo-labels with reliance on the original labeled examples.

The method has provable behavior at two extremes. If the pseudo-labels are entirely wrong, it reduces to training only on labeled data. If they are completely correct, it becomes training on both labeled and pseudo-labeled data, increasing the effective sample size. These endpoint properties explain the intended robustness: the method can retain the labeled-data training process or exploit the larger dataset when the pseudo-labels support it.

The authors evaluate the doubly-robust loss on ImageNet image classification and nuScenes 3D object detection. In those experiments, it outperforms the self-training baseline. The contribution combines theoretical endpoint guarantees with evidence across two different prediction tasks. Its stated findings show a way to make the usefulness of additional unlabeled data depend more carefully on the quality of the labels assigned to it.
summary.tldr: Doubly-robust self-training has provable fallback and full-data behavior at the extremes of pseudo-label accuracy and improves the tested self-training baseline.

title: Doubly-Robust Self-Training

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms typically consider discrete-time dynamics, even though the underlying systems are often continuous in time. In this paper, we introduce a model-based reinforcement learning algorithm that represents continuous-time dynamics using nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). We capture epistemic uncertainty using well-calibrated probabilistic models, and use the optimistic principle for exploration. Our regret bounds surface the importance of the measurement selection strategy (MSS), since in continuous time we not only must decide how to explore, but also when to observe the underlying system. Our analysis demonstrates that the regret is sublinear when modeling ODEs with Gaussian Processes (GP) for common choices of MSS, such as equidistant sampling. Additionally, we propose an adaptive, data-dependent, practical MSS that, when combined with GP dynamics, also achieves sublinear regret with significantly fewer samples. We showcase the benefits of continuous-time modeling over its discrete-time counterpart, as well as our proposed adaptive MSS over standard baselines, on several applications.

Our regret bounds surface the importance of the measurement selection strategy (MSS), since in continuous time we not only must decide how to explore, but also when to observe the underlying system. paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning methods represent change in discrete steps, although the systems they control evolve continuously. This paper models those dynamics with nonlinear ordinary differential equations. It uses calibrated probabilistic models to represent uncertainty caused by limited knowledge, then applies optimistic exploration to guide learning about the system.

Continuous time introduces an additional decision: when to take measurements. The authors make this measurement-selection strategy explicit in their regret analysis. With Gaussian-process models of the dynamics, they establish sublinear regret for common measurement strategies, including equally spaced observations. Sublinear regret means the accumulated performance gap grows more slowly than the learning horizon.

The paper also proposes an adaptive strategy that chooses measurements using available data. Combined with Gaussian-process dynamics, it retains sublinear regret while requiring significantly fewer samples. Applications demonstrate benefits from continuous-time modeling and from adaptive measurement selection relative to the compared alternatives. The work thus treats observation timing as part of efficient exploration, alongside the choice of actions.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time reinforcement-learning method jointly addresses exploration and observation timing, with sublinear-regret guarantees and fewer measurements through adaptive sampling.

title: Efficient Exploration in Continuous-time Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Today's online advertisers procure digital ad impressions through interacting with autobidding platforms: advertisers convey high level procurement goals via setting levers such as budget, target return-on-investment, max cost per click, etc.. Then ads platforms subsequently procure impressions on advertisers' behalf, and report final procurement conversions (e.g. click) to advertisers. In practice, advertisers may receive minimal information on platforms' procurement details, and procurement outcomes are subject to non-stationary factors like seasonal patterns, occasional system corruptions, and market trends which make it difficult for advertisers to optimize lever decisions effectively. Motivated by this, we present an online learning framework that helps advertisers dynamically optimize ad platform lever decisions while subject to general long-term constraints in a realistic bandit feedback environment with non-stationary procurement outcomes. In particular, we introduce a primal-dual algorithm for online decision making with multi-dimension decision variables, bandit feedback and long-term uncertain constraints. We show that our algorithm achieves low regret in many worlds when procurement outcomes are generated through procedures that are stochastic, adversarial, adversarially corrupted, periodic, and ergodic, respectively, without having to know which procedure is the ground truth. Finally, we emphasize that our proposed algorithm and theoretical results extend beyond the applications of online advertising.

paragraphs: Advertisers often control automated buying through settings such as budgets or return targets, while seeing little about the platform's underlying purchases. The outcomes can change with seasonality, market trends, or disruptions. This paper formulates the advertiser's problem as online learning: repeatedly choose those settings using limited feedback while respecting constraints over time.

The proposed primal-dual algorithm handles multiple decision variables, bandit feedback, and uncertain long-term constraints. Bandit feedback means the learner must work with the outcomes of its chosen actions rather than complete information about all alternatives. The primal-dual formulation combines the search for good decisions with the need to manage constraints across the sequence.

The authors establish low regret for several outcome-generating settings, including stochastic, adversarial, adversarially corrupted, periodic, and ergodic processes. The algorithm does not need to know which of these settings generated the observations. This adaptability is the main theoretical result, and the framework also applies to constrained online decision problems beyond advertising.
summary.tldr: A constrained online-learning algorithm adapts advertising controls under limited feedback and achieves low regret across several unknown outcome-generating settings.

title: Online Ad Procurement in Non-stationary Autobidding Worlds

abstract: Open-world classification systems should discern out-of-distribution (OOD) data whose labels deviate from those of in-distribution (ID) cases, motivating recent studies in OOD detection. Advanced works, despite their promising progress, may still fail in the open world, owing to the lacking knowledge about unseen OOD data in advance. Although one can access auxiliary OOD data (distinct from unseen ones) for model training, it remains to analyze how such auxiliary data will work in the open world. To this end, we delve into such a problem from a learning theory perspective, finding that the distribution discrepancy between the auxiliary and the unseen real OOD data is the key to affect the open-world detection performance. Accordingly, we propose Distributional-Augmented OOD Learning (DAOL), alleviating the OOD distribution discrepancy by crafting an OOD distribution set that contains all distributions in a Wasserstein ball centered on the auxiliary OOD distribution. We justify that the predictor trained over the worst OOD data in the ball can shrink the OOD distribution discrepancy, thus improving the open-world detection performance given only the auxiliary OOD data. We conduct extensive evaluations across representative OOD detection setups, demonstrating the superiority of our DAOL over its advanced counterparts.

paragraphs: An open-world classifier needs to recognize when an input belongs to a class outside its training categories. Auxiliary examples of out-of-distribution data can help, but they may differ from the unfamiliar data encountered later. This paper studies that mismatch through learning theory and identifies distribution discrepancy as a key influence on detection performance.

The proposed Distributional-Augmented OOD Learning method, or DAOL, expands training beyond one auxiliary distribution. It constructs a set of distributions inside a Wasserstein ball centered on the available auxiliary OOD distribution. The predictor is then trained against the worst OOD data within that set, accounting for a range of distributional alternatives.

The authors justify that this worst-case training can reduce the relevant discrepancy and improve open-world detection using only the auxiliary OOD data. Evaluations across representative detection settings report better performance than advanced competing methods. The approach matters because it treats uncertainty about future unfamiliar inputs as a distribution-level training problem, directly addressing the gap between available auxiliary examples and later OOD encounters.
summary.tldr: DAOL trains against distributional variations around auxiliary OOD data to improve detection of unfamiliar inputs encountered later.

title: Learning to Augment Distributions for Out-of-distribution Detection

abstract: Transformers have achieved remarkable success in a wide range of natural language processing and computer vision applications. However, the representation capacity of a deep transformer model is degraded due to the over-smoothing issue in which the token representations become identical when the model's depth grows. In this work, we show that self-attention layers in transformers minimize a functional which promotes smoothness, thereby causing token uniformity. We then propose a novel regularizer that penalizes the norm of the difference between the smooth output tokens from self-attention and the input tokens to preserve the fidelity of the tokens. Minimizing the resulting regularized energy functional, we derive the Neural Transformer with a Regularized Nonlocal Functional (NeuTRENO), a novel class of transformer models that can mitigate the over-smoothing issue. We empirically demonstrate the advantages of NeuTRENO over the baseline transformers and state-of-the-art methods in reducing the over-smoothing of token representations on various practical tasks, including object classification, image segmentation, and language modeling.

paragraphs: As a transformer becomes deeper, its token representations can become increasingly alike. This over-smoothing reduces its capacity to preserve distinctions among tokens. The paper investigates the mechanism behind that behavior by showing that self-attention layers minimize a mathematical functional that favors smoothness, linking the attention operation to token uniformity.

The authors modify this functional with a regularizer that penalizes differences between the input tokens and the smoothed output tokens. This introduces pressure to preserve the information carried by the inputs while attention combines information across tokens. Minimizing the revised energy functional leads to a class of models called NeuTRENO, making the architectural change follow from the proposed mathematical account.

Experiments compare NeuTRENO with baseline transformers and state-of-the-art methods on object classification, image segmentation, and language modeling. The reported results show advantages in reducing over-smoothing of token representations. The contribution combines an explanation of why token distinctions can disappear with a derived mechanism for retaining them across the evaluated practical tasks.
summary.tldr: NeuTRENO derives transformer layers from a regularized smoothing objective to preserve token distinctions and reduce over-smoothing.

title: Mitigating Over-smoothing in Transformers via Regularized Nonlocal Functionals

abstract: The field of graph learning has been substantially advanced by the development of deep learning models, in particular graph neural networks. However, one salient yet largely under-explored challenge is detecting Out-of-Distribution (OOD) nodes on graphs. Prevailing OOD detection techniques developed in other domains like computer vision, do not cater to the interconnected nature of graphs. This work aims to fill this gap by exploring the potential of a simple yet effective method -- OOD score propagation, which propagates OOD scores among neighboring nodes along the graph structure. This post hoc solution can be easily integrated with existing OOD scoring functions, showcasing its excellent flexibility and effectiveness in most scenarios. However, the conditions under which score propagation proves beneficial remain not fully elucidated. Our study meticulously derives these conditions and, inspired by this discovery, introduces an innovative edge augmentation strategy with theoretical guarantee. Empirical evaluations affirm the superiority of our proposed method, outperforming strong OOD detection baselines in various scenarios and settings.

paragraphs: Detecting graph nodes that differ from the training distribution requires accounting for connections between nodes. Detection methods developed for other data types may overlook that structure. This paper studies score propagation, a simple procedure that passes out-of-distribution scores among neighboring nodes after the original scores have been computed.

Because propagation operates on scores, it can be combined with existing scoring functions. However, using neighboring information is not automatically beneficial. The authors derive conditions under which propagation helps, providing a theoretical basis for understanding its effectiveness. This moves the analysis beyond observing that a convenient post-processing operation often works.

Those conditions motivate an edge augmentation strategy with a theoretical guarantee. The strategy changes the graph connections used by the method in light of the analysis. Empirical evaluations show improvements over strong out-of-distribution detection baselines across various settings. The central contribution is the connection between a flexible existing operation, a characterization of when it is beneficial, and a graph modification strategy informed by that characterization.
summary.tldr: The paper derives when graph-based OOD score propagation helps and uses those conditions to design a theoretically supported edge augmentation strategy.

title: Revisiting Score Propagation in Graph Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods effectively adapt large language models (LLMs) to diverse downstream tasks, reducing storage and GPU memory demands. Despite these advantages, several applications pose new challenges to PEFT beyond mere parameter efficiency. One notable challenge involves the efficient deployment of LLMs equipped with multiple task- or user-specific adapters, particularly when different adapters are needed for distinct requests within the same batch. Another challenge is the interpretability of LLMs, which is crucial for understanding how LLMs function. Previous studies introduced various approaches to address different challenges. In this paper, we introduce a novel method, RoAd, which employs a straightforward 2D rotation to adapt LLMs and addresses all the above challenges: (1) RoAd is remarkably parameter-efficient, delivering optimal performance on GLUE, eight commonsense reasoning tasks and four arithmetic reasoning tasks with <0.1% trainable parameters; (2) RoAd facilitates the efficient serving of requests requiring different adapters within a batch, with an overhead comparable to element-wise multiplication instead of batch matrix multiplication; (3) RoAd enhances LLM's interpretability through integration within a framework of distributed interchange intervention, demonstrated via composition experiments.

paragraphs: Adapting a large language model can require very few trainable parameters yet still create deployment challenges. A service may need to answer several requests together while applying a different task or user adapter to each request. RoAd addresses this combination of training efficiency, mixed-adapter batching, and model interpretability through a simple two-dimensional rotation.

The method uses these rotations to adapt the model with less than 0.1% of its parameters trainable. The authors report strong performance on GLUE, eight commonsense reasoning tasks, and four arithmetic reasoning tasks. For serving, the important property is that applying different adapters within one batch has overhead comparable to element-wise multiplication rather than batch matrix multiplication.

RoAd also integrates with distributed interchange intervention, a framework used here to investigate model behavior through composition experiments. Those experiments demonstrate an interpretability benefit alongside the efficiency results. The contribution is therefore a single adaptation mechanism that connects three concerns often addressed separately: how much must be trained, how adapters are served together, and how their effects can be investigated.
summary.tldr: RoAd uses two-dimensional rotations to combine parameter-efficient adaptation, efficient mixed-adapter batching, and composition-based interpretability.

title: 3-in-1: 2D Rotary Adaptation for Efficient Finetuning, Efficient Batching and Composability

abstract: ``The right to be forgotten'' ensured by laws for user data privacy becomes increasingly important. Machine unlearning aims to efficiently remove the effect of certain data points on the trained model parameters so that it can be approximately the same as if one retrains the model from scratch. We propose to leverage projected noisy stochastic gradient descent for unlearning and establish its first approximate unlearning guarantee under the convexity assumption. Our approach exhibits several benefits, including provable complexity saving compared to retraining, and supporting sequential and batch unlearning. Both of these benefits are closely related to our new results on the infinite Wasserstein distance tracking of the adjacent (un)learning processes. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves a similar utility under the same privacy constraint while using $2\%$ and $10\%$ of the gradient computations compared with the state-of-the-art gradient-based approximate unlearning methods for mini-batch and full-batch settings, respectively.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of selected training examples without rebuilding a model from scratch. The intended result is approximately what training without those examples would have produced. This paper studies projected noisy stochastic gradient descent as a way to obtain that result with a formal guarantee.

The guarantee assumes convexity. Under that assumption, the authors establish approximate unlearning and prove computational savings relative to retraining. The method supports both sequential deletion requests and batch deletion. Their analysis tracks the infinite Wasserstein distance between related learning and unlearning processes, providing the mathematical basis for these guarantees and capabilities.

Experiments compare the approach with leading gradient-based approximate unlearning methods under the same privacy constraint. The reported utility is similar while requiring only 2% of their gradient computations in the mini-batch setting and 10% in the full-batch setting. These findings indicate a substantial reduction in gradient work for the evaluated settings. The theoretical contribution is specifically an approximate unlearning guarantee under convexity, rather than an unrestricted guarantee for arbitrary training problems.
summary.tldr: Projected noisy stochastic gradient descent enables certified approximate unlearning under convexity with reduced gradient computation.

title: Certified Machine Unlearning via Noisy Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Bayesian optimisation (BO) is a powerful framework for global optimisation of costly functions, using predictions from Gaussian process models (GPs). In this work, we apply BO to functions that exhibit invariance to a known group of transformations. We show that vanilla and constrained BO algorithms are inefficient when optimising such invariant objectives, and provide a method for incorporating group invariances into the kernel of the GP to produce invariance-aware algorithms that achieve significant improvements in sample efficiency. We derive a bound on the maximum information gain of these invariant kernels, and provide novel upper and lower bounds on the number of observations required for invariance-aware BO algorithms to achieve $\epsilon$-optimality. We demonstrate our method's improved performance on a range of synthetic invariant and quasi-invariant functions. We also apply our method in the case where only some of the invariance is incorporated into the kernel, and find that these kernels achieve similar gains in sample efficiency at significantly reduced computational cost. Finally, we use invariant BO to design a current drive system for a nuclear fusion reactor, finding a high-performance solution where non-invariant methods failed.

paragraphs: When evaluating an objective is expensive, optimization should make good use of each observation. This paper considers objectives whose values stay unchanged under a known group of transformations. It shows that standard and constrained Bayesian optimization can use observations inefficiently when they fail to incorporate this known structure.

The proposed method builds group invariances into the kernel of the Gaussian process used to predict objective values. The resulting optimization algorithms can exploit those invariances when selecting evaluations. The authors bound the maximum information gain of the invariant kernels and derive upper and lower bounds on the observations needed to reach a specified level of near-optimality.

Incorporating only part of the invariance achieves similar gains at substantially lower computational cost in the reported tests. The method is also applied to designing a current drive system for a nuclear fusion reactor, finding a high-performance solution where the evaluated non-invariant approaches failed.
summary.tldr: Encoding known transformation invariances in Gaussian-process kernels makes Bayesian optimization more sample-efficient in theory and reported applications.

title: Sample-efficient Bayesian Optimisation Using Known Invariances

abstract: The recently introduced Consistency models pose an efficient alternative to diffusion algorithms, enabling rapid and good quality image synthesis. These methods overcome the slowness of diffusion models by directly mapping noise to data, while maintaining a (relatively) simpler training. Consistency models enable a fast one- or few-step generation, but they typically fall somewhat short in sample quality when compared to their diffusion origins. In this work we propose a novel and highly effective technique for post-processing Consistency-based generated images, enhancing their perceptual quality. Our approach utilizes a joint classifier-discriminator model, in which both portions are trained adversarially. While the classifier aims to grade an image based on its assignment to a designated class, the discriminator portion of the very same network leverages the softmax values to assess the proximity of the input image to the targeted data manifold, thereby serving as an Energy-based Model. By employing example-specific projected gradient iterations under the guidance of this joint machine, we refine synthesized images and achieve an improved FID scores on the ImageNet 64x64 dataset for both Consistency-Training and Consistency-Distillation techniques.

paragraphs: Consistency models generate images in one or a few steps, offering a fast alternative to diffusion-based generation. Their speed can come with somewhat lower sample quality. This paper addresses that quality gap through post-processing: it starts with images produced by a consistency model and refines them using an additional learned guide.

The guide combines a classifier and a discriminator in one network, with both parts trained adversarially. The classifier assesses how well an image fits its designated class. The discriminator uses the same network's softmax values to assess proximity to the target data manifold, providing an energy-based signal about how closely the image resembles the intended data.

The method applies projected gradient iterations tailored to each generated example under this joint guidance. On ImageNet at 64-by-64 resolution, the authors report improved FID scores for images produced through both consistency training and consistency distillation. The findings support refinement as a way to improve consistency-generated images, with class assignment and data resemblance contributing complementary guidance.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained classifier and energy-based discriminator guide post-processing that improves the quality of consistency-generated images.

title: Enhancing Consistency-Based Image Generation via Adversarialy-Trained Classification and Energy-Based Discrimination

abstract: Foundation models have made significant strides in understanding the genomic language of DNA sequences. However, previous models typically adopt the tokenization methods designed for natural language, which are unsuitable for DNA sequences due to their unique characteristics. In addition, the optimal approach to tokenize DNA remains largely under-explored, and may not be intuitively understood by humans even if discovered. To address these challenges, we introduce MxDNA, a novel framework where the model autonomously learns an effective DNA tokenization strategy through gradient decent. MxDNA employs a sparse Mixture of Convolution Experts coupled with a deformable convolution to model the tokenization process, with the discontinuous, overlapping, and ambiguous nature of meaningful genomic segments explicitly considered. On Nucleotide Transformer Benchmarks and Genomic Benchmarks, MxDNA demonstrates superior performance to existing methods with less pretraining data and time, highlighting its effectiveness. Finally, we show that MxDNA learns unique tokenization strategy distinct to those of previous methods and captures genomic functionalities at a token level during self-supervised pretraining. Our MxDNA aims to provide a new perspective on DNA tokenization, potentially offering broad applications in various domains and yielding profound insights. Code is available at https://github.com/qiaoqiaoLF/MxDNA.

Earlier genomic foundation models commonly borrow tokenization methods from natural language, even though meaningful genomic segments can overlap, be discontinuous, or have ambiguous boundaries. The paper treats tokenization as a learnable part of the model instead of fixing that interpretation in advance.

The framework learns its strategy through gradient descent. It combines a sparse mixture of convolution experts with deformable convolution to represent the tokenization process. These components explicitly account for the unusual structure of genomic segments. This connects the choice of tokens to model training, allowing the representation of the sequence to develop alongside the model's understanding of it.

On the Nucleotide Transformer Benchmarks and Genomic Benchmarks, the authors report better performance than existing methods while using less pretraining data and time. They also show a learned tokenization strategy distinct from previous approaches and token-level capture of genomic functionality during self-supervised pretraining. These findings support adaptive tokenization for the evaluated genomic tasks; broader applications are presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: MxDNA learns DNA tokenization during training, accommodating complex genomic segments and improving benchmark performance with less pretraining data and time.

title: Model Decides How to Tokenize: Adaptive DNA Sequence Tokenization with MxDNA

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are non-Euclidean deep learning models for graph-structured data. Despite their successful and diverse applications, oversmoothing prohibits deep architectures due to node features converging to a single fixed point. This severely limits their potential to solve complex tasks. To counteract this tendency, we propose a plug-and-play module consisting of three steps: Cluster→Normalize→Activate (CNA). By applying CNA modules, GNNs search and form super nodes in each layer, which are normalized and activated individually. We demonstrate in node classification and property prediction tasks that CNA significantly improves the accuracy over the state-of-the-art. Particularly, CNA reaches 94.18% and 95.75% accuracy on Cora and CiteSeer, respectively. It further benefits GNNs in regression tasks as well, reducing the mean squared error compared to all baselines. At the same time, GNNs with CNA require substantially fewer learnable parameters than competing architectures.

paragraphs: The paper addresses oversmoothing in graph neural networks, where node features converge toward a shared fixed point as processing deepens. This makes different nodes harder to distinguish and limits the usefulness of deeper architectures. The proposed Cluster-Normalize-Activate module, or CNA, changes how features are organized and processed within each layer.

With CNA, the network searches for and forms super nodes, then normalizes and activates them individually. The module is designed to be inserted into existing GNNs. Its central idea is to counteract convergence toward a single representation by introducing group-specific processing at successive layers, giving the architecture another way to preserve useful distinctions in graph-structured data.

Experiments on node classification and property prediction show significant accuracy improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The abstract reports 94.18% accuracy on Cora and 95.75% on CiteSeer. Regression tasks also benefit, with lower mean squared error than all tested baselines. These results accompany substantially fewer learnable parameters than competing architectures, linking the proposed module to both predictive gains and parameter efficiency.
summary.tldr: CNA modules counter graph-network oversmoothing through per-layer clustering and separate processing, improving tested prediction tasks with fewer parameters.

title: Graph Neural Networks Need Cluster-Normalize-Activate Modules

abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-image (T2I) models have greatly benefited from large-scale datasets, but they also pose significant risks due to the potential generation of unsafe content. To mitigate this issue, researchers proposed unlearning techniques that attempt to induce the model to unlearn potentially harmful prompts. However, these methods are easily bypassed by adversarial attacks, making them unreliable for ensuring the safety of generated images. In this paper, we propose Direct Unlearning Optimization (DUO), a novel framework for removing NSFW content from T2I models while preserving their performance on unrelated topics. DUO employs a preference optimization approach using curated paired image data, ensuring that the model learns to remove unsafe visual concepts while retain unrelated features. Furthermore, we introduce an output-preserving regularization term to maintain the model's generative capabilities on safe content. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUO can robustly defend against various state-of-the-art red teaming methods without significant performance degradation on unrelated topics, as measured by FID and CLIP scores. Our work contributes to the development of safer and more reliable T2I models, paving the way for their responsible deployment in both closed-source and open-source scenarios.
