paragraphs: This paper develops exploration for agents that must learn through interaction without an external reward. Its motivation is that exploration methods successful in deterministic simulations can struggle with stochastic dynamics or require too much interaction for real robots. The authors draw on active learning to define what makes an action worth exploring.

They train an ensemble of dynamics models and encourage the agent to seek situations where those models disagree. This disagreement becomes a self-supervised objective for acquiring skills. The authors also use the objective to optimize the policy through differentiation, without reinforcement learning, producing a sample-efficient exploration procedure.

The approach is demonstrated in stochastic Atari environments, Mujoco, and Unity. The differentiable exploration method is also implemented on a real robot that learns to interact with objects from scratch. These results show the proposed objective operating across simulated and physical settings. Its central contribution is connecting disagreement among learned dynamics models to both the choice of exploratory behavior and a direct way to optimize that behavior.
summary.tldr: An agent learns to explore without external rewards by maximizing disagreement among dynamics models and directly differentiating the exploration objective.

title: Self-Supervised Exploration via Disagreement

abstract: Self-play, where the algorithm learns by playing against itself without requiring any direct supervision, has become the new weapon in modern Reinforcement Learning (RL) for achieving superhuman performance in practice. However, the majority of exisiting theory in reinforcement learning only applies to the setting where the agent plays against a fixed environment; it remains largely open whether self-play algorithms can be provably effective, especially when it is necessary to manage the exploration/exploitation tradeoff. We study self-play in competitive reinforcement learning under the setting of Markov games, a generalization of Markov decision processes to the two-player case. We introduce a self-play algorithm—Value Iteration with Upper/Lower Confidence Bound (VI-ULCB)—and show that it achieves regret $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ after playing $T$ steps of the game, where the regret is measured by the agent’s performance against a fully adversarial opponent who can exploit the agent’s strategy at any step. We also introduce an explore-then-exploit style algorithm, which achieves a slightly worse regret of $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(T^{2/3})$, but is guaranteed to run in polynomial time even in the worst case. To the best of our knowledge, our work presents the first line of provably sample-efficient self-play algorithms for competitive reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Self-play allows an agent to learn through competition with itself, but guarantees for learning against a fixed environment do not directly resolve the competitive case. This paper studies two-player Markov games, with particular attention to exploration and exploitation. Its performance criterion allows an adversarial opponent to exploit the agent's current strategy at any step.

The first algorithm, Value Iteration with Upper/Lower Confidence Bound, achieves regret growing as the square root of the total number of game steps, up to logarithmic factors. Measuring regret against a fully adversarial opponent makes the result relevant to vulnerability during learning, rather than only performance against a single fixed competitor.

A second algorithm separates exploration from exploitation. Its regret grows at the slightly worse rate of T to the two-thirds power, again up to logarithmic factors, but it has a worst-case polynomial running-time guarantee. The two results expose a tradeoff between the stated regret rate and the available computational guarantee. The authors present the work as, to their knowledge, the first line of provably sample-efficient self-play algorithms for competitive reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Two self-play algorithms provide regret guarantees against adversarial opponents, with a tradeoff between regret rate and worst-case computational guarantees.

title: Provable Self-Play Algorithms for Competitive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Maximizing on k-submodular functions subject to size constraint has received extensive attention recently. In this paper, we investigate a more realistic scenario of this problem that (1) obtaining exact evaluation of an objective function is impractical, instead, its noisy version is acquired; and (2) algorithms are required to take only one single pass over dataset, producing solutions in a timely manner. We propose two novel streaming algorithms, namely DStream and RStream, with their theoretical performance guarantees. We further demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms in two application, showing that our algorithms can return comparative results to state-of-the-art non-streaming methods while using a much fewer number of queries.

paragraphs: The paper studies size-constrained maximization of k-submodular objectives under two practical restrictions. Objective evaluations are noisy because exact values are impractical to obtain, and the algorithm can make only one pass through the dataset. The aim is to produce useful solutions promptly despite uncertainty in the values used to guide selection.

The authors propose two streaming algorithms, DStream and RStream, and establish theoretical performance guarantees for them. Their setting combines the size constraint, noisy evaluations, and single-pass processing in one optimization problem. This matters because an approach designed around repeated access or exact objective values may not fit the intended streaming use.

Experiments in two applications show that the algorithms can achieve results comparable to leading non-streaming methods while making far fewer objective queries. The empirical finding concerns those applications, while the theoretical guarantees provide a separate basis for evaluating the algorithms. Together, the results support single-pass optimization as a useful option when objective queries are costly or available only in noisy form.
summary.tldr: DStream and RStream optimize noisy k-submodular objectives in one pass, with guarantees and competitive reported results using fewer queries.

title: Streaming k-Submodular Maximization under Noise subject to Size Constraint

abstract: Contrastive representation learning has been outstandingly successful in practice. In this work, we identify two key properties related to the contrastive loss: (1) alignment (closeness) of features from positive pairs, and (2) uniformity of the induced distribution of the (normalized) features on the hypersphere. We prove that, asymptotically, the contrastive loss optimizes these properties, and analyze their positive effects on downstream tasks. Empirically, we introduce an optimizable metric to quantify each property. Extensive experiments on standard vision and language datasets confirm the strong agreement between both metrics and downstream task performance. Directly optimizing for these two metrics leads to representations with comparable or better performance at downstream tasks than contrastive learning.

Directly optimizing for these two metrics leads to representations with comparable or better performance at downstream tasks than contrastive learning.

paragraphs: This paper explains contrastive representation learning through two geometric properties of learned features. Alignment means that features from positive pairs lie close together. Uniformity means that normalized features spread evenly across the hypersphere, the surface occupied by vectors of equal length. These properties describe both relationships between paired examples and the overall distribution of representations.

The authors prove that contrastive loss optimizes alignment and uniformity asymptotically, and analyze how these properties benefit downstream tasks. They also introduce an optimizable metric for each property. This turns the geometric explanation into quantities that can be measured during evaluation and used directly as learning objectives.

Experiments on standard vision and language datasets show strong agreement between the two metrics and downstream performance. Directly optimizing the metrics produces representations with comparable or better downstream results than contrastive learning in those experiments. The work thus provides both an asymptotic account of what contrastive loss encourages and empirical support for using those properties to guide representation learning.
summary.tldr: Contrastive learning asymptotically promotes positive-pair alignment and uniform feature distributions, which can also serve as effective direct objectives.

title: Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere

abstract: Federated Learning is a distributed learning setting where the goal is to train a centralized model with training data distributed over a large number of heterogeneous clients, each with unreliable and relatively slow network connections. A common optimization approach used in federated learning is based on the idea of local SGD: each client runs some number of SGD steps locally and then the updated local models are averaged to form the updated global model on the coordinating server. In this paper, we investigate the performance of an asynchronous version of local SGD wherein the clients can communicate with the server at arbitrary time intervals. Our main result shows that for smooth strongly convex and smooth nonconvex functions we achieve convergence rates that match the synchronous version that requires all clients to communicate simultaneously.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a central model using data held by many clients whose network connections may be slow or unreliable. A common method is local stochastic gradient descent: clients take several training steps on their own data, then send their models to a server for averaging.

This paper studies an asynchronous form of that procedure. Clients can communicate with the server at arbitrary time intervals instead of participating in simultaneous communication rounds. The central question is whether relaxing that coordination requirement changes the theoretical rate at which training converges.

For smooth strongly convex objectives and smooth nonconvex objectives, the authors establish convergence rates matching the synchronous version. This shows that, in the analyzed settings, a matching rate is compatible with clients communicating at different times. The result addresses the mathematical cost of asynchronous communication rather than reporting a specific wall-clock speedup. Its practical relevance comes from aligning the learning procedure with heterogeneous clients while retaining the stated convergence-rate comparison.
summary.tldr: Asynchronous local SGD matches synchronous convergence rates for the analyzed smooth convex and nonconvex objectives while allowing arbitrary client communication intervals.

title: Federated Learning under Arbitrary Communication Patterns

abstract: To assess generalization, machine learning scientists typically either (i) bound the generalization gap and then (after training) plug in the empirical risk to obtain a bound on the true risk; or (ii) validate empirically on holdout data. However, (i) typically yields vacuous guarantees for overparameterized models; and (ii) shrinks the training set and its guarantee erodes with each re-use of the holdout set. In this paper, we leverage unlabeled data to produce generalization bounds. After augmenting our (labeled) training set with randomly labeled data, we train in the standard fashion. Whenever classifiers achieve low error on the clean data but high error on the random data, our bound ensures that the true risk is low. We prove that our bound is valid for 0-1 empirical risk minimization and with linear classifiers trained by gradient descent. Our approach is especially useful in conjunction with deep learning due to the early learning phenomenon whereby networks fit true labels before noisy labels but requires one intuitive assumption. Empirically, on canonical computer vision and NLP tasks, our bound provides non-vacuous generalization guarantees that track actual performance closely. This work enables practitioners to certify generalization even when (labeled) holdout data is unavailable and provides insights into the relationship between random label noise and generalization.

Bounds can be uninformative for overparameterized models, while holdout data reduces the training set and loses guarantee strength with reuse. RATT explores another source of evidence: how a trained classifier behaves on additional examples assigned random labels.

The procedure mixes randomly labeled examples into the labeled training set and trains normally. When the classifier achieves low error on clean examples but high error on random ones, the proposed bound certifies low true risk in its applicable setting. The authors prove validity for 0–1 empirical risk minimization and for linear classifiers trained by gradient descent.

For deep learning, the approach uses the observed tendency of networks to learn genuine labels before noisy ones, with an additional assumption required. Experiments on computer vision and language tasks produce non-vacuous bounds that closely track actual performance. The work therefore offers a route to generalization certification without labeled holdout data, using resistance to fitting random labels as informative evidence.
summary.tldr: RATT uses errors on randomly labeled added data to certify generalization under its stated conditions, without requiring a labeled holdout set.

title: RATT: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Guarantee Generalization

abstract: Incorporating graph side information into recommender systems has been widely used to better predict ratings, but relatively few works have focused on theoretical guarantees. Ahn et al. (2018) firstly characterized the optimal sample complexity in the presence of graph side information, but the results are limited due to strict, unrealistic assumptions made on the unknown latent preference matrix and the structure of user clusters. In this work, we propose a new model in which 1) the unknown latent preference matrix can have any discrete values, and 2) users can be clustered into multiple clusters, thereby relaxing the assumptions made in prior work. Under this new model, we fully characterize the optimal sample complexity and develop a computationally-efficient algorithm that matches the optimal sample complexity. Our algorithm is robust to model errors and outperforms the existing algorithms in terms of prediction performance on both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Recommender systems can use graph information alongside observed ratings to estimate users' underlying preferences. The paper investigates how much rating data is needed to do this reliably. Its starting point is that earlier theoretical guarantees relied on restrictive assumptions about preference values and the structure of user groups.

The authors introduce a model allowing arbitrary discrete preference values and multiple user clusters. Within this model, they fully characterize the optimal sample complexity: the amount of data needed for the estimation problem. They also construct a computationally efficient algorithm that attains this statistical requirement, connecting a fundamental data limit to an achievable method.

The contribution therefore broadens the setting in which graph-assisted recommendation has matching sample-complexity guarantees. It does not remove the model's discrete-valued and clustered structure; it relaxes particular restrictions within that structure. The authors additionally report robustness to model errors and better prediction performance than existing algorithms on both synthetic and real data, providing empirical support alongside the theoretical characterization.
summary.tldr: A broader model of graph-assisted recommendation admits an efficient estimator that matches the optimal sample complexity.

title: Discrete-Valued Latent Preference Matrix Estimation with Graph Side Information

abstract: In real-world applications, data often come in a growing manner, where the data volume and the number of classes may increase dynamically. This will bring a critical challenge for learning: given the increasing data volume or the number of classes, one has to instantaneously adjust the neural model capacity to obtain promising performance. Existing methods either ignore the growing nature of data or seek to independently search an optimal architecture for a given dataset, and thus are incapable of promptly adjusting the architectures for the changed data. To address this, we present a neural architecture adaptation method, namely Adaptation eXpert (AdaXpert), to efficiently adjust previous architectures on the growing data. Specifically, we introduce an architecture adjuster to generate a suitable architecture for each data snapshot, based on the previous architecture and the different extent between current and previous data distributions. Furthermore, we propose an adaptation condition to determine the necessity of adjustment, thereby avoiding unnecessary and time-consuming adjustments. Extensive experiments on two growth scenarios (increasing data volume and number of classes) demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: A neural network that suits a dataset today may need different capacity as more examples or new classes arrive. This paper addresses that changing setting with AdaXpert, a method for adapting an existing network architecture as its training data grow. The central problem is deciding how the model should change alongside the data.

AdaXpert uses an architecture adjuster that considers both the previous architecture and the extent of the difference between the current and previous data distributions. It generates an architecture suited to the new data snapshot. This makes the earlier design part of the adaptation process, allowing the method to build on work already done.

The method also includes a condition for deciding whether an architectural adjustment is necessary. That decision matters because repeatedly changing architectures can be time-consuming even when the data do not warrant it. Experiments cover growth in both dataset size and number of classes and demonstrate the method's effectiveness in those two scenarios.
summary.tldr: AdaXpert adapts existing neural architectures to growing datasets and checks whether each adjustment is necessary.

title: AdaXpert: Adapting Neural Architecture for Growing Data

abstract: We propose an algorithm for stochastic and adversarial multiarmed bandits with switching costs, where the algorithm pays a price $\lambda$ every time it switches the arm being played. Our algorithm is based on adaptation of the Tsallis-INF algorithm of Zimmert and Seldin (2021) and requires no prior knowledge of the regime or time horizon. In the oblivious adversarial setting it achieves the minimax optimal regret bound of $ O( (\lambda K)^{1/3}T^{2/3} + \sqrt{KT})$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $K$ is the number of arms. In the stochastically constrained adversarial regime, which includes the stochastic regime as a special case, it achieves a regret bound of $O((\lambda K)^{2/3} T^{1/3} + \ln T)\sum_{i \neq i^*} \Delta_i^{-1})$, where $\Delta_i$ are suboptimality gaps and $i^*$ is the unique optimal arm. In the special case of $\lambda = 0$ (no switching costs), both bounds are minimax optimal within constants. We also explore variants of the problem, where switching cost is allowed to change over time. We provide experimental evaluation showing competitiveness of our algorithm with the relevant baselines in the stochastic, stochastically constrained adversarial, and adversarial regimes with fixed switching cost.

paragraphs: In a multiarmed bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses among alternatives while learning from limited feedback. This paper adds a charge each time the chosen alternative changes. That charge creates a tension between trying different arms and avoiding expensive switches. The proposed algorithm adapts Tsallis-INF without requiring advance knowledge of the environment’s regime or the number of rounds.

For an oblivious adversary, the algorithm achieves a minimax-optimal regret bound combining a switching-cost term proportional to T^(2/3) with a square-root term. In a stochastically constrained adversarial regime, which includes stochastic bandits, it obtains a different guarantee involving T^(1/3), logarithmic growth, and gaps from the unique best arm. These gaps make the guarantee sensitive to how distinguishable the alternatives are.

When switching is free, both guarantees are minimax optimal within constant factors. The authors also investigate costs that vary over time. Experiments with fixed switching costs show competitiveness with relevant baselines across stochastic, constrained-adversarial, and adversarial regimes, supporting the usefulness of one algorithm across these environments.
summary.tldr: One bandit algorithm adapts to stochastic and adversarial environments while accounting for switching costs and requiring no known time horizon.

title: An Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits with Switching Costs

abstract: Stochastic gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo (SGMCMC) is a scalable algorithm for asymptotically exact Bayesian inference in parameter-rich models, such as Bayesian neural networks. However, since mixing can be slow in high dimensions, practitioners often resort to variational inference (VI). Unfortunately, VI makes strong assumptions on both the factorization and functional form of the posterior. To relax these assumptions, this work proposes a new non-parametric variational inference scheme that combines ideas from both SGMCMC and coordinate-ascent VI. The approach relies on a new Langevin-type algorithm that operates on a "self-averaged" posterior energy function, where parts of the latent variables are averaged over samples from earlier iterations of the Markov chain. This way, statistical dependencies between coordinates can be broken in a controlled way, allowing the chain to mix faster. This scheme can be further modified in a "dropout" manner, leading to even more scalability. We test our scheme for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and FMNIST. In all cases, we find improvements in convergence speed and/or final accuracy compared to SGMCMC and parametric VI.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference in models with many parameters faces a trade-off between flexible uncertainty modeling and computational efficiency. Stochastic gradient MCMC can be asymptotically exact, but its sampling chain may explore high-dimensional distributions slowly. Variational inference offers another route, often at the cost of strong assumptions about the posterior’s form and factorization.

This paper combines ideas from stochastic gradient MCMC and coordinate-ascent variational inference in a non-parametric variational scheme. Its Langevin-type algorithm uses a self-averaged posterior energy: some latent variables are averaged using samples collected in earlier chain iterations. This breaks dependencies between coordinates in a controlled way, allowing the chain to mix faster. A dropout-style modification provides additional scalability.

The method is evaluated with ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and FMNIST. In every evaluated case, the authors report improvements in convergence speed, final accuracy, or both compared with stochastic gradient MCMC and parametric variational inference. The contribution offers a way to relax restrictive posterior assumptions while improving practical inference behavior. The stated results do not require both speed and accuracy to improve simultaneously in every case.
summary.tldr: A non-parametric inference scheme uses earlier samples to control coordinate dependencies, improving convergence speed and/or accuracy in the evaluated models.

title: Structured Stochastic Gradient MCMC

abstract: Recently, deep neural networks have gained increasing popularity in the field of time series forecasting. A primary reason for their success is their ability to effectively capture complex temporal dynamics across multiple related time series. The advantages of these deep forecasters only start to emerge in the presence of a sufficient amount of data. This poses a challenge for typical forecasting problems in practice, where there is a limited number of time series or observations per time series, or both. To cope with this data scarcity issue, we propose a novel domain adaptation framework, Domain Adaptation Forecaster (DAF). DAF leverages statistical strengths from a relevant domain with abundant data samples (source) to improve the performance on the domain of interest with limited data (target). In particular, we use an attention-based shared module with a domain discriminator across domains and private modules for individual domains. We induce domain-invariant latent features (queries and keys) and retrain domain-specific features (values) simultaneously to enable joint training of forecasters on source and target domains. A main insight is that our design of aligning keys allows the target domain to leverage source time series even with different characteristics. Extensive experiments on various domains demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on synthetic and real-world datasets, and ablation studies verify the effectiveness of our design choices.

A target application may contain too few series, too few observations per series, or both. Domain Adaptation Forecaster, or DAF, addresses this shortage by transferring statistical information from a relevant source domain with more data.

DAF combines a shared attention module and domain discriminator with modules specific to each domain. This arrangement supports joint training while distinguishing the information used to match temporal patterns from the information that remains particular to each forecasting domain.

A central design insight is that aligning attention keys allows target forecasts to draw on source time series even when those series have different characteristics. Experiments across synthetic and real-world datasets show performance improvements over leading baselines. Ablation studies also support the effectiveness of the design choices. Together, these findings support sharing selected components of attention as a way to improve forecasting when target data are scarce.
summary.tldr: DAF improves forecasting with limited target data by sharing attention features across domains while retaining domain-specific information.

title: Domain Adaptation for Time Series Forecasting via Attention Sharing

abstract: Knowledge and language understanding of models evaluated through question answering (QA) has been usually studied on static snapshots of knowledge, like Wikipedia. However, our world is dynamic, evolves over time, and our models’ knowledge becomes outdated. To study how semi-parametric QA models and their underlying parametric language models (LMs) adapt to evolving knowledge, we construct a new large-scale dataset, StreamingQA, with human written and generated questions asked on a given date, to be answered from 14 years of time-stamped news articles. We evaluate our models quarterly as they read new articles not seen in pre-training. We show that parametric models can be updated without full retraining, while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. For semi-parametric models, adding new articles into the search space allows for rapid adaptation, however, models with an outdated underlying LM under-perform those with a retrained LM. For questions about higher-frequency named entities, parametric updates are particularly beneficial. In our dynamic world, the StreamingQA dataset enables a more realistic evaluation of QA models, and our experiments highlight several promising directions for future research.

paragraphs: Question-answering benchmarks based on a fixed knowledge snapshot do not capture how a model responds when the world changes. StreamingQA instead pairs dated questions with 14 years of timestamped news articles. It includes human-written and generated questions, enabling evaluation of knowledge adaptation at particular points in time.

The authors evaluate models quarterly as they encounter articles absent from pretraining. They study both parametric models, which retain knowledge in their parameters, and semi-parametric models that also search external material. Their experiments show that parametric models can be updated without full retraining while avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

Adding new articles to a semi-parametric model's search space enables rapid adaptation, but keeping its underlying language model outdated produces worse results than using a retrained one. Parameter updates are particularly helpful for questions about more frequently occurring named entities. These findings show that refreshing searchable documents and updating the language model address related aspects of evolving knowledge, and the benchmark makes that distinction observable over time.
summary.tldr: StreamingQA evaluates knowledge adaptation over time and shows benefits from both refreshed retrieval collections and language-model updates.

title: StreamingQA: A Benchmark for Adaptation to New Knowledge over Time in Question Answering Models

abstract: We study approximation of probability measures supported on n-dimensional manifolds embedded in R^m by injective flows—neural networks composed of invertible flows and injective layers. We show that in general, injective flows between R^n and R^m universally approximate measures supported on images of extendable embeddings, which are a subset of standard embeddings: when the embedding dimension m is small, topological obstructions may preclude certain manifolds as admissible targets. When the embedding dimension is sufficiently large, m >= 3n+1, we use an argument from algebraic topology known as the clean trick to prove that the topological obstructions vanish and injective flows universally approximate any differentiable embedding. Along the way we show that the studied injective flows admit efficient projections on the range, and that their optimality can be established "in reverse," resolving a conjecture made in Brehmer & Cranmer 2020.

paragraphs: Some probability distributions occupy a lower-dimensional manifold inside a larger space. This paper studies how injective flows can approximate such distributions. These networks combine invertible flows with injective layers, and the question is whether they can represent both the manifold's geometry and the probability measure supported on it.

The authors establish universal approximation for measures supported on images of extendable embeddings, a particular subset of embeddings. When the surrounding dimension is small, topology can prevent some manifolds from being valid targets. Thus, the representational question depends on geometric structure as well as the dimensions of the manifold and its surrounding space.

When the surrounding dimension m satisfies m ≥ 3n + 1 for an n-dimensional manifold, the authors use an algebraic-topology argument to show that these obstructions disappear, allowing approximation of any differentiable embedding. This is a sufficient dimensional condition. They additionally establish efficient projection onto the flows' range and show that optimality can be established in reverse, resolving the conjecture identified in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Injective flows have universal approximation guarantees for manifold-supported measures, with topological obstructions disappearing under a sufficient dimension bound.

title: Universal Joint Approximation of Manifolds and Densities by Simple Injective Flows

abstract: Extremely large pre-trained language models (PTMs) such as GPT-3 are usually released as a service. It allows users to design task-specific prompts to query the PTMs through some black-box APIs. In such a scenario, which we call Language-Model-as-a-Service (LMaaS), the gradients of PTMs are usually unavailable. Can we optimize the task prompts by only accessing the model inference APIs? This paper proposes the black-box tuning framework to optimize the continuous prompt prepended to the input text via derivative-free optimization. Instead of optimizing in the original high-dimensional prompt space, which is intractable for traditional derivative-free optimization, we perform optimization in a randomly generated subspace due to the low intrinsic dimensionality of large PTMs. The experimental results show that the black-box tuning with RoBERTa on a few labeled samples not only significantly outperforms manual prompt and GPT-3’s in-context learning, but also surpasses the gradient-based counterparts, i.e., prompt tuning and full model tuning.

paragraphs: Large pretrained language models are often accessed through inference services that do not expose gradients. This makes ordinary gradient-based adaptation unavailable to users. The paper asks whether task-specific prompts can still be optimized through model queries alone, using a small amount of labeled task data.

Its black-box tuning framework optimizes a continuous prompt placed before the input text. It uses derivative-free optimization, which does not require gradients. Searching directly over the full prompt space would be intractable for traditional methods of this kind, so the authors search within a randomly generated lower-dimensional subspace, motivated by the low intrinsic dimensionality of large pretrained models.

Experiments using RoBERTa and a few labeled examples report stronger performance than manual prompts, GPT-3's in-context learning, and gradient-based prompt or full-model tuning. These are empirical comparisons in the studied settings. The broader contribution is a concrete way to adapt continuous prompts when inference access is available but access to the model's gradients is not.
summary.tldr: Black-box tuning optimizes continuous prompts in a random low-dimensional subspace using inference queries without model gradients.

title: Black-Box Tuning for Language-Model-as-a-Service

abstract: Modern platforms leverage randomized experiments to make informed decisions from a given set of alternatives. As a particularly challenging scenario, these alternatives can potentially have (i) high volume, with thousands of new items being released each hour, and (ii) short lifetime, either due to the contents’ transient nature, or some underlying non-stationarity that impels the learner to treat the same item as non-identical copies across time. We consider a multiplay bandits model. In each round a set of $k=n^\rho$ actions that will be available for $w$ rounds arrives, each of whose mean reward is drawn from a fixed known distribution. The learner selects a multiset of $n$ actions at a time. We propose an $\ell$-Layered Sieve Policy that recursively refines the action space for $\ell\leq w$ times. We show that for any given $\rho>0$, with suitable $\ell$, the policy achieves $\tilde O (n^{-\min \{\rho, \frac 12 (1+\frac 1w)^{-1}\}})$ regret. We also complement this result with an $\Omega (n^{-\min \{\rho, \frac 12\}})$ lower bound. We further validate the effectiveness of our Sieve Policy via numerical simulations and a field experiment in a large content card serving platform.

We consider a multiplay bandits model. In each round a set of $k=n^\rho$ actions that will be available for $w$ rounds arrives, each of whose mean reward is drawn from a fixed known distribution. The learner selects a multiset of $n$ actions at a time. We propose an $\ell$-Layered Sieve Policy that recursively refines the action space for $\ell\leq w$ times. We show that for any given $\rho>0$, with suitable $\ell$, the policy achieves $\tilde O (n^{-\min \{\rho, \frac 12 (1+\frac 1w)^{-1}\}})$ regret. We also complement this result with an $\Omega (n^{-\min \{\rho, \frac 12\}})$ lower bound. We further validate the effectiveness of our Sieve Policy via numerical simulations and a field experiment in a large content card serving platform.

paragraphs: When new alternatives arrive rapidly and disappear soon afterward, an online learner has little time to decide which ones deserve attention. This paper studies that setting using a multiplay bandit model. Each round introduces n^ρ actions that remain available for w rounds, and the learner makes n selections at a time, allowing repeated selections.

The model assumes action means are drawn from a fixed, known distribution. The proposed Layered Sieve Policy progressively narrows the action space through at most w refinement layers. This organizes learning around the limited lifetime of each action: the policy must refine its choices while those choices are still available.

For any positive ρ, a suitable number of layers gives a regret upper bound whose dependence on n reflects both arrival volume and lifetime. A complementary lower bound shows a fundamental limit with a related, though different, exponent. The authors also validate the policy through simulations and a field experiment on a large content-card platform. The work links theoretical performance to settings where substantial decision volume coexists with rapidly expiring options.
summary.tldr: A layered sieve progressively filters rapidly arriving, short-lived actions, with regret bounds and validation in simulations and a content-platform field experiment.

title: Short-lived High-volume Bandits

abstract: We consider the problem of computing bounds for causal queries on quasi-Markovian graphs with unobserved confounders and discrete valued observed variables, where identifiability does not hold. Existing non-parametric approaches for computing such bounds use multilinear programming (MP) formulations that are often intractable for existing solvers when the degree of the polynomial objective is greater than two. Hence, one often has to resort to either fast approximate heuristics which are not guaranteed to contain the true query value, or more accurate but computationally intensive procedures. We show how to construct an equivalent MP with a polynomial objective of lower degree. In particular, the degree of the objective in the new MP is equal to only the number of C-components that are intervened upon, instead of the total number of C-components. As a result, we can compute exact bounds for significantly larger causal inference problems as compared to what is possible using existing techniques. We also propose a very efficient Frank-Wolfe heuristic that produces very high quality bounds, and scales to large multilinear problems of higher degree.

paragraphs: When unobserved confounders prevent a causal query from being identified, the available information may still constrain its possible values. This paper studies how to compute those bounds for quasi-Markovian graphs with discrete observed variables. Existing formulations use multilinear optimization, which can become difficult for solvers when the polynomial objective has degree greater than two.

The main contribution is an equivalent optimization formulation with a lower-degree objective. Its degree depends only on the number of C-components affected by the intervention, rather than the total number of these components in the graph. This ties the complexity of the objective more closely to the particular causal query being asked.

The reformulation enables exact bounds for substantially larger problems than existing techniques can handle. The authors also introduce an efficient Frank-Wolfe heuristic that produces high-quality bounds for large, higher-degree problems. These are two distinct computational contributions: an equivalent formulation that supports exact calculation and a scalable heuristic whose reported quality should not be confused with an exactness guarantee.
summary.tldr: An equivalent lower-degree optimization formulation makes exact causal bounds tractable for larger problems with unobserved confounding.

title: Causal Bounds in Quasi-Markovian Graphs

abstract: Training normalizing flow generative models can be challenging due to the need to calculate computationally expensive determinants of Jacobians. This paper studies the likelihood-free training of flows and proposes the energy objective, an alternative sample-based loss based on proper scoring rules. The energy objective is determinant-free and supports flexible model architectures that are not easily compatible with maximum likelihood training, including semi-autoregressive energy flows, a novel model family that interpolates between fully autoregressive and non-autoregressive models. Energy flows feature competitive sample quality, posterior inference, and generation speed relative to likelihood-based flows; this performance is decorrelated from the quality of log-likelihood estimates, which are generally very poor. Our findings question the use of maximum likelihood as an objective or a metric, and contribute to a scientific study of its role in generative modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/ps789/SAEF.

paragraphs: Training normalizing flows through maximum likelihood can require expensive Jacobian determinant calculations. This paper explores a sample-based alternative called the energy objective. Based on proper scoring rules, it avoids determinant calculations during training and supports architectures that are difficult to accommodate within ordinary maximum-likelihood training.

The authors introduce semi-autoregressive energy flows, a model family spanning fully autoregressive and non-autoregressive designs. The alternative objective therefore changes more than the loss function: it permits exploration of a wider range of architectural choices. The study evaluates these flows in terms of sample quality, posterior inference, and generation speed relative to likelihood-trained flows.

Energy flows achieve competitive performance on those measures even though their log-likelihood estimates are generally very poor. The observed performance is decorrelated from likelihood-estimation quality. This finding questions how maximum likelihood should be used as a training objective or evaluation metric in generative modeling, while keeping the claim grounded in the behavior of the studied models.
summary.tldr: A determinant-free energy objective trains flexible normalizing flows with competitive generation despite generally poor log-likelihood estimates.

title: Semi-Autoregressive Energy Flows: Exploring Likelihood-Free Training of Normalizing Flows

abstract: We introduce a gradient-based approach for the problem of Bayesian optimal experimental design to learn causal models in a batch setting — a critical component for causal discovery from finite data where interventions can be costly or risky. Existing methods rely on greedy approximations to construct a batch of experiments while using black-box methods to optimize over a single target-state pair to intervene with. In this work, we completely dispose of the black-box optimization techniques and greedy heuristics and instead propose a conceptually simple end-to-end gradient-based optimization procedure to acquire a set of optimal intervention target-value pairs. Such a procedure enables parameterization of the design space to efficiently optimize over a batch of multi-target-state interventions, a setting which has hitherto not been explored due to its complexity. We demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms baselines and existing acquisition strategies in both single-target and multi-target settings across a number of synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships often requires interventions: deliberately changing variables and observing what happens. Because interventions can be expensive or risky, choosing informative experiments matters. This paper studies Bayesian experimental design when several experiments must be selected together, including experiments that intervene on multiple variables at once.

Existing approaches described by the authors assemble batches greedily and use black-box optimization to choose an individual intervention target and value. The proposed method instead makes the design process differentiable and optimizes a batch through gradients. A parameterization of the design space allows the procedure to jointly search over which variables to intervene on and which values to assign them.

This joint formulation makes a complicated experimental design problem accessible to a single end-to-end optimization procedure. Across synthetic datasets, the authors report better performance than the evaluated baselines and acquisition strategies in both single-target and multiple-target settings. The findings support gradient-based batch design as a useful approach to selecting causal experiments, with the reported empirical evidence specifically coming from synthetic data.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly optimizes batches of causal interventions through gradients and reports improvements over existing strategies on synthetic datasets.

title: Differentiable Multi-Target Causal Bayesian Experimental Design

abstract: The behavior of a GP regression depends on the choice of covariance function. Stationary covariance functions are preferred in machine learning applications. However, (non-periodic) stationary covariance functions are always mean reverting and can therefore exhibit pathological behavior when applied to data that does not relax to a fixed global mean value. In this paper we show that it is possible to use improper GP priors with infinite variance to define processes that are stationary but not mean reverting. To this aim, we use of non-positive kernels that can only be defined in this limit regime. The resulting posterior distributions can be computed analytically and it involves a simple correction of the usual formulas. The main contribution of the paper is the introduction of a large family of smooth non-reverting covariance functions that closely resemble the kernels commonly used in the GP literature (e.g. squared exponential and Matérn class). By analyzing both synthetic and real data, we demonstrate that these non-positive kernels solve some known pathologies of mean reverting GP regression while retaining most of the favorable properties of ordinary smooth stationary kernels.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression depends strongly on its covariance function. Stationary choices are popular, but ordinary non-periodic stationary covariance functions bring mean reversion: predictions tend back toward a fixed global mean. That behavior can be inappropriate for data whose values do not settle toward such a mean.

The paper constructs stationary processes without mean reversion by using improper Gaussian process priors with infinite variance. This limiting setting permits non-positive kernels that are unavailable in the ordinary formulation. Despite the unusual prior, posterior distributions remain analytically computable through a simple correction to the standard formulas.

The authors introduce a broad family of smooth, non-reverting covariance functions resembling familiar squared-exponential and Matérn kernels. Analyses of synthetic and real data show that these kernels resolve some known problems caused by mean reversion while preserving most favorable properties of ordinary smooth stationary kernels. The contribution expands the modeling choices available when stationarity is desirable but attraction toward a fixed global mean conflicts with the data.
summary.tldr: Improper infinite-variance Gaussian process priors enable stationary, non-mean-reverting models with analytically computable posteriors.

title: Stationarity without mean reversion in improper Gaussian processes

abstract: Our study addresses the challenge of distinguishing human-written text from Large Language Model (LLM) outputs. We provide evidence that this differentiation is consistently feasible, except when human and machine text distributions are indistinguishable across their entire support. Employing information theory, we show that while detecting machine-generated text becomes harder as it nears human quality, it remains possible with adequate text data. We introduce guidelines on the required text data quantity, either through sample size or sequence length, for reliable AI text detection, through derivations of sample complexity bounds. This research paves the way for advanced detection methods. Our comprehensive empirical tests, conducted across various datasets (Xsum, Squad, IMDb, and Kaggle FakeNews) and with several state-of-the-art text generators (GPT-2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama, Llama-2-13B-Chat-HF, Llama-2-70B-Chat-HF), assess the viability of enhanced detection methods against detectors like RoBERTa-Large/Base-Detector and GPTZero, with increasing sample sizes and sequence lengths. Our findings align with OpenAI's empirical data related to sequence length, marking the first theoretical substantiation for these observations.

paragraphs: This position paper examines whether human-written and machine-generated text can be distinguished as language models improve. Its argument centers on the distributions of the two kinds of text. The authors provide evidence for detection being feasible with sufficient data, except when those distributions are indistinguishable across their entire support.

Using information theory, they derive sample-complexity bounds that relate reliable detection to the amount of text available. That quantity can increase through more samples or longer sequences. As machine text becomes closer to human text, detection becomes harder, but the analysis supports its remaining possible when adequate evidence is available. This is a conditional possibility claim rather than a guarantee for every individual passage.

The empirical study varies sample sizes and sequence lengths across several datasets, text generators, and detection methods. The findings support the theoretical account and align with previously reported observations about the usefulness of longer sequences. The contribution is therefore both an argument about detectability and guidance on the quantity of evidence that reliable detection may require.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that AI-text detection remains possible with enough data when human and machine text distributions are distinguishable.

title: Position: On the Possibilities of AI-Generated Text Detection

abstract: We introduce iterative reasoning through energy diffusion (IRED), a novel framework for learning to reason for a variety of tasks by formulating reasoning and decision-making problems with energy-based optimization. IRED learns energy functions to represent the constraints between input conditions and desired outputs. After training, IRED adapts the number of optimization steps during inference based on problem difficulty, enabling it to solve problems outside its training distribution — such as more complex Sudoku puzzles, matrix completion with large value magnitudes, and path finding in larger graphs. Key to our method’s success is two novel techniques: learning a sequence of annealed energy landscapes for easier inference and a combination of score function and energy landscape supervision for faster and more stable training. Our experiments show that IRED outperforms existing methods in continuous-space reasoning, discrete-space reasoning, and planning tasks, particularly in more challenging scenarios.

paragraphs: IRED treats reasoning and decision-making as optimization problems. It learns energy functions that represent constraints linking an input to a desired output. Producing an answer then involves optimizing against those learned constraints, giving the model an iterative procedure that can continue for different numbers of steps depending on the difficulty of the problem.

Two techniques support this design. First, the method learns a sequence of annealed energy landscapes to make inference easier. Second, training combines supervision of the score function with supervision of the energy landscape, which the authors describe as making training faster and more stable. These techniques address both learning the constraints and using them effectively afterward.

The reported experiments show stronger performance than existing methods on continuous reasoning, discrete reasoning, and planning, especially in harder cases. IRED also solves examples beyond its training distribution, including more complex Sudoku puzzles, matrix completion with larger values, and path finding in larger graphs. These findings support adapting inference effort to difficulty as a way to extend the usefulness of learned reasoning constraints.
summary.tldr: IRED learns energy-based constraints and adapts its optimization effort to solve harder reasoning and planning problems beyond its training distribution.

title: Learning Iterative Reasoning through Energy Diffusion

abstract: Private selection mechanisms (e.g., Report Noisy Max, Sparse Vector) are fundamental primitives of differentially private (DP) data analysis with wide applications to private query release, voting, and hyperparameter tuning. Recent work (Liu and Talwar, 2019; Papernot and Steinke, 2022) has made significant progress in both generalizing private selection mechanisms and tightening their privacy analysis using modern numerical privacy accounting tools, e.g., Rényi DP. But Rényi DP is known to be lossy when $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP is ultimately needed, and there is a trend to close the gap by directly handling privacy profiles, i.e., $\delta$ as a function of $\epsilon$ or its equivalent dual form known as $f$-DPs. In this paper, we work out an easy-to-use recipe that bounds the privacy profiles of ReportNoisyMax and PrivateTuning using the privacy profiles of the base algorithms they corral. Numerically, our approach improves over the RDP-based accounting in all regimes of interest and leads to substantial benefits in end-to-end private learning experiments. Our analysis also suggests new distributions, e.g., binomial distribution for randomizing the number of rounds that leads to more substantial improvements in certain regimes.

paragraphs: Private selection mechanisms are building blocks for tasks such as choosing queries, aggregating votes, and tuning hyperparameters under differential privacy. Their usefulness depends partly on how tightly privacy loss can be accounted for. Analyses based on Rényi differential privacy can lose precision when converted to the final epsilon-delta privacy guarantee that an application needs.

This paper works directly with privacy profiles, which describe delta as a function of epsilon. It provides a recipe for bounding the profiles of ReportNoisyMax and PrivateTuning from the profiles of their underlying algorithms. This makes the privacy accounting compositional: information about the component algorithms is used to analyze the larger selection procedure.

Numerical results improve on Rényi-based accounting across all regimes of interest studied, and end-to-end private-learning experiments show substantial benefits. The analysis also suggests alternative distributions for randomizing the number of rounds, including a binomial distribution that gives larger improvements in certain regimes. The contribution combines tighter accounting with guidance about mechanism design, while keeping those extra gains conditional on the regime.
summary.tldr: Direct privacy-profile analysis tightens accounting for private selection and tuning, with reported benefits in private learning and certain randomized-round designs.

title: Privacy Profiles for Private Selection

abstract: In this paper, we consider multi-objective reinforcement learning, which arises in many real-world problems with multiple optimization goals. We approach the problem with a max-min framework focusing on fairness among the multiple goals and develop a relevant theory and a practical model-free algorithm under the max-min framework. The developed theory provides a theoretical advance in multi-objective reinforcement learning, and the proposed algorithm demonstrates a notable performance improvement over existing baseline methods.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we consider multi-objective reinforcement learning, which arises in many real-world problems with multiple optimization goals. We approach the problem with a max-min framework focusing on fairness among the multiple goals and develop a relevant theory and a practical model-free algorithm under the max-min framework. The developed theory provides a theoretical advance in multi-objective reinforcement learning, and the proposed algorithm demonstrates a notable performance improvement over existing baseline methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning problems can involve several goals that must be pursued together. This paper focuses on fairness among those goals through a max-min formulation. In this formulation, the weakest objective is central to the optimization criterion, making the balance among goals an explicit part of what the learning process seeks to improve.

The authors develop both theory for this formulation and a practical model-free learning algorithm. These are complementary contributions: the theoretical work studies the proposed approach to multiple objectives, while the algorithm provides a way to learn under that approach. The fairness criterion therefore shapes the learning problem itself, rather than appearing only as a separate consideration when assessing results.

The paper reports a notable performance improvement over existing baseline methods. Its stated contribution connects a fairness-oriented objective with theoretical development and an operational learning method. For applications with multiple optimization goals, the work supports max-min reinforcement learning as an approach worth considering when performance on the least well-served goal is a central concern.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theory and a model-free algorithm for max-min reinforcement learning that prioritizes fairness among multiple goals.

title: The Max-Min Formulation of Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning: From Theory to a Model-Free Algorithm

abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) has recently emerged in as a lightweight technique to encourage prompt-adherence in generations, yet has not yet been successfully applied to language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate across a wide array of benchmarks that CFG can be used broadly as an inference-time technique in pure language modeling. We show that CFG (1) improves the performance of Pythia, GPT-2 and LLaMA-family models across: Q&A, reasoning, code generation, and machine translation, achieving SOTA on LAMBADA with LLaMA-7B over PaLM-540B; (2) brings improvements equivalent to a model with twice the parameter-count; (3) can stack alongside other inference-time methods like Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, yielding further improvements in difficult tasks; (4) can be used to increase the faithfulness and coherence of assistants in challenging form-driven and content-driven prompts: in human evaluations we show a 75% preference for using CFG over baseline.

paragraphs: Classifier-free guidance is a technique for encouraging generated outputs to follow a prompt. This paper demonstrates its use during inference in language models, investigating whether guidance can improve both task performance and adherence to user instructions. The study covers Pythia, GPT-2, and models in the LLaMA family across a broad collection of benchmarks.

Reported improvements span question answering, reasoning, code generation, and translation. On LAMBADA, the authors report a state-of-the-art result with LLaMA-7B exceeding PaLM-540B. They also describe gains equivalent to those of a model with twice as many parameters. These comparisons concern the reported evaluations, showing that generation-time guidance can provide substantial benefits without making parameter count the only route to improvement.

Guidance can also be combined with Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, producing additional gains on difficult tasks. For challenging prompts specifying form or content, the authors report improved faithfulness and coherence, with human evaluators preferring guided outputs 75% of the time. The findings connect benchmark gains with better adherence in assistant-style generation.
summary.tldr: Classifier-free guidance improves language-model task performance and prompt adherence, with guided outputs preferred in 75% of the reported human evaluations.

title: Stay on Topic with Classifier-Free Guidance

abstract: Model-based methods have significantly contributed to distinguishing task-irrelevant distractors for visual control. However, prior research has primarily focused on heterogeneous distractors like noisy background videos, leaving homogeneous distractors that closely resemble controllable agents largely unexplored, which poses significant challenges to existing methods. To tackle this problem, we propose Implicit Action Generator (IAG) to learn the implicit actions of visual distractors, and present a new algorithm named implicit Action-informed Diverse visual Distractors Distinguisher (AD3), that leverages the action inferred by IAG to train separated world models. Implicit actions effectively capture the behavior of background distractors, aiding in distinguishing the task-irrelevant components, and the agent can optimize the policy within the task-relevant state space. Our method achieves superior performance on various visual control tasks featuring both heterogeneous and homogeneous distractors. The indispensable role of implicit actions learned by IAG is also empirically validated.

paragraphs: A visual control agent must separate the parts of an image that matter for its task from distracting activity. Earlier work has largely addressed visually different distractions, such as background videos. This paper also targets distractors that closely resemble the controllable agent, making their appearance alone a difficult basis for deciding what belongs in the task representation.

The proposed Implicit Action Generator learns actions that describe how visual distractors behave. AD3 uses these inferred actions to train separate world models. The idea is to use behavior as additional evidence for separating irrelevant visual components from the state that the agent needs to control, then optimize its policy within that task-relevant state space.

The authors report superior performance across visual control tasks containing both visually distinct and agent-like distractors. Their empirical analysis also supports the essential contribution of the inferred actions within the method. The findings suggest that modeling distracting behavior explicitly can improve the separation needed for control, including when appearance makes that separation especially difficult.
summary.tldr: AD3 infers distractors’ implicit actions to separate world models and improve visual control amid both distinct and agent-like distractions.

title: AD3: Implicit Action is the Key for World Models to Distinguish the Diverse Visual Distractors

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as formidable tools, showing their strong capability in handling various open-vocabulary tasks in image recognition, text-driven visual content generation, and visual chatbots, to name a few. In recent years, considerable efforts and resources have been devoted to adaptation methods for improving downstream performance of VLMs, particularly on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like prompt learning. However, a crucial aspect that has been largely overlooked is the confidence calibration problem in fine-tuned VLMs, which could greatly reduce reliability when deploying such models in the real world. This paper bridges the gap by systematically investigating the confidence calibration problem in the context of prompt learning and reveals that existing calibration methods are insufficient to address the problem, especially in the open-vocabulary setting. To solve the problem, we present a simple and effective approach called Distance-Aware Calibration (DAC), which is based on scaling the temperature using as guidance the distance between predicted text labels and base classes. The experiments with 7 distinct prompt learning methods applied across 11 diverse downstream datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DAC, which achieves high efficacy without sacrificing the inference speed.

paragraphs: Adapting a vision-language model can improve its predictions without ensuring that its confidence remains reliable. This paper studies that calibration problem for prompt-based fine-tuning of CLIP, especially when recognition involves an open vocabulary. The authors find that existing calibration methods do not adequately address the problem in this setting.

Their proposed Distance-Aware Calibration method, DAC, adjusts the temperature used to scale confidence. The adjustment is guided by the distance between predicted text labels and the base classes. This makes calibration sensitive to the relationship between the predicted label and the classes that anchor the adaptation setting, using that relationship as additional information for confidence adjustment.

Experiments cover seven prompt learning methods and eleven downstream datasets. The authors report that DAC improves calibration effectively without sacrificing inference speed. The findings highlight confidence reliability as a distinct concern in adapting vision-language models and support label-distance information as a practical signal for calibrating predictions in an open-vocabulary setting.
summary.tldr: DAC improves confidence calibration for prompt-tuned CLIP by adjusting temperature according to predicted labels’ distance from base classes.

title: Open-Vocabulary Calibration for Fine-tuned CLIP

abstract: Research on adversarial robustness has predominantly focused on continuous inputs, leaving categorical inputs, especially tabular attributes, less examined. To echo this challenge, our work aims to evaluate and enhance the robustness of classification over categorical attributes against adversarial perturbations through efficient attack-free approaches. We propose a robustness evaluation metric named Integrated Gradient-Smoothed Gradient (IGSG). It is designed to evaluate the attributional sensitivity of each feature and the decision boundary of the classifier, two aspects that significantly influence adversarial risk, according to our theoretical analysis. Leveraging this metric, we develop an IGSG-based regularization to reduce adversarial risk by suppressing the sensitivity of categorical attributes. We conduct extensive empirical studies over categorical datasets of various application domains. The results affirm the efficacy of both IGSG and IGSG-based regularization. Notably, IGSG-based regularization surpasses the state-of-the-art robust training methods by a margin of approximately 0.4% to 12.2% on average in terms of adversarial accuracy, especially on high-dimension datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/YujunZhou/IGSG.

summary.tldr: IGSG evaluates categorical classifiers’ sensitivity and uses it to improve adversarial robustness without generating attacks.

title: Attack-free Evaluating and Enhancing Adversarial Robustness on Categorical Data

abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle diverse tasks by incorporating multiple input-output examples, known as demonstrations, into the input of LLMs. More recently, advancements in the expanded context windows of LLMs have led to many-shot ICL, which uses hundreds of demonstrations and outperforms few-shot ICL, which relies on fewer examples. However, this approach is often hindered by the high cost of obtaining large amounts of labeled data. To address this challenge, we propose Many-Shot Adaptive Pseudo-LabEling, namely MAPLE, a novel influence-based many-shot ICL framework that utilizes pseudo-labeled samples to compensate for the lack of label information. We first identify a subset of impactful unlabeled samples and perform pseudo-labeling on them by querying LLMs. These pseudo-labeled samples are then adaptively selected and tailored to each test query as input to improve the performance of many-shot ICL, without significant labeling costs. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, showcasing its ability to enhance LLM adaptability and performance with limited labeled data. Our code is provided at https://github.com/Chen-1031/MAPLE_ICL.

paragraphs: In-context learning gives a language model examples of inputs and outputs inside its prompt. Larger context windows allow hundreds of demonstrations, which can improve performance over using only a few. The difficulty is obtaining enough labeled examples without making the approach expensive to use.

MAPLE supplements limited labels with model-generated pseudo-labels. It first identifies an influential subset of unlabeled samples, then queries language models to label those samples. For each test query, it adaptively selects and tailors pseudo-labeled demonstrations. This connects the initial choice of samples worth labeling with the later choice of examples useful for a particular input.

Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate improved adaptability and performance when labeled data is limited, without significant labeling costs. The contribution is a framework for using a large context window more effectively when human-provided labels are scarce. Its two selection stages focus the available labeling effort and prompt content on useful samples, allowing many-shot learning to draw on unlabeled data through pseudo-labeling.
summary.tldr: MAPLE selects influential unlabeled examples, generates pseudo-labels, and adapts demonstrations to each query for many-shot in-context learning.

title: MAPLE: Many-Shot Adaptive Pseudo-Labeling for In-Context Learning

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive progress in tasks such as visual question answering and visual understanding, but they still face significant challenges in emotional reasoning. Current methods to enhance emotional understanding typically rely on fine-tuning or manual annotations, which are resource-intensive and limit scalability. In this work, we focus on improving the ability of MLLMs to capture emotions during the inference phase. Specifically, MLLMs encounter two main issues: they struggle to distinguish between semantically similar emotions, leading to misclassification, and they are overwhelmed by redundant or irrelevant visual information, which distracts from key emotional cues. To address these, we propose Sharpening Emotion Perception in MLLMs (SEPM), which incorporates a Confidence-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Inference framework to refine emotion classification by guiding the model through simpler tasks. Additionally, SEPM employs Focus-on-Emotion Visual Augmentation to reduce visual redundancy by directing the attention of models to relevant emotional cues in images. Experimental results demonstrate that SEPM significantly improves MLLM performance on emotion-related tasks, providing a resource-efficient and scalable solution for emotion recognition.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can understand many aspects of images yet still struggle to recognize emotions. The paper identifies two obstacles: closely related emotions are easily confused, and irrelevant visual information can distract the model from emotional cues. It focuses on improving the inference process, addressing the resource demands associated with approaches based on fine-tuning or manual annotation.

The proposed SEPM method combines two mechanisms. A confidence-guided process moves from coarse judgments toward finer distinctions, guiding the model through simpler tasks to refine emotion classification. A visual augmentation component directs attention toward emotionally relevant image content and reduces redundant information. Together, these mechanisms address both the difficulty of choosing among similar emotions and the difficulty of finding useful visual evidence.

Experiments show significant improvements on emotion-related tasks. The stated significance is that better emotional perception can come from changing how a model examines an image and organizes its judgments during inference. The authors present this as a resource-efficient, scalable approach to emotion recognition, with the reported evidence centered on performance in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: SEPM improves emotion recognition during inference by refining uncertain judgments and focusing visual attention on emotional cues.

title: Catch Your Emotion: Sharpening Emotion Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have opened up greater opportunities to enable fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) to behave as more powerful interactive agents through improved instruction-following ability. However, understanding how this impacts confidence calibration for reliable model output has not been researched in full. In this work, we examine various open-sourced LLMs, identifying significant calibration degradation after instruction tuning in each. Seeking a practical solution, we look towards label smoothing, which has been shown as an effective method to regularize for overconfident predictions but has yet to be widely adopted in the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of LLMs. We first provide insight as to why label smoothing is sufficient to maintain calibration throughout the SFT process. However, settings remain where the effectiveness of smoothing is severely diminished, in particular the case of large vocabulary LLMs (LV-LLMs). We posit the cause to stem from the ability to become over-confident, which has a direct relationship with the hidden size and vocabulary size, and justify this theoretically and experimentally. Finally, we address an outstanding issue regarding the memory footprint of the cross-entropy loss computation in the label smoothed loss setting, designing a customized kernel to dramatically reduce memory consumption without sacrificing speed or performance in comparison to existing solutions for non-smoothed losses.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning makes language models better at following requests, but it can also weaken the relationship between their confidence and correctness. The authors examine several open-source models and find substantial calibration degradation after instruction tuning in each. They investigate whether label smoothing can preserve more reliable confidence during supervised fine-tuning.

Label smoothing softens training targets to discourage overly confident predictions. The paper explains why this can be sufficient to maintain calibration during fine-tuning, while identifying settings where its effectiveness drops sharply. Large-vocabulary models are a particular concern. The authors propose that the ability to become overconfident depends directly on hidden size and vocabulary size, and support this account with theoretical and experimental analysis.

The work also addresses the computational cost of using a smoothed cross-entropy loss. A custom kernel substantially reduces its memory footprint without sacrificing speed or performance relative to existing non-smoothed loss implementations. Together, the findings connect a practical calibration technique to architectural factors that affect its usefulness and an implementation that makes applying it less memory-intensive.
summary.tldr: Label smoothing can preserve calibration during instruction tuning, but its effectiveness depends on model dimensions, especially vocabulary size.

title: Calibrated Language Models and How to Find Them with Label Smoothing

abstract: Designing effective reward functions remains a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), as it often requires extensive human effort and domain expertise. While RL from human feedback has been successful in aligning agents with human intent, acquiring high-quality feedback is costly and labor-intensive, limiting its scalability. Recent advancements in foundation models present a promising alternative–leveraging AI-generated feedback to reduce reliance on human supervision in reward learning. Building on this paradigm, we introduce ERL-VLM, an enhanced rating-based RL method that effectively learns reward functions from AI feedback. Unlike prior methods that rely on pairwise comparisons, ERL-VLM queries large vision-language models (VLMs) for absolute ratings of individual trajectories, enabling more expressive feedback and improved sample efficiency. Additionally, we propose key enhancements to rating-based RL, addressing instability issues caused by data imbalance and noisy labels. Through extensive experiments across both low-level and high-level control tasks, we demonstrate that ERL-VLM significantly outperforms existing VLM-based reward generation methods. Our results demonstrate the potential of AI feedback for scaling RL with minimal human intervention, paving the way for more autonomous and efficient reward learning.
