paragraphs: Reward design is a major source of human effort in reinforcement learning. Human feedback can communicate desired behavior, but collecting enough high-quality judgments is costly. ERL-VLM explores an alternative: learning reward functions from feedback generated by large vision-language models, with the aim of reducing the amount of direct human supervision needed.

The method asks a vision-language model to assign an absolute rating to each individual trajectory, meaning a sequence of agent behavior. This differs from asking which of two trajectories is better. The paper argues that individual ratings provide more expressive feedback and improve sample efficiency. It also introduces enhancements to address training instability caused by imbalanced data and noisy labels.

Experiments span both low-level and high-level control tasks. ERL-VLM significantly outperforms the evaluated methods for generating rewards with vision-language models. The results support the potential of AI-provided ratings for scalable reward learning, while the treatment of imbalance and noise highlights that obtaining ratings and learning reliably from them are both important parts of the approach.
summary.tldr: ERL-VLM learns rewards from vision-language-model ratings of individual trajectories and improves training stability under imbalanced, noisy feedback.

title: Enhancing Rating-Based Reinforcement Learning to Effectively Leverage Feedback from Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: We consider the generative modeling of speech over multiple minutes, a requirement for long-form multimedia generation and audio-native voice assistants. However, textless spoken language models struggle to generate plausible speech past tens of seconds, due to high temporal resolution of speech tokens causing loss of coherence, architectural issues with long-sequence training or extrapolation, and memory costs at inference time. From these considerations we derive SpeechSSM, the first speech language model family to learn from and sample long-form spoken audio (e.g., 16 minutes of read or extemporaneous speech) in a single decoding session without text intermediates. SpeechSSMs leverage recent advances in linear-time sequence modeling to greatly surpass current Transformer spoken LMs in coherence and efficiency on multi-minute generations while still matching them at the utterance level. As we found current spoken language evaluations uninformative, especially in this new long-form setting, we also introduce: LibriSpeech-Long, a benchmark for long-form speech evaluation; new embedding-based and LLM-judged metrics; and quality measurements over length and time. Speech samples, the LibriSpeech-Long dataset, and any future code or model releases can be found at https://google.github.io/tacotron/publications/speechssm/.

paragraphs: Generating speech directly over several minutes creates unusually long token sequences. The authors identify coherence loss, difficulties with long-sequence training or extrapolation, and inference memory costs as obstacles for textless spoken language models. These problems motivate SpeechSSM, a model family designed for sustained speech generation without an intermediate text representation.

SpeechSSM uses advances in linear-time sequence modeling to learn from and generate long spoken audio in a single decoding session. The abstract gives 16-minute read or extemporaneous speech as an example. The authors report substantially better coherence and efficiency than current Transformer spoken language models on multi-minute outputs, while matching their performance at the utterance level.

The paper also addresses evaluation, finding existing speech-language assessments uninformative for this longer setting. It introduces LibriSpeech-Long, embedding-based and language-model-judged metrics, and measurements of quality over length and time. These additions matter because success at generating a short utterance does not adequately describe how a model performs throughout an extended spoken passage.
summary.tldr: SpeechSSM generates multi-minute speech without text intermediates and introduces evaluation tools for sustained audio generation.

title: Long-Form Speech Generation with Spoken Language Models

abstract: We present Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs), a framework for uncovering and aligning interpretable concepts spanning multiple pretrained deep neural networks. Unlike existing concept-based interpretability methods, which focus on a single model, USAEs jointly learn a universal concept space that can reconstruct and interpret the internal activations of multiple models at once. Our core insight is to train a single, overcomplete sparse autoencoder (SAE) that ingests activations from any model and decodes them to approximate the activations of any other model under consideration. By optimizing a shared objective, the learned dictionary captures common factors of variation—concepts—across different tasks, architectures, and datasets. We show that USAEs discover semantically coherent and important universal concepts across vision models; ranging from low-level features (e.g., colors and textures) to higher-level structures (e.g., parts and objects). Overall, USAEs provide a powerful new method for interpretable cross-model analysis and offers novel applications—such as coordinated activation maximization—that open avenues for deeper insights in multi-model AI systems.

paragraphs: Understanding a single neural network does not automatically reveal how its concepts correspond to those of another network. Universal Sparse Autoencoders address this comparison problem by learning one concept space shared across multiple pretrained models. The aim is to reconstruct and interpret their internal activations within a common representation.

The framework trains a single overcomplete sparse autoencoder that can take activations from any model under consideration and decode them into approximate activations of another. A shared training objective encourages its dictionary to capture common factors of variation across architectures, tasks, and datasets. Cross-model reconstruction therefore provides a basis for aligning concepts rather than analyzing each network entirely separately.

In vision models, the authors find semantically coherent and important shared concepts ranging from colors and textures to parts and objects. They also identify applications such as coordinated activation maximization. The contribution is a framework for interpretable comparison across the models being studied: a common concept dictionary makes it possible to investigate representational correspondences at several levels of visual abstraction.
summary.tldr: Universal Sparse Autoencoders learn a shared interpretable concept space by reconstructing activations across multiple pretrained models.

title: Universal Sparse Autoencoders: Interpretable Cross-Model Concept Alignment

abstract: We analyze the Accelerated Noisy Power Method, an algorithm for Principal Component Analysis in the setting where only inexact matrix-vector products are available, which can arise for instance in decentralized PCA. While previous works have established that acceleration can improve convergence rates compared to the standard Noisy Power Method, these guarantees require overly restrictive upper bounds on the magnitude of the perturbations, limiting their practical applicability. We provide an improved analysis of this algorithm, which preserves the accelerated convergence rate under much milder conditions on the perturbations. We show that our new analysis is worst-case optimal, in the sense that the convergence rate cannot be improved, and that the noise conditions we derive cannot be relaxed without sacrificing convergence guarantees. We demonstrate the practical relevance of our results by deriving an accelerated algorithm for decentralized PCA, which has similar communication costs to non-accelerated methods. To our knowledge, this is the first decentralized algorithm for PCA with provably accelerated convergence.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis can require repeated matrix-vector products that are only approximately available, including when computation is decentralized. The Accelerated Noisy Power Method addresses this setting. Earlier guarantees showed faster convergence than the standard noisy method, but required perturbations to be so small that the results had limited practical applicability.

This paper improves the analysis while retaining the accelerated convergence rate. Its main advance is to permit substantially milder conditions on the errors in matrix-vector products. The authors also establish worst-case optimality: within the analyzed setting, neither the convergence rate nor the permitted noise conditions can be improved without losing convergence guarantees.

The analysis leads to an accelerated decentralized PCA algorithm with communication costs similar to those of non-accelerated alternatives. Thus, its theoretical improvement supports faster convergence without requiring a corresponding increase in communication costs. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first decentralized PCA algorithm with provably accelerated convergence, connecting a sharper perturbation analysis to a distributed computational setting.
summary.tldr: A sharper noise analysis preserves accelerated PCA convergence under milder perturbations and yields a provably accelerated decentralized algorithm.

title: Improved Analysis of the Accelerated Noisy Power Method with Applications to Decentralized PCA

abstract: Stochastic optimization (SO) plays a central role in decision-making under uncertainty. Among SO problems, time-varying stochastic optimization (TV-SO) is particularly important due to its applications in adaptive control and machine learning. Non-parametric approaches have been proposed for time-varying deterministic optimization; however, they have not been developed for their stochastic counterparts. This work addresses that gap by developing a stochastic variational framework based on Malliavin calculus. This framework yields non-parametric optimality conditions for SO problems with stochastic decisions and supports the design of a scalable deep-learning algorithm that is insensitive to the parameterization dimension. This algorithm, called the Stochastic Path Follower (SPF), is applied to two important problems under distribution drift, namely least-squares recovery and logistic regression. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based and gradient-based methods in both performance and scalability.

paragraphs: Decision-making under uncertainty often requires optimizing while the underlying distribution changes over time. Although non-parametric approaches had been developed for time-varying deterministic optimization, this paper extends that direction to stochastic problems. Its focus includes settings where the decisions themselves are stochastic, adding randomness to the objects being optimized.

The authors develop a stochastic variational framework using Malliavin calculus. It provides non-parametric optimality conditions and supports a deep-learning algorithm called Stochastic Path Follower. The framework is designed to make the algorithm insensitive to the dimension of the parameterization, addressing scalability alongside the problem of adapting to changing distributions.

In these evaluations, it outperforms the compared state-of-the-art learning-based and gradient-based approaches in performance and scalability. The contribution connects a mathematical extension of non-parametric optimization to a practical learning method, showing how optimality conditions for stochastic decisions can guide computation in changing environments.
summary.tldr: A stochastic variational framework yields Stochastic Path Follower, a scalable learning algorithm evaluated on optimization problems under distribution drift.

title: Non-Parametric Optimization for Scalable Learning in Stochastic Decision Problems

abstract: Aligning large visual generative models with human feedback is often performed through pairwise preference optimization. While such approaches are conceptually simple, they fundamentally rely on annotated pairs, limiting scalability in settings where feedback is collected as independent scalar ratings. In this work, we revisit the KL-regularized alignment objective and show that the optimal policy implicitly compares each sample’s reward to an instance-specific baseline that is generally intractable. We propose a threshold-guided alignment framework that replaces this oracle baseline with a data-driven global threshold estimated from empirical score statistics. This formulation turns alignment into a binary decision task on unpaired data, enabling effective optimization directly from scalar feedback. We further incorporate a confidence weighting term to emphasize samples whose scores deviate strongly from the threshold, improving sample efficiency. Experiments across both diffusion and masked generative paradigms, spanning three test sets and five reward models, show that our method consistently improves preference alignment over previous methods. These results position our threshold-guided framework as a simple yet principled alternative for aligning visual generative models without paired comparisons.

paragraphs: Preference optimization often trains visual generators using annotated pairs, but feedback may instead arrive as separate numerical ratings. This paper develops a way to learn directly from those unpaired scores. It starts by analyzing a KL-regularized alignment objective and identifying the comparison implicit in its optimal policy.

That comparison measures each sample’s reward against an instance-specific baseline, which is generally intractable. The proposed framework replaces it with a single threshold estimated from empirical score statistics. This converts alignment into a binary decision task on independently rated examples. A confidence weight places greater emphasis on samples whose scores are farther from the threshold.

Experiments span diffusion and masked generative models, three test sets, and five reward models. The method consistently improves preference alignment over previous methods in those evaluations, while confidence weighting improves sample efficiency. Its practical significance is that scalar feedback can directly support alignment without annotated pairs. The global threshold is a data-driven replacement for the theoretical baseline, rather than a claim that the baseline itself has become tractable.
summary.tldr: A data-driven score threshold lets visual generators learn preference alignment directly from unpaired scalar feedback.

title: Threshold-Guided Optimization for Visual Generative Models

abstract: Despite the rapid development of AI reviewers, evaluating such systems remains challenging: metrics favor overlap with human reviews over correctness. However, since human reviews often cover only a subset of salient issues and sometimes contain mistakes, they are unreliable as gold references. To address this, we build category-specific benchmark subsets and skip evaluation when the corresponding human reviews are missing to strengthen Completeness. We also leverage reviewer–author–meta-review discussions as expert annotations and filter unreliable reviews accordingly to strengthen Correctness. Finally, we introduce CoCoReviewBench, which curates 3,900 papers from ICLR and NeurIPS to enable reliable and fine-grained evaluation of AI reviewers. Analysis shows that AI reviewers remain limited in correctness and are prone to hallucinations, and highlights reasoning models as more effective reviewers, motivating further directions for improving AI reviewers. Benchmarks and models are available at https://github.com/hexuandeng/CoCoReviewBench.
originalAbstract: Despite the rapid development of AI reviewers, evaluating such systems remains challenging: metrics favor overlap with human reviews over correctness. However, since human reviews often cover only a subset of salient issues and sometimes contain mistakes, they are unreliable as gold references. To address this, we build category-specific benchmark subsets and skip evaluation when the corresponding human reviews are missing to strengthen Completeness. We also leverage reviewer–author–meta-review discussions as expert annotations and filter unreliable reviews accordingly to strengthen Correctness. Finally, we introduce CoCoReviewBench, which curates 3,900 papers from ICLR and NeurIPS to enable reliable and fine-grained evaluation of AI reviewers. Analysis shows that AI reviewers remain limited in correctness and are prone to hallucinations, and highlights reasoning models as more effective reviewers, motivating further directions for improving AI reviewers. Benchmarks and models are available at https://github.com/hexuandeng/CoCoReviewBench.

paragraphs: Evaluating an AI reviewer by its overlap with a human review can reward agreement without establishing correctness. Human reviews may overlook relevant issues or make mistakes themselves. CoCoReviewBench addresses this problem by changing how reference material is organized and checked, aiming to assess both the coverage and validity of an AI reviewer’s observations.

For completeness, the authors construct subsets for specific issue categories and omit an evaluation when the corresponding human review material is absent. This makes the available reference coverage part of the evaluation design. For correctness, they use discussions involving reviewers, authors, and meta-reviewers as expert annotations and filter reviews judged unreliable through that process.

The resulting benchmark contains 3,900 papers from ICLR and NeurIPS and supports more detailed evaluation of reviewing behavior. Its analysis finds that AI reviewers still struggle with correctness and produce hallucinated claims. Reasoning models perform more effectively as reviewers in the reported analysis. The benchmark therefore helps distinguish convincing review language from criticism supported by the paper and its expert discussion.
summary.tldr: CoCoReviewBench uses category-specific references and expert review discussions to assess AI reviewers’ completeness and correctness more reliably.

title: CoCoReviewBench: A Completeness- and Correctness-Oriented Benchmark for AI Reviewers

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often assign disproportionate attention to the first token, a phenomenon known as the attention sink. Several recent approaches aim to address this issue, including Sink Attention in GPT-OSS and Gated Attention in Qwen3-Next. However, a comprehensive analysis of the relationship among these attention mechanisms is lacking. In this work, we provide both theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrating that the sink in Vanilla Attention and Sink Attention naturally construct a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism within attention layers. This insight explains the head collapse phenomenon observed in prior work, where only a fixed subset of attention heads contributes to generation. To mitigate head collapse, we propose a sink-aware training algorithm with an auxiliary load balancing loss designed for attention layers. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves effective head load balancing and improves model performance across Vanilla Attention, Sink Attention, and Gated Attention. We hope this study offers a new perspective on attention mechanisms and encourages further exploration of the inherent MoE structure within attention layers.

paragraphs: Language models often direct unusually large amounts of attention toward the first token, a pattern called an attention sink. Several attention variants address this behavior, but their relationships have remained incompletely understood. This paper connects the sink to another observed pattern: only a fixed subset of attention heads contributes to generation.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors show that sinks in Vanilla Attention and Sink Attention naturally create a mixture-of-experts mechanism inside attention layers. This interpretation explains head collapse in terms of how contributions are distributed across heads. It gives a common perspective on behavior that otherwise appears to be an isolated attention anomaly.

The proposed training method adds an auxiliary loss that balances head loads while accounting for sinks. Experiments report more balanced contributions and improved model performance across Vanilla Attention, Sink Attention, and Gated Attention. The practical contribution is a training intervention informed by the analysis; the conceptual contribution is recognizing an inherent expert-like structure within attention itself.
summary.tldr: Interpreting attention sinks as an internal mixture-of-experts mechanism motivates a load-balancing loss that reduces head collapse and improves performance.

title: Attention Sink Forges Native MoE in Attention Layers: Sink-Aware Training to Address Head Collapse

abstract: High-resolution visual encoders in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) substantially improve fine-grained perception, yet incur prohibitive computational costs.Existing token pruning methods are effective on natural images but struggle with spatially sparse structured inputs (e.g., charts), where critical high-frequency information is sparse, localized, and structurally essential. To address this challenge, we propose Adaptive Dual-Branch Token Sparsification (AD-BTS), a density-aware framework that dynamically allocates computation according to input signal characteristics. Specifically, AD-BTS introduces a Gradient-based Routing Gate (GRG) that uses lightweight pixel-level gradient statistics to estimate structural flatness and guide routing. Then, AD-BTS activates either a Redundancy Selection Branch (RSB) for aggressive token pruning with a frozen encoder, or a Structural Fusion Branch (SFB) with conditional LoRA and context fusion to preserve sparse structural information.Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL demonstrate that AD-BTS establishes a new Pareto frontier between efficiency and accuracy. Under extreme compression (20% token retention), AD-BTS outperforms the strongest baseline by 12.1% on ChartQA while achieving a 1.8$\times$ prefill speedup, effectively reconciling computational efficiency with structural robustness.

paragraphs: High-resolution visual encoders help multimodal models recognize fine details, but processing all their image tokens is expensive. Removing tokens can save computation, yet charts present a particular problem: important structure may occupy only small, isolated regions. A pruning rule that works on natural photographs can therefore discard information essential to interpreting a structured image.

AD-BTS chooses between two processing branches according to the image’s spatial information density. A lightweight gate examines pixel gradients to estimate how flat or structurally varied the input is. One branch aggressively removes redundant tokens while keeping the encoder frozen. The other uses conditional LoRA adaptation and context fusion to preserve sparse structural information.

Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL report an improved tradeoff between accuracy and computation. With 20% of tokens retained, AD-BTS outperforms the strongest baseline by 12.1% on ChartQA and achieves a 1.8× prefill speedup. These results support adapting the compression strategy to the input’s structure, rather than applying the same token-selection behavior to every image.
summary.tldr: AD-BTS routes images through different token-compression branches to preserve sparse visual structure while reducing computation.

title: AD-BTS: Adaptive Dual-Branch Token Sparsification via Spatial Information Density

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) may memorize sensitive cross-modal information during pretraining, making machine unlearning (MU) crucial. Existing methods typically evaluate unlearning effectiveness based on output deviations, while overlooking the generation quality after unlearning. This can easily lead to hallucinated or rigid responses, thereby affecting the usability and safety of the unlearned model. To address this issue, we propose ASRU, a controllable multimodal unlearning framework that incorporates generation quality as a core evaluation objective. ASRU first induces initial refusal behavior through activation redirection, and then optimizes fine-grained refusal boundaries using a customized reward function, thereby achieving a better trade-off between target knowledge unlearning and model utility. Experiments on Qwen3-VL show that ASRU significantly improves unlearning effectiveness (+24.6%) on average and generation quality (5.8$\times$) on average while effectively preserving model utility, using only a small amount of retained supervision data.

paragraphs: ASRU addresses the problem of removing sensitive knowledge from models that process multiple modalities while keeping their responses useful. The authors argue that judging unlearning mainly by changes in model outputs can overlook response quality. A model might stop producing the targeted information yet respond with hallucinations or inflexible refusals, undermining the usefulness of the unlearning procedure.

The framework makes generation quality an explicit objective. It first redirects internal activations to induce refusal behavior. It then uses reinforcement learning with a customized reward to refine the boundary between requests that should be refused and those the model should still handle. These stages connect an initial behavioral change with more selective control over that behavior.

Experiments on Qwen3-VL report average improvements of 24.6% in unlearning effectiveness and 5.8 times in generation quality while preserving model utility. The method uses only a small amount of retained supervision data. The results support evaluating unlearning through both targeted forgetting and the quality of the model that remains.
summary.tldr: ASRU combines activation steering and reinforcement learning to improve targeted multimodal unlearning while preserving useful, higher-quality responses.

title: ASRU: Activation Steering Meets Reinforcement Unlearning for Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Despite its importance to applications in protein design, predicting protein properties like binding affinity and thermostability from sparse experimental data remains a significant challenge. Accordingly, we introduce a class of sequence kernels that exploit evolutionary substitution matrices as well as local linearity and demonstrate that the resulting Gaussian processes provide data-efficient models of protein property landscapes, frequently outperforming alternatives that rely on foundation model embeddings. Furthermore–by learning what are in effect structure-aware substitution matrices–we show that our kernels can readily incorporate structural information from foundation models. We demonstrate that these structure-conditioned kernels are well suited to multi-task learning across multiple protein property landscapes and can decisively outperform local supervised learning methods.

paragraphs: Protein design often requires predicting properties such as binding affinity or heat stability from relatively few experimental measurements. This paper develops sequence kernels for that sparse-data setting. A kernel specifies how protein sequences relate to one another, allowing a Gaussian process to use those relationships when predicting a protein’s properties.

The proposed kernels combine evolutionary substitution matrices with local linearity. This supplies structure about sequence changes instead of relying only on representations extracted from a foundation model. The authors report that the resulting Gaussian processes learn protein property landscapes efficiently from limited data and frequently outperform alternatives based on foundation-model embeddings.

The approach can also incorporate structural information supplied by foundation models. It does so by learning substitution relationships that effectively depend on protein structure. These structure-conditioned kernels support learning across multiple protein property landscapes, and the authors show that they can substantially outperform local supervised methods. The contribution therefore includes both a sequence-based predictor and a way to use foundation-model information within a flexible kernel framework.
summary.tldr: Flexible sequence and structure-conditioned kernels enable data-efficient protein property prediction, often outperforming embedding-based alternatives.

title: Flexible Kernels for Protein Property Prediction

abstract: While existing text-to-speech (TTS) models exhibit high expressiveness, fine-grained control over composite instructions remains challenging due to the structural mismatch between discrete textual intents and continuous acoustic realizations. Inspired by human cognitive decoupling, we introduce AgentSteerTTS, a multi-agent closed-loop framework designed for intent-faithful expressive control of composite instructions. First, in our framework, an adversarial disentanglement module mitigates speaker-emotion leakage through gradient reversal and cross-covariance regularization. Next, a Dual-Stream Anchoring Controller grounds abstract intents using a large-scale acoustic prototype library: a Retrieval Agent selects expressive anchors, while a Synthesis Agent fuses them into continuous control vectors via gated attention. Finally, a Fast–Slow Feedback Agent refines output intensity through latent gradient correction and resolves semantic–acoustic mismatches using high-level perceptual critique. Experiments on a composite-instruction benchmark and public test sets show that AgentSteerTTS yields consistent and significant improvements to the baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. Our code and models will be released.

paragraphs: Expressive speech synthesis does not automatically provide precise control over several instructions at once. Text describes intentions in discrete terms, while speech realizes them through continuously varying sound. AgentSteerTTS addresses this mismatch by separating instruction interpretation, speech control, and feedback into cooperating agents.

The framework first reduces interference between speaker identity and emotion using adversarial disentanglement, gradient reversal, and cross-covariance regularization. A retrieval agent then selects expressive examples from a large acoustic prototype library. These examples anchor abstract instructions in acoustic patterns. A synthesis agent combines the selected anchors through gated attention to produce continuous control vectors.

A feedback agent closes the loop at two levels. Latent gradient corrections adjust output intensity, while higher-level perceptual critiques address mismatches between the intended meaning and the resulting sound. Experiments on a composite-instruction benchmark and public test sets report consistent, significant improvements over the evaluated baselines. The contribution is a coordinated control process that connects textual intent to acoustic examples and then uses feedback to refine the result.
summary.tldr: AgentSteerTTS combines acoustic-example retrieval, speech synthesis, and feedback agents to improve control over composite speech instructions.

title: AgentSteerTTS: A Multi-Agent Closed-Loop Framework for Composite-Instruction Text-to-Speech

abstract: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) is a training method that seeks to find flat minima in deep learning, resulting in state-of-the-art performance across various domains. Instead of minimizing the loss of the current weights, SAM minimizes the worst-case loss in its neighborhood in the parameter space. In this paper, we investigate the convergence instability of SAM near a saddle point. Using the qualitative theory of dynamical systems, we explain how SAM becomes stuck in the saddle point and theoretically prove that the saddle point can become an attractor under SAM dynamics. Additionally, we show that this convergence instability can also occur in stochastic dynamical systems by establishing the diffusion of SAM. We prove that SAM diffusion is worse than that of vanilla gradient descent in terms of saddle point escape. Finally, we demonstrate that often overlooked training tricks, momentum and batch-size, might be important to mitigate the convergence instability and achieve high generalization performance. Our theoretical and empirical results are thoroughly verified through experiments on several well-known optimization problems and benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization trains a model against the worst loss in a neighborhood around its current parameters, with the aim of finding flatter solutions. This paper investigates a potential difficulty in those dynamics near saddle points. A saddle is a location where the loss landscape offers different behavior in different directions, making escape important for optimization.

Using dynamical-systems theory, the authors prove that a saddle point can become an attractor under SAM. They also derive a diffusion description of stochastic SAM and show that the instability can persist in that setting. In their saddle-escape analysis, SAM's diffusion behaves worse than that of ordinary gradient descent. These results identify a possible failure mechanism rather than asserting that every SAM run becomes trapped.

The paper examines momentum and batch size as factors that might mitigate the instability and help achieve strong generalization. Experiments on optimization problems and benchmark tasks support the theoretical and empirical analysis. The contribution is an explanation of how a method designed to favor flat solutions can develop undesirable local dynamics, together with evidence that familiar training choices can matter for managing them.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that SAM can make saddle points attractive and examines momentum and batch size as possible mitigations.

title: Stability Analysis of Sharpness-Aware Minimization

abstract: SLM-LLM routing accelerates generation by strategically invoking LLMs for critical tokens. However, existing methods typically train routers to mimic the LLM, capping performance at the reference trajectory’s limit. In this work, we demonstrate that the SLM-LLM collaborative inference space offers a richer solution set, yielding correct answers even when the LLM fails. To exploit this, we propose AlphaRouter, a routing framework learning optimal collaborative inference paths via a search and iterative update paradigm. Formulating routing as a Markov Decision Process, we introduce Collaborative Inference Tree Search (CITS) to explore the solution space. To tackle the severe credit assignment challenge posed by sparse rewards, we propose Tree-Advantage Policy Optimization (TAPO) to optimize the routing policy. By leveraging counterfactual advantages within the tree structure, TAPO effectively attributes the final reward to specific routing decisions, stabilizing training without dense supervision. Extensive experiments show that AlphaRouter advances the Pareto frontier of accuracy-efficiency trade-offs by exploiting better inference trajectories in the collaborative space. Code is available at https://github.com/StripeLife0217/AlphaRouter.

paragraphs: AlphaRouter studies how a small language model and a large language model can share generation one token at a time. Existing routers often learn to imitate the larger model, tying their behavior to its reference generation path. The authors show that combining the two models can produce correct answers even in cases where the larger model alone fails.

The method treats routing as a sequential decision problem and alternates search with policy updates. Collaborative Inference Tree Search explores different sequences of model choices. Tree-Advantage Policy Optimization then uses comparisons between alternative branches to estimate how individual routing decisions contributed to the final result. This addresses the difficulty of learning from a reward that arrives only after a full answer.

The experiments report an improved accuracy–efficiency frontier, meaning the method finds more favorable combinations of answer quality and computational cost. The contribution is therefore broader than avoiding expensive tokens: it uses search to discover productive collaborations and trains a router to reproduce useful decision patterns without dense supervision.
summary.tldr: AlphaRouter learns token-level collaboration between small and large language models through tree search and reinforcement learning, improving the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

title: AlphaRouter: Token-level Routing Between SLM and LLM with Reinforcement Learning and Tree Search

abstract: We present adversarial flow models, a class of generative models that belongs to both the adversarial and flow families. Our method supports native one-step and multi-step generation and is trained with an adversarial objective. Unlike traditional GANs, in which the generator learns an arbitrary transport map between the noise and data distributions, our generator is encouraged to learn a deterministic noise-to-data mapping. This significantly stabilizes adversarial training. Unlike consistency-based methods, our model directly learns one-step or few-step generation without having to learn the intermediate timesteps of the probability flow for propagation. This preserves model capacity and avoids error accumulation. Under the same 1NFE setting on ImageNet-256px, our B/2 model approaches the performance of consistency-based XL/2 models, while our XL/2 model achieves a new best FID of 2.38. We additionally demonstrate end-to-end training of 56-layer and 112-layer models without any intermediate supervision, achieving FIDs of 2.08 and 1.94 with a single forward pass and surpassing the corresponding 28-layer 2NFE and 4NFE counterparts with equal compute and parameters.

paragraphs: Adversarial flow models combine adversarial training with a flow-based approach to generation. They support both one-step and multi-step sampling. The proposed generator is encouraged to learn a deterministic noise-to-data mapping, which the authors report substantially stabilizes adversarial training compared with allowing an arbitrary transport map.

The method directly learns generation in one or a few steps without learning intermediate probability-flow timesteps for propagation. The authors argue that this preserves model capacity and avoids accumulated propagation errors. They also train deeper generators end to end without intermediate supervision, exploring whether additional depth can deliver strong single-pass generation.

On ImageNet at 256-pixel resolution with one function evaluation, the B/2 model approaches consistency-based XL/2 models, while the proposed XL/2 reaches an FID of 2.38. Models with 56 and 112 layers achieve FIDs of 2.08 and 1.94 in one forward pass. They outperform corresponding 28-layer models using two and four evaluations at equal compute and parameter counts, supporting the reported effectiveness of deeper single-pass generators.
summary.tldr: Adversarial flow models directly learn one-step or few-step generation, with reported training stability and strong single-pass image-generation results.

title: Adversarial Flow Models

abstract: Stochastic programming is often challenged by epistemic uncertainty, where critical probability distributions are poorly characterized or unknown due to a lack of data. To address this, we pioneer a novel framework for stochastic programming that minimizes an upper confidence bound (UCB) on the expected random cost, acting as a robustness-seeking strategy. Our central contribution is the Average Percentile Upper Bound (APUB), a new statistical construct that serves as both a statistically rigorous upper bound for population means and an approximate risk metric for sample means. We rigorously prove the asymptotic correctness and consistency of APUB, establishing a reliable foundation for data-driven decision-making. We also develop practical solution methods, including a bootstrap sampling approximation method and an L-shaped method, to solve APUB optimization problems, with a specific focus on two-stage linear stochastic optimization with random recourse. Empirical demonstrations on a two-stage product mix problem reveal the significant benefits of our APUB optimization framework, which fortifies the process against epistemic uncertainty while reinforcing key decision-making attributes like reliability and consistency. The implementation and source code are available at https://github.com/8Wings/APUB-Optimization.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization chooses actions when costs depend on uncertain outcomes. With limited data, even the probability distributions governing those outcomes may be poorly known. This paper proposes choosing decisions by minimizing an upper confidence bound on expected cost, making uncertainty about the estimated cost part of the optimization objective.

The central statistical construct is the Average Percentile Upper Bound, or APUB. It serves as an upper bound for population means and as an approximate risk measure for sample means. The authors prove asymptotic correctness and consistency, providing theoretical support for its behavior as the amount of data grows. These are specifically asymptotic properties rather than an unrestricted claim about every finite dataset.

The paper develops a bootstrap approximation and an L-shaped solution method, focusing on two-stage linear stochastic problems with random recourse. Demonstrations on a two-stage product mix problem report benefits for reliability and consistency under uncertainty about the underlying distribution. The approach connects statistical uncertainty to the decision rule itself, seeking robust choices through a conservative estimate of expected cost.
summary.tldr: APUB optimization minimizes an upper confidence bound on expected cost to account for poorly known probability distributions.

title: Minimizing Upper Confidence Bounds: A Data-Driven Framework for Stochastic Programming

abstract: We introduce NetDiff, a node-conditioned denoising diffusion model that generates directional link topologies and a two-slot transmit/receive parity for mobile ad hoc networks. Directional antennas can yield high throughput but require globally consistent link decisions under sector, interference, connectivity, and half-duplex constraints. NetDiff improves global coherence with Absolute Cross-Attentive Modulation (ACAM) tokens, which provide permutation-invariant global signals and help the model match graph-level counts (e.g., density and sector usage). We also propose partial diffusion to update an existing topology with a small number of denoising steps, enabling fast reconfiguration under mobility. NetDiff reaches over 95 % of target performance with constant inference time, outperforms heuristic and omnidirectional baselines, and improves over a strong diffusion graph-transformer baseline on key metrics.

NetDiff improves global coherence with Absolute Cross-Attentive Modulation (ACAM) tokens, which provide permutation-invariant global signals and help the model match graph-level counts (e.g., density and sector usage). paragraphs: Directional antennas can support high throughput in mobile ad hoc networks, but their link choices must work together across the network. Decisions must account for interference, connectivity, antenna sectors, and half-duplex operation. NetDiff generates directional connection topologies together with a two-slot transmit/receive parity, treating these coupled decisions as a graph generation problem.

The model uses node-conditioned denoising diffusion. To improve global consistency, it adds Absolute Cross-Attentive Modulation tokens that supply network-wide signals independent of node ordering. These signals help the generated graph match overall quantities such as density and sector usage, bringing aggregate network requirements into a process that must also decide individual connections.

For changing node positions, partial diffusion updates an existing topology using only a few denoising steps. The reported results reach more than 95% of target performance with constant inference time. NetDiff outperforms heuristic and omnidirectional baselines and improves key metrics over a strong diffusion graph-transformer baseline, supporting both its global coordination mechanism and its use for rapid reconfiguration.
summary.tldr: NetDiff uses globally informed graph diffusion and partial updates to generate and rapidly reconfigure directional mobile-network topologies.

title: NetDiff: Graph Diffusion with Improved Global Capabilities to Generate and Update Mobile Network Topologies

abstract: Reliable epidemic forecasting is critical for public health decision-making yet remains challenging due to data sparsity and the non-stationary nature of disease dynamics. While recent hybrid models attempt to integrate mechanistic principles with data-driven approaches, they often relegate mechanistic priors to merely auxiliary features or regularization terms. This design not only obscures the interpretability of the mechanistic contribution but also fails to inherit the capability of physical models to generalize under non-stationary dynamics, as the core architecture remains predominantly data-driven. To address these limitations, we propose EpiDiff, a unified framework that synergizes epidemiological domain knowledge with the generative power of diffusion models. Unlike methods that rigidly fuse features, EpiDiff employs a novel uncertainty-aware steering mechanism during inference. Specifically, we quantify the posterior uncertainty of mechanistic estimations and use it to dynamically modulate the diffusion process. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that EpiDiff consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and robustness, particularly under non-stationary distributions, while offering transparent insights into model reliance by explicitly visualizing when the forecast is governed by mechanistic laws versus data-driven patterns.

title: Bridging Dynamics and Data: A Unified Diffusion Framework for Mechanistically-Informed Epidemic Forecasting

abstract: We introduce FlowOptimizer, a deep unfolded, flow-based framework for learning iterative optimizers. Motivated by the expressiveness of flow models, we represent each optimization iteration via a velocity field that operates on a population of candidate solutions, i.e., a set of parallel iterates, conditioned on contextual information including their objective values and gradients, as well as population-level statistics. The velocity field is initially trained in a simulation-free manner by matching displacements from source populations to improved target ones obtained through sampling. Subsequently, we unfold the flow model across optimization iterations and fine-tune the entire sequence end-to-end by directly optimizing objective values over a targeted class of problems. Notably, FlowOptimizer is a self-supervised framework whose training relies solely on objective evaluations without requiring knowledge of solutions. We evaluate our approach on a series of tasks from standard non-convex optimization benchmarks to real-world problems from robotics, power grid and supply chain applications. FlowOptimizer consistently outperforms well-established sampling-based/gradient-based traditional optimization and learning-to-optimize methods by orders of magnitude in terms of solution quality. We further highlight its ability to be trained on low-dimensional problems and successfully generalize to substantially higher-dimensional $(\times 10)$ ones.

These results support learning coordinated search updates from objective-based feedback.
summary.tldr: FlowOptimizer learns population-based optimization steps through flow models, achieving large reported solution-quality gains without needing known optimal solutions.

title: Learning-to-Optimize via Deep Unfolded Flows

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for embodied intelligence. However, most existing approaches are built on large-scale Transformers, resulting in substantial inference latency and energy consumption that limit their practical deployment in low-power, real-time scenarios. We propose SpikeVLA, an end-to-end spiking VLA framework for embodied navigation with energy-efficient inference, consisting of three key components. (i) a spiking vision encoder, Spike-V, that replaces dense continuous computation with event-driven spiking representations to reduce the energy cost of visual representation learning, (ii) a multimodal spiking large language model, Spike-L, that reformulates cross-modal reasoning with spiking dynamics and token-level event-driven sparsity to further lower inference overhead, and (iii) a spiking action policy network, Spike-A, that uses Laplacian-kernel population coding and end-to-end reinforcement learning to produce stable, robust continuous control under low-energy constraints. Experiments on multimodal interaction and robotic control tasks show that SpikeVLA significantly reduces energy consumption and computational overhead while maintaining competitive performance, highlighting its potential for low-power, real-time embodied intelligence.

The contribution therefore extends spiking computation across the full perception-to-action chain rather than limiting it to one component. Experiments on multimodal interaction and robotic control report significant reductions in energy consumption and computational overhead while maintaining competitive performance. These results indicate potential for low-power, real-time embodied systems, with the reported evidence emphasizing efficiency alongside retained task capability.
summary.tldr: SpikeVLA uses spiking networks throughout perception, reasoning, and action to reduce energy and computation while retaining competitive performance.

title: SpikeVLA: Vision-Language-Action Models with Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems remain brittle under realistic retrieval noise, even when the required evidence appears in the top-$K$ results. A key reason is that retrievers and rerankers optimize solely for relevance, often selecting either trivial, answer-revealing passages or evidence that lacks the critical information required to answer the question, without considering whether the evidence is suitable for the generator. We propose BAR-RAG, which reframes the reranker as a boundary-aware evidence selector that targets the generator’s Goldilocks Zone—evidence that is neither trivially easy nor fundamentally unanswerable for the generator, but is challenging yet sufficient for inference and thus provides the strongest learning signal. BAR-RAG trains the selector with reinforcement learning using generator feedback, and adopts a two-stage pipeline that fine-tunes the generator under the induced evidence distribution to mitigate the distribution mismatch between training and inference. Experiments on knowledge-intensive question answering benchmarks show that BAR-RAG consistently improves end-to-end performance under noisy retrieval, achieving an average gain of 10.3% over strong RAG and reranking baselines while substantially improving robustness.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can fail even when useful evidence is present among retrieved passages. This paper argues that relevance alone does not determine whether evidence suits the generator. Some passages reveal the answer too directly to provide a strong learning signal, while others omit information needed to answer at all.

BAR-RAG trains a selector to target evidence that is challenging but still sufficient for the generator to reason from. The selector learns through reinforcement learning using feedback from the generator. A two-stage pipeline also fine-tunes the generator on the evidence distribution produced by selection, reducing the mismatch between its training inputs and what it encounters during inference.

The approach therefore coordinates evidence selection with the capabilities and learning needs of the answering model. On knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks with noisy retrieval, BAR-RAG consistently improves end-to-end performance. The authors report an average gain of 10.3% over strong retrieval-augmented generation and reranking baselines, alongside substantially improved robustness. The findings support treating evidence suitability as more than topical relevance.
summary.tldr: BAR-RAG selects challenging but sufficient evidence using generator feedback, improving question answering and robustness under noisy retrieval.

title: Rethinking the Reranker: Boundary-Aware Evidence Selection for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%. Project Page & Code: https://lems-svd.github.io

paragraphs: Low-rank compression reduces the computational demands of language models by approximating their weight matrices with smaller representations. Its success depends on two decisions: how much capacity to retain in each layer, and how to construct each approximation. This paper addresses both, arguing that existing error estimates miss propagation across layers and that some Fisher-based decompositions suffer severe rank collapse.

Layer-wise Error Modeling Search, or LEMS, estimates compression error using local layer importance, global importance, and a propagation bias. It then allocates ranks across the model through an integer linear programming formulation. The accompanying KFAC-SVD method changes the decomposition itself, using token-level statistics to mitigate the rank deficiency found in earlier Fisher-based approaches.

Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama3 families, LEMS outperforms the tested search strategies, with zero-shot accuracy gains reaching 4.8 percentage points and results extending to 70-billion-parameter models. KFAC-SVD delivers an average perplexity improvement of 15%. These findings show benefits from improving both the allocation of compressed capacity and the quality of the retained representation.
summary.tldr: LEMS and KFAC-SVD improve language-model compression by refining layer-wise rank allocation and low-rank decomposition quality.

title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search

abstract: Flow-based methods have achieved significant success in various generative modeling tasks, capturing nuanced details within complex data distributions. However, few existing works have exploited this unique capability to resolve fine-grained structural details beyond generation tasks. This paper presents a flow-inspired framework for representation learning. First, we demonstrate that a rectified flow trained using independent coupling is zero everywhere at $t=0.5$ if and only if the source and target distributions are identical. We term this property the zero-flow criterion. Second, we show that this criterion can certify conditional independence, thereby extracting sufficient information from the data. Third, we translate this criterion into a tractable, simulation-free loss function that enables learning amortized Markov blankets in graphical models and latent representations in self-supervised learning tasks. Experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Zero-Flow Encoders adapts ideas from flow-based generation to learning informative representations. Its starting point is a precise mathematical criterion: for a rectified flow trained with independent coupling, the flow is zero everywhere at the midpoint exactly when the source and target distributions are identical. The independent-coupling setting is part of the stated result.

The authors show how this zero-flow criterion can certify conditional independence. That connection lets the framework identify representations containing sufficient information from the data. The contribution moves from comparing distributions to determining whether a learned representation retains the information needed for the relevant conditional relationships.

To make the idea usable in training, the paper derives a tractable loss that does not require simulation. It applies this loss to learning amortized Markov blankets in graphical models and latent representations for self-supervised learning. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness. Together, these results establish a route from a distribution-equality criterion to practical representation-learning objectives.
summary.tldr: Zero-Flow Encoders turns a midpoint flow criterion for distribution equality into a simulation-free objective for learning sufficient representations.

title: Zero-Flow Encoders

abstract: Quaternion neural networks are parameter-efficient and model multidimensional dependencies by representing four related features as a single entity. However, existing quaternion self-attention computes component-wise scores and applies independent softmax operations to each component, which increases the computational cost and allows attention distributions to diverge across components. We propose a shared-score quaternion self-attention mechanism that computes a single real-valued score using the quaternion inner product and applies a shared attention distribution across all components. This reduces score-computation multiplications by 75% and the number of softmax operations from four to one. We prove that, when queries and keys are produced by quaternion linear projections that induce component pre-mixing, the component-wise and shared scores lie in the same interaction subspace, indicating that independent component-wise attention primarily re-parameterizes the same interactions rather than expanding the feature interaction space. In speech enhancement, our method reduces inference time by up to 44.3% on a GPU and 58.1% on a CPU while maintaining quality, with consistent trends across vision and natural language processing.

paragraphs: Quaternion networks represent four related features together, allowing them to model dependencies with relatively few parameters. Existing quaternion attention mechanisms nevertheless calculate separate scores and softmax distributions for the four components. This adds computation and permits the components to attend differently. The paper replaces these separate calculations with a shared attention distribution.

The proposed mechanism uses the quaternion inner product to produce one real-valued score. It reduces score-computation multiplications by 75% and replaces four softmax operations with one. The authors also prove a conditional result: when quaternion linear projections mix components before producing queries and keys, shared and component-wise scores occupy the same interaction subspace. Under that condition, independent component attention mainly re-parameterizes existing interactions.

In speech enhancement, the shared-score method reduces inference time by up to 44.3% on a GPU and 58.1% on a CPU while maintaining quality. Vision and language experiments show consistent trends. These findings connect a targeted computational simplification with a theoretical explanation of why it can retain useful interactions. The subspace result depends on the stated component-mixing condition, while the runtime benefits are empirical.
summary.tldr: Shared-score quaternion attention reduces redundant computation and speeds inference, with a conditional proof that it retains the same interaction subspace.

title: Quaternion Self-Attention with Shared Scores

abstract: The known stylistic biases in LLM judges, such as a preference for verbosity or specific sentence structures, present an underexplored security vulnerability. In this work, we introduce BITE (BIas exploraTion and Exploitation), a black-box adversarial framework that learns semantics-preserving edits to mislead an LLM judge and artificially inflate the scores it assigns. We cast the selection of stylistic edits as a contextual bandit problem and use a LinUCB policy to adaptively choose edits that maximize the judge’s score without access to model parameters or gradients. Empirically, we test BITE across a diverse range of LLM judges and tasks, including both pointwise and pairwise comparisons on chatbot leaderboards and AI-reviewer benchmarks. BITE achieves an attack success rate exceeding 65% and raises scores by 1–2 points on a 9-point scale, all while preserving semantic equivalence. We further assess the attack’s stealthiness, showing that BITE evades standard style-control methods and several detection baselines. Our findings expose a fundamental weakness in the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm and motivate robust, attack-aware evaluation. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianglinyang/llm-as-a-judge-attack.

paragraphs: Language models used as judges can favor particular writing styles, including verbosity or sentence patterns. BITE investigates whether these preferences can be deliberately exploited to increase scores without improving the underlying content. It treats stylistic bias as a vulnerability in automated evaluation, rather than merely a source of incidental scoring variation.

summary.tldr: BITE adaptively selects meaning-preserving style edits that exploit LLM judges’ biases and inflate evaluation scores.

title: Turning Bias into Bugs: Bandit-Guided Style Manipulation Attacks on LLM Judges

abstract: Gradient-variation online learning has drawn increasing attention due to its deep connections to game theory and optimization. It has been studied extensively in the full-information setting, but is underexplored with bandit feedback. In this work, we focus on gradient variation in Bandit Convex Optimization (BCO) with two-point feedback. By proposing a refined analysis of the non-consecutive gradient variation, a fundamental quantity in gradient variation with bandit feedback, we improve the dimension dependence for both convex and strongly convex functions compared with the best known results (Chiang et al., 2013). Our improved analysis of the non-consecutive gradient variation also implies other favorable problem-dependent guarantees, such as gradient-variance and small-loss regret bounds. Beyond the two-point setup, we demonstrate the versatility of our technique by achieving the first gradient-variation bound for one-point bandit linear optimization over hyper-rectangular domains. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our results in more challenging tasks such as dynamic and universal regret minimization, establishing the first gradient-variation dynamic and universal regret bounds for two-point BCO.

paragraphs: Online optimization studies decisions made over a sequence of changing losses. With bandit feedback, the learner sees limited evaluations rather than complete information about each loss function. This paper develops guarantees that reflect gradient variation, allowing the analysis to account for how the optimization problem changes across the sequence.

The main contribution is a refined treatment of non-consecutive gradient variation in bandit convex optimization with two-point feedback. It improves how the guarantees depend on dimension for both convex and strongly convex losses compared with the previous best results. The same analysis also produces guarantees expressed through gradient variance and small loss, connecting performance to additional properties of the particular problem.

The technique extends beyond this setting. The paper establishes the first gradient-variation guarantee for one-point bandit linear optimization over hyper-rectangular domains. It also derives the first gradient-variation bounds for dynamic and universal regret in two-point bandit convex optimization. These are theoretical advances in making limited-feedback guarantees more responsive to problem structure.
summary.tldr: A refined gradient-variation analysis improves dimension dependence and extends problem-dependent guarantees in bandit optimization.

title: Improved Dimension Dependence for Bandit Convex Optimization with Gradient Variation

abstract: Evaluation metrics establish a standard assessment framework for models, playing a pivotal role in model optimization and advancement. However, widely adopted pixel-wise metrics (e.g., IoU, Dice) rely heavily on pixel-level statistics, often failing to capture the structural integrity of predictions. While the S-measure (S-m) incorporates structural perception to some extent, it struggles to differentiate critical structural violations and remains insensitive to background false positives and small objects. To address these limitations, we propose the Topology-aware measure (T-m), a novel metric designed to explicitly quantify topological consistency. T-m employs the Fuzzy Jaccard Index as a foundational score, integrates a Topological Integrity term (I-topo) to penalize critical structural fragmentation, and utilizes a Boundary Alignment term (A-bdy) to evaluate boundary alignment. These three components synergize to achieve robust evaluation of prediction maps at the topological level. We establish a rigorous Meta-Measure validation framework and benchmark our method against nine mainstream metrics across diverse complex scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that T-m performs exceptionally in downstream tasks and maintains high consistency with human visual perception.

paragraphs: Binary segmentation metrics determine how predicted foreground regions are judged against reference masks. Pixel-based scores such as IoU and Dice can miss structural damage because their statistics do not directly describe connectivity or fragmentation. The paper also identifies weaknesses in S-measure, including sensitivity to small objects, background false positives, and critical structural violations.

T-measure combines three complementary components. A Fuzzy Jaccard score provides the foundational comparison. A topological integrity term penalizes important structural fragmentation, while a boundary alignment term assesses how well predicted borders match the reference. Together, these components aim to account for both regional agreement and the organization of the predicted shape.

The authors introduce a Meta-Measure validation framework and compare T-measure with nine mainstream metrics across complex scenarios. They report strong downstream performance and high agreement with human visual perception. The contribution is an evaluation criterion that explicitly incorporates topology, making structural integrity part of the score used to assess segmentation quality rather than relying entirely on pixel-level agreement.
summary.tldr: T-measure evaluates binary segmentation using regional agreement, structural integrity, and boundary alignment to better reflect perceived quality.

title: T-measure: A Topology-Consistent Metric for Binary Segmentation

abstract: Transparent objects pose a fundamental challenge for depth estimation and 3D reconstruction due to their violation of Lambertian assumptions, leading to severe geometry degradation in downstream tasks. To address this, we propose a novel geometry-guided preprocessing framework GHOST that leverages visual foundation models to transform transparent regions into opaque, structurally consistent representations without requiring downstream model retraining. Specifically, our pipeline utilizes (1) TransDINO and (2) TransDecomp to disentangle masks and transparency physical properties, while (3) DAF-Net recovers surface normal priors to encode geometric curvature. Subsequently, (4) GeoSemTransNet integrates these multi-modal cues to synthesize a texture-rich opaque RGB image that preserves the transparent object’s 3D structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the accuracy of state-of-the-art depth estimation and reconstruction models on transparent objects by restoring essential photometric cues.

Specifically, our pipeline utilizes (1) TransDINO and (2) TransDecomp to disentangle masks and transparency physical properties, while (3) DAF-Net recovers surface normal priors to encode geometric curvature. Subsequently, (4) GeoSemTransNet integrates these multi-modal cues to synthesize a texture-rich opaque RGB image that preserves the transparent object’s 3D structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the accuracy of state-of-the-art depth estimation and reconstruction models on transparent objects by restoring essential photometric cues.

paragraphs: Transparent objects are difficult for depth estimation and 3D reconstruction because their appearance violates the Lambertian assumptions used by these systems. The resulting visual cues can lead to severe errors in recovered geometry. GHOST addresses this at the input stage, transforming transparent regions into opaque representations that existing downstream models can process without retraining.

The pipeline combines several sources of information. TransDINO and TransDecomp separate object masks and physical properties of transparency. DAF-Net estimates surface-normal priors, providing information about curvature and surface orientation. GeoSemTransNet then combines these cues to synthesize a textured, opaque RGB image while preserving the transparent object's three-dimensional structure.

The added texture supplies photometric cues that are otherwise unreliable or missing for transparent surfaces. Experiments show significant accuracy improvements for state-of-the-art depth estimation and reconstruction models on transparent objects. The stated contribution is therefore a geometry-guided preprocessing strategy: it changes the visual evidence presented to downstream systems while retaining the structure those systems are meant to recover.
summary.tldr: GHOST synthesizes geometry-consistent opaque textures on transparent objects to improve depth estimation and reconstruction without downstream retraining.

title: GHOST: Geometry-Guided Hallucination of Opaque Surface Textures

abstract: This position paper argues that documentation is infrastructure for reproducible geometry reasoning, and more broadly that mathematical benchmarks built around formal domain-specific languages (DSLs) need an executable interface contract: documented vocabulary should be matched by executable, versioned behavior and runnable examples. We use JGEX (as implemented by Newclid and AlphaGeometry) as a prototypical case study of how documentation–implementation gaps, missing examples, and nontrivial encoding choices can constrain expressivity, affect solver behavior, fragment tool interoperability, and bias benchmark construction. We introduce JGEXDiv, a curated collection of $137$ Euclidean geometry problems with released JGEX formalizations, natural-language rewrites, and metadata, covering $51.4%$ of admissible construction-pattern bins under our signature-based analysis. We also release a conformance suite for the documented JGEX interface, including minimal runnable examples, validation scripts, and a predicate-level support matrix. This audit surfaces cross-tool discrepancies, including documented predicates that execute under pinned Newclid v3.0.1 but are not recognized by Yuclid, as well as predicates that are unsupported or unstable under Newclid itself. Finally, we provide an executable NL$\rightarrow$JGEX baseline under the same backend. We argue that these artifacts together form an executable interface contract for mathematical DSL benchmarks, and should be treated as first-class research artifacts alongside datasets and evaluation code.

paragraphs: This paper argues that reproducible mathematical reasoning benchmarks need documentation tied to executable, versioned behavior. It studies JGEX, a formal language for geometry, to show how gaps between documented vocabulary and actual implementation can affect what problems can be expressed, how solvers behave, and whether tools work together.

The authors introduce JGEXDiv, containing 137 Euclidean geometry problems with formalizations, natural-language rewrites, and metadata. The paper argues that this interface contract deserves the same research status as datasets and evaluation code.
summary.tldr: A JGEX dataset and conformance audit show why mathematical benchmarks need documentation backed by versioned execution and runnable examples.

abstract: This position paper argues that AI agents with chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities are predisposed to exhibit collusive behavior and should be required to obtain behavioral certification before making decisions that affect economic markets. This is because integrating these agents into society could collapse the legal evidentiary distinction between competition and collusion among independent firms without eroding the economic harm distinction. Experiments with DeepSeek-R1 agents in the Bertrand oligopoly pricing domain reveal a tendency towards tacit collusion that persists even when humans prompt the agents not to collude. We further show that the chain-of-thought of these agents can be steered toward either extremely collusive or highly competitive behavior in a way that is not semantically detectable by another LLM analyzing the reasoning traces. As a result, deploying reasoning agents for market decisions leads to collusive economic outcomes without any evidence of conspiracy or intent. Thus, certification based on observed behavior in representative situations is necessary to prevent collusion. We provide preliminary evidence that such agents can be steered in a generalizable way toward efficient competitive equilibria. However, developing a comprehensive behavioral certification will be required before these models can be deployed in real-world markets while ensuring their stability and efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper argues that reasoning agents should receive behavioral certification before making decisions affecting economic markets. Its concern is that agents can produce harmful coordination between firms without the evidence of conspiracy or intent typically used to distinguish collusion from competition. Economic harm could therefore persist even when familiar evidentiary signals are absent.

In experiments involving DeepSeek-R1 agents in a Bertrand oligopoly pricing setting, the authors observed a tendency toward tacit collusion even when people instructed the agents not to collude. They also steered reasoning toward strongly collusive or highly competitive behavior in ways another LLM could not detect semantically by inspecting the reasoning traces. These findings motivate evaluating decisions directly rather than relying on instructions or readable reasoning as assurances.

The authors propose certification based on behavior in representative situations. They report preliminary evidence that steering can generalize toward efficient competitive outcomes, offering a possible path for intervention. However, they explicitly call for comprehensive certification before real-world deployment can ensure market stability and efficiency. The experimental results support that agenda within the studied pricing setting.
summary.tldr: Pricing experiments motivate behavioral certification because reasoning agents can collude despite instructions and apparently uninformative reasoning traces.

abstract: Hill-climbing search is the most commonly used search algorithm in ILP systems because it permits the generation of theories in short running times. However, a well known drawback of this greedy search strategy is its myopia. Macro-operators (or macros for short), a recently proposed technique to reduce the search space explored by exhaustive search, can also be argued to reduce the myopia of hill-climbing search by automatically performing a variable-depth look-ahead in the search space. Surprisingly, macros have not been employed in a greedy learner. In this paper, we integrate macros into a hill-climbing learner. In a detailed comparative study in several domains, we show that indeed a hill-climbing learner using macros performs significantly better than current state-of-the-art systems involving other techniques for reducing myopia, such as fixed-depth look-ahead, template-based look-ahead, beam-search, or determinate literals. In addition, macros, in contrast to some of the other approaches, can be computed fully automatically and do not require user involvement nor special domain properties such as determinacy.
