paragraphs: Hill-climbing search builds a solution by repeatedly choosing a promising nearby change. In inductive logic programming, this makes it possible to learn theories quickly, but it also creates short-sightedness: an immediately attractive step may hide a better sequence of changes. This paper investigates a way to give that search a longer view.

The authors integrate macro-operators into a hill-climbing learner. A macro packages multiple search steps into a larger move, allowing the learner to look ahead by a variable number of steps. This differs from always looking a fixed distance ahead or relying on templates to specify which longer moves should be considered.

Across several domains, the macro-based learner performs significantly better than the compared systems using fixed-depth look-ahead, template-based look-ahead, beam search, or determinate literals. The reported advantage is empirical. A further practical benefit is that the macros can be computed automatically, without user input or special domain properties such as determinacy.
summary.tldr: Automatically generated macro-operators improve a hill-climbing learner’s ability to look ahead and outperform several alternatives in the reported comparisons.

title: A comparative study on methods for reducing myopia of hill-climbing search in multirelational learning

abstract: Kernel conditional random fields (KCRFs) are introduced as a framework for discriminative modeling of graph-structured data. A representer theorem for conditional graphical models is given which shows how kernel conditional random fields arise from risk minimization procedures defined using Mercer kernels on labeled graphs. A procedure for greedily selecting cliques in the dual representation is then proposed, which allows sparse representations. By incorporating kernels and implicit feature spaces into conditional graphical models, the framework enables semi-supervised learning algorithms for structured data through the use of graph kernels. The framework and clique selection methods are demonstrated in synthetic data experiments, and are also applied to the problem of protein secondary structure prediction.

paragraphs: This paper introduces kernel conditional random fields as a framework for discriminative modeling of graph-structured data. The framework brings kernels and their implicit feature spaces into conditional graphical models. It connects the representation of structured relationships with the feature representations made available by kernel methods.

A representer theorem establishes how these models arise from risk minimization using Mercer kernels on labeled graphs. The authors then propose a greedy procedure for selecting cliques in the dual representation. This selection procedure allows sparse representations, giving the framework a way to retain selected components of the model rather than requiring a dense representation.

The use of graph kernels also enables semi-supervised learning algorithms for structured data within the framework. The authors demonstrate the models and clique selection procedures on synthetic data and apply them to protein secondary structure prediction. The contribution combines a theoretical representation result, a sparsity mechanism, and demonstrations of their use in structured prediction.
summary.tldr: Kernel conditional random fields combine implicit kernel features with graphical models and use greedy clique selection to obtain sparse representations.

title: Kernel conditional random fields: representation and clique selection

abstract: We consider a variant of Q-learning in continuous state spaces under the totalexpected discounted cost criterion combined with local function approximationmethods. Provided that the function approximator satisfies certaininterpolation properties, the resulting algorithm is shown to converge withprobability one. The limit function is shown to satisfy a fixed point equationof the Bellman type, where the fixed point operator depends on the stationarydistribution of the exploration policy and the function approximation method.The basic algorithm is extended in several ways. In particular, a variant ofthe algorithm is obtained that is shown to converge in probability to theoptimal Q function. Preliminary computer simulations are presented thatconfirm the validity of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies Q-learning in continuous state spaces, where a local function approximator represents values across states. Its objective is total expected discounted cost. The central theoretical question is whether combining Q-learning with this approximation strategy leads to a stable limiting function, and how that function relates to optimal decision making.

The basic algorithm converges with probability one provided the approximator satisfies specified interpolation properties. Its limit obeys a Bellman-type fixed-point equation. Crucially, the operator in that equation depends on both the stationary distribution of the exploration policy and the approximation method. The convergence result therefore characterizes a limit shaped by how states are explored and how values are represented.

The authors also develop extensions, including a variant shown to converge in probability to the optimal Q function. That is a distinct result from almost-sure convergence of the basic method to its own fixed point. Preliminary simulations support the approach, complementing the theoretical analysis without replacing the stated conditions or merging the two convergence guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under interpolation conditions, approximate Q-learning converges almost surely, while an extended variant converges in probability to the optimal Q function.

title: Interpolation-based Q-learning

abstract: Kernelizing partial least squares (PLS), an algorithm which has been particularly popular in chemometrics, leads to kernel PLS which has several interesting properties, including a sub-cubic runtime for learning, and an iterative construction of directions which are relevant for predicting the outputs. We show that the kernelization of PLS introduces interesting properties not found in ordinary PLS, giving novel insights into the workings of kernel PLS and the connections to kernel ridge regression and conjugate gradient descent methods. Furthermore, we show how to correctly define the degrees of freedom for kernel PLS and how to efficiently compute an unbiased estimate. Finally, we address the practical problem of model selection. We demonstrate how to use the degrees of freedom estimate to perform effective model selection, and discuss how to implement crossvalidation schemes efficiently.

Furthermore, we show how to correctly define the degrees of freedom for kernel PLS and how to efficiently compute an unbiased estimate. Finally, we address the practical problem of model selection. paragraphs: Partial least squares builds directions that are useful for predicting outputs. Its kernel version combines this iterative construction with a learning runtime described as sub-cubic. The paper examines what changes when PLS is kernelized, with attention to properties that do not occur in ordinary PLS and to their implications for understanding the algorithm.

The analysis develops connections between kernel PLS, kernel ridge regression, and conjugate gradient descent. It also addresses degrees of freedom, a way of describing the flexibility of the fitted model. The authors show how to define this quantity correctly for kernel PLS and efficiently compute an unbiased estimate of it.

These theoretical contributions are tied to the practical task of selecting a model. The paper demonstrates effective model selection using the degrees-of-freedom estimate and discusses efficient cross-validation implementations. Its significance is that understanding the method's structure leads to tools for choosing model complexity, alongside a clearer account of how kernel PLS relates to other learning and optimization procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes kernel PLS, derives an efficiently computed unbiased degrees-of-freedom estimate, and uses it for effective model selection.

title: Kernelizing PLS, degrees of freedom, and efficient model selection

abstract: We propose a deterministic method to evaluate the integral of a positive function based on soft-binning functions that smoothly cut the integral into smaller integrals that are easier to approximate. The use of mean-field approximations for each individual sub-part leads to a tractable algorithm that alternates between the optimization of the bins and the approximation of the local integrals. We introduce suitable choices for the binning functions such that a standard mean field approximation can be extended to a split mean field approximation without the need for extra derivations. The method can be seen as a revival of the ideas underlying the mixture mean field approach. We discuss the relation between the two algorithms.

We introduce suitable choices for the binning functions such that a standard mean field approximation can be extended to a split mean field approximation without the need for extra derivations. paragraphs: This paper proposes a deterministic method for approximating the integral of a positive function. Its central idea is to use smooth binning functions to divide the original integral into smaller pieces that are easier to approximate. These soft divisions allow the method to organize the calculation into local subproblems.

Each piece receives its own mean-field approximation. The resulting algorithm alternates between improving the bins and improving the approximations to the local integrals. Thus, the subdivision and the approximations are optimized together: the method adjusts how the integral is split as well as how each resulting part is evaluated.

The authors identify binning functions that allow an existing mean-field approximation to be extended into a split version without additional derivations. This makes the method useful as an extension of an established approximation procedure. They also explain its relationship to mixture mean-field methods, presenting it as a revival of related ideas. The contribution is a tractable construction for combining multiple local approximations within one integral calculation.
summary.tldr: Split variational inference smoothly divides an integral into parts and jointly optimizes their bins and local mean-field approximations.

title: Split variational inference

abstract: We present a novel approach for learning nonlinear dynamic models, which leads to a new set of tools capable of solving problems that are otherwise difficult. We provide theory showing this new approach is consistent for models with long range structure, and apply the approach to motion capture and high-dimensional video data, yielding results superior to standard alternatives.
originalAbstract: We present a novel approach for learning nonlinear dynamic models, which leads to a new set of tools capable of solving problems that are otherwise difficult. We provide theory showing this new approach is consistent for models with long range structure, and apply the approach to motion capture and high-dimensional video data, yielding results superior to standard alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper concerns learning nonlinear dynamic models, which describe changing systems whose behavior is not captured by a linear relationship. The authors introduce a new learning approach intended to make difficult modeling problems tractable. Its stated scope includes models with long-range structure, so the work addresses dependencies that extend beyond only nearby moments in a sequence.

The theoretical contribution is a consistency result for models with that long-range structure. Consistency provides an asymptotic justification for learning within the setting covered by the theory. This matters because the approach is supported by an argument about its learning behavior, in addition to demonstrations of what it can do on observed data.

The empirical applications involve motion capture and high-dimensional video, two settings where dynamic structure is central to the observations. The authors report results superior to standard alternatives on those applications. Taken together, the theory and experiments support the proposed approach as a tool for nonlinear dynamics with extended temporal structure, with empirical improvements specifically established in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A new nonlinear-dynamics learning approach has a consistency result for long-range structure and outperforms standard alternatives on motion-capture and video applications.

title: Learning nonlinear dynamic models

abstract: We propose a new dimensionality reduction method, the elastic embedding (EE), that optimises an intuitive, nonlinear objective function of the low-dimensional coordinates of the data. The method reveals a fundamental relation betwen a spectral method, Laplacian eigenmaps, and a nonlinear method, stochastic neighbour embedding; and shows that EE can be seen as learning both the coordinates and the affinities between data points. We give a homotopy method to train EE, characterise the critical value of the homotopy parameter, and study the method's behaviour. For a fixed homotopy parameter, we give a globally convergent iterative algorithm that is very effective and requires no user parameters. Finally, we give an extension to out-of-sample points. In standard datasets, EE obtains results as good or better than those of SNE, but more efficiently and robustly.

The method reveals a fundamental relation betwen a spectral method, Laplacian eigenmaps, and a nonlinear method, stochastic neighbour embedding; and shows that EE can be seen as learning both the coordinates and the affinities between data points. We give a homotopy method to train EE, characterise the critical value of the homotopy parameter, and study the method's behaviour. For a fixed homotopy parameter, we give a globally convergent iterative algorithm that is very effective and requires no user parameters. Finally, we give an extension to out-of-sample points. paragraphs: Elastic embedding is a dimensionality reduction method that optimizes a nonlinear objective over low-dimensional coordinates. The paper connects this method to both Laplacian eigenmaps and stochastic neighbor embedding, bringing a spectral approach and a nonlinear approach into a shared analysis. It also interprets elastic embedding as learning both point coordinates and affinities between points.

The authors develop a homotopy training method, characterize a critical value of its parameter, and study the resulting behavior. For a fixed homotopy parameter, they provide a globally convergent iterative algorithm that requires no additional user parameters. The parameter-free statement applies to that fixed-parameter iterative procedure, while the homotopy method has its own parameter.

The paper also extends the method to points outside the original training sample. On standard datasets, elastic embedding produces results as good as or better than stochastic neighbor embedding, with greater efficiency and robustness. These findings support the method as a practical embedding approach, while its analysis clarifies relationships between existing families of dimensionality reduction techniques.
summary.tldr: Elastic embedding connects spectral and nonlinear dimensionality reduction and matches or improves on SNE results with greater efficiency and robustness.

title: The Elastic Embedding Algorithm for Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: Advances in sensing technologies and the growth of the internet have resulted in an explosion in the size of modern datasets, while storage and processing power continue to lag behind. This motivates the need for algorithms that are efficient, both in terms of the number of measurements needed and running time. To combat the challenges associated with large datasets, we propose a general framework for active hierarchical clustering that repeatedly runs an off-the-shelf clustering algorithm on small subsets of the data and comes with guarantees on performance, measurement complexity and runtime complexity. We instantiate this framework with a simple spectral clustering algorithm and provide concrete results on its performance, showing that, under some assumptions, this algorithm recovers all clusters of size Omega(log n) using O(n log^2 n) similarities and runs in O(n log^3 n) time for a dataset of n objects. Through extensive experimentation we also demonstrate that this framework is practically alluring.

We instantiate this framework with a simple spectral clustering algorithm and provide concrete results on its performance, showing that, under some assumptions, this algorithm recovers all clusters of size Omega(log n) using O(n log^2 n) similarities and runs in O(n log^3 n) time for a dataset of n objects. Through extensive experimentation we also demonstrate that this framework is practically alluring.

paragraphs: Large datasets make clustering expensive in two ways: acquiring similarity measurements can be costly, and processing those measurements takes time. The paper proposes an active hierarchical clustering framework that repeatedly applies an existing clustering algorithm to small subsets. This makes subset-level computation a building block for recovering a larger clustering hierarchy.

The framework comes with guarantees covering clustering performance, the number of measurements, and runtime. For a particular version using a simple spectral clustering algorithm, the authors show that, under their assumptions, it recovers every cluster whose size is at least on the order of log n. It uses O(n log^2 n) similarity measurements and O(n log^3 n) time for n objects.

These bounds connect the size of recoverable clusters to the resources needed for discovery. The recovery claim is conditional on the stated assumptions and cluster-size threshold. Extensive experiments also support the framework's practical appeal. Together, the theory and experiments suggest that running familiar clustering tools on carefully used small subsets can offer an efficient route to hierarchical clustering at larger scales.
summary.tldr: An active clustering framework uses small subsets to recover hierarchical clusters with conditional guarantees on accuracy, measurements, and runtime.

title: Efficient Active Algorithms for Hierarchical Clustering
